10121-the-literature-of-arabia-with-crit:
Epiphanius Wilson's 1900 volume on the literature of Arabia opens with the Romance of Antar. Its hero loves Ibla, fair as the full moon, and his early fortunes unfold among the Absians and Fazareans.

Arabian poetry and the Arabian Nights follow, with the seven voyages of Sindbad and Aladdin's wonderful lamp. Wilson's critical and biographical sketches set each work in its tradition. Readers get the great Arab story world in English: heroes, voyages, magic, and poetry, in one accessible volume. The volume belongs to the Oriental Literature series. The tales suit readers new to Arab letters.
10222-the-pilgrims-of-new-england-a-tale:
Mrs. J. B. Webb wrote this tale of the early American settlers, opening with the Mayflower off a stern New England coast in November 1620. The Pilgrims land on granite rock, face cold, and begin a hard new life in a wild land. Webb writes for young readers, with a moral and religious tone.

Storms, hunger, Native neighbors, and the building of homes and a church fill the story. Faith and endurance carry families through loss and fear. Readers get a Victorian-era retelling of the Pilgrim landing, earnest, simple, and full of period feeling about courage and God.
10478-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-02:
John Lord published this second volume of Beacon Lights of History, on Jewish heroes and prophets, treating faith through biography. Lord, author of The Old Roman World and Modern Europe, opens with Abraham as spiritual father of nations, in an age that had largely forgotten God. The tone is earnest, moral, and readable.

Abraham's call, migrations, stay in Egypt, parting from Lot, meeting with Melchizedek, covenant with God, and sacrifice of Isaac fill the opening lecture. Trials, obedience, and defects all shape his portrait. Readers get a classic, old-style history of Israel's heroes, through lives rather than dates alone.
10521-the-primadonna-a-sequel-to-fair-ma:
F. Marion Crawford published this sequel to Fair Margaret in 1908, following the singer Cordova. The book opens as Cordova sings the mad scene in Lucia for the last time that season, never better, in powder, chalked hands, and a lace nightdress like an expensive shroud. Crawford, author of Saracinesca, writes with operatic color.

The accident that follows will test Cordova's voice, pride, and love, as she moves through opera houses and society. Crawford treats the stage as a world of art, jealousy, and passion. Readers get a rich, romantic novel of a prima donna, full of music, drama, and period glamour.
10742-the-picture-alphabet:
The Picture Alphabet, printed by Oliver Spafford at Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1850, taught young children their letters with animal pictures. A stands for antelope, B for bull, C for cat, D for dog, and so on through hawk, ibex, kite, lynx, monkey, owl, and walrus. For X the book honestly notes that no English word begins with the letter.

Each letter pairs a capital, a small letter, and a picture, with numbers at the start. The book is simple, sturdy, and made for the nursery. Modern readers get a charming example of early American alphabet books, when learning to read began with beasts and birds.
10743-moonfleet:
J. Meade Falkner published Moonfleet in 1898, a tale of smugglers on the Dorset coast, dedicated to the Mohunes of Fleet and Moonfleet. The story opens in Moonfleet village, runs through floods, a discovery, a vault, a rescue, and an assault, and follows its boy hero toward a sea-cave, a well, and a jewel. Smugglers slipping the revenue men haunt its verses.

Falkner writes with a antiquarian's love of place and a storyteller's grip, blending adventure with local legend. The novel has become a classic of children's adventure, though adults enjoy it too. Readers get smuggling, treasure, and the Dorset shore, told in clear, atmospheric prose.
1122-hamlet:
Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, learns from his father's ghost that his uncle Claudius murdered the old king and married his mother. William Shakespeare's tragedy follows the prince as he feigns madness, stages a play to trap the king, and drifts toward a bloody end that kills nearly the whole court.

"To be, or not to be" crowns a play of delay, wit, and grief, where every act of revenge breeds a new wrong. Ophelia, Polonius, Laertes, and Gertrude all fall in the final duel. Hamlet stands as the most debated play in English, and its hero as the modern mind's first portrait.
11231-bartleby-the-scrivener-a-story-of-:
Herman Melville's short tale is narrated by a Wall Street lawyer who hires a pale copyist named Bartleby to work in his chambers. At first Bartleby copies steadily, but soon he answers every new request with a quiet refusal: he would prefer not to. The lawyer, a man who prides himself on an easy life, cannot fire him, reason with him, or understand him.

Bartleby's refusals spread from copying to errands to leaving the office at all, and the story ends in prison and death. Melville leaves the cause unexplained, apart from a rumor about a dead-letter office. The tale endures because its central puzzle stays open, inviting readers to weigh charity, duty, and the limits of kindness.
11280-maggie-miller-the-story-of-old-hag:
Mary J. Holmes's Maggie Miller, subtitled the Story of Old Hagar's Secret, opens at an old house by a mill among New England hills, where a brook once drove a creaking sawmill wheel. Hagar's secret, guarded through chapters on girlhood, trifles, junior and senior partners, society, and Madam Conway's disasters, is finally told in chapter nineteen, with results, sisters, mourning, Niagara, and home following. Arthur Carrollton and Maggie anchor the romance.

Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine, was among America's best-selling novelists, and Maggie Miller shows her domestic-sensation method: a hidden identity, virtuous heroines, and providential sorting. The novel's New England setting and mill imagery give its melodrama a local texture. It remains a representative bestseller of its era.
11957-the-wing-and-wing-or-le-feu-follet:
James Fenimore Cooper's The Wing-and-Wing, or Le Feu-Follet, opens on the Tyrrhenian Sea, whose charms, the narrator notes, have been sung since the days of Homer. The Mediterranean, bounded by Alps and Apennines, provides the setting for a tale of ships, coasts, and shifting loyalties.

Cooper's preface frames the story with a reflection on religion and revolution, contrasting blind belief in dogmas with presumptuous cavilling on revelation. Noting the impression that France exemplified the latter at the height of her great revolution. The novel that follows tests those ideas in action, aboard a vessel whose French name, will-o'-the-wisp, suits its elusive course.
12287-somerset:
G. W. Wade and J. H. Wade wrote this county guide to Somerset for Methuen, with thirty-two illustrations and two maps. The book opens with a map of Somerset railways and views of Cheddar pinnacles, and quotes Wordsworth on Quantock airy ridge.

Chapters cover situation and extent, climate, communications, physical features and geology, fauna and flora, history, and antiquities. A mid-book passage describes lake dwellings built on timber and brushwood over marsh, with clay floors and stone hearths. The guide mixes walking information with archaeology and natural history. It serves as a period portrait of an English county, written for travelers who wanted more than hotels and timetables.
12470-a-perilous-secret:
Charles Reade's 1884 novel, A Perilous Secret, builds its plot from two children, a poor man's child and a rich man's child, and two fathers. Chapters follow an old servant, Mary's peril, sharp practice, the course of true love, lovers parted, a Gordian knot cut and another tied, and a clandestine marriage.

Later chapters loose a serpent, put the secret in danger, explode a false accusation, let a woman outwit two men, and bury a man alive, twice over in chapter titles. Reade, author of Hard Cash and It Is Never Too Late to Mend, writes in a sensational, moral manner. The novel is Victorian melodrama at full pace, where a secret, once kept, threatens everyone who touches it.
12939-the-brighton-boys-with-the-submari:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll's Brighton Boys with the Submarine Fleet follows Jack Hammond and Ted from Brighton into Uncle Sam's undersea service in European waters. A newspaper call for young men to man submarines against Germany starts the adventure, leading to the North Sea, mine fields, U-boat captures, and Zeebrugge. Sealed orders and fog add mystery.

A sick-bay scene shows Jack winning praise for saving his commander, with talk of an American Croix de Guerre and a visit to the faint Lieutenant McClure. Driscoll, writing as a naval officer, gives the undersea war a boy's-eye view. The book is brisk wartime adventure of 1918 vintage.
13379-the-two-elsies-a-sequel-to-elsie-a:
Martha Finley's The Two Elsies, tenth in the long Elsie series, follows the Dinsmore and Raymond families through talk, travel, and moral counsel. Lulu, Evelyn, Rosie, Christine, and Alma discuss patience, work, and faith, with Viamede, Magnolia Hall, and family friends always near at hand.

A sterner passage warns young readers about Mormon missionaries, picturing dupes promised paradise who find the Bible set aside and Joseph Smith exalted. Edward insists that Mormon teaching leaves women no choice to remain single. Finley mixes family affection with firm Protestant teaching, as her heroines weigh duty, courtship, and the right use of patience in daily life.
13817-with-marlborough-to-malplaquet:
Herbert Strang and Richard Stead wrote this boys' adventure novel set in Queen Anne's reign. A young hero joins Marlborough's army and marches through the War of the Spanish Succession. Battles, sieges, and camp life fill the chapters, ending at Malplaquet in 1709. Four colour illustrations and a map support the text.

Strang keeps history close: uniforms, drill, and strategy appear in plain detail. The hero learns courage, loyalty, and discipline under fire. Scenes in Durham and on campaign contrast home and war. The book belongs to a series on great reigns, from Edward III onward. It offers young readers adventure with a solid historical frame.
13835-the-amulet:
Hendrik Conscience, the Flemish novelist, set The Amulet in sixteenth-century Antwerp. A dark and bloody deed, worked up from a real incident, brings swift and terrible retribution. The translator's preface stresses how the tale shows divine justice laughing at sinners' schemes. Conscience, author of The Lion of Flanders, wrote for a wide popular audience.

A rich girl appears with a chamois-skin purse clasped with precious stones, her father's arms on stained glass. Wealth, pride, and crime tangle through the plot. Conscience keeps the moral plain and the action brisk. The novel belongs to his series of Flemish historical tales. It offers romance, history, and a stern moral in one volume.
14034-king-alfred-s-viking-a-story-of-th:
Charles W. Whistler's historical novel follows King Alfred in his darkest years, hiding in the Somerset fens at Athelney while Danish armies hold the land. Drawn from Asser's life of the king and later chronicles, it gives Alfred a band of Norse seamen for his first fleet. Their chief goes unnamed in the records, so Whistler invents a Viking captain and his crew.

Sea raids, fen camps, and night attacks on Danish tents drive the action. A party of twenty-two men cuts tent lines in silence, then turns back with a war shout to spread panic. Thanes, herdsmen, and holy signs from Saint Cuthbert mix with shipcraft and swordplay. Young readers meet Alfred as a leader learning to fight at sea, and the novel keeps its history close while letting adventure carry the tale.
14118-legend-of-moulin-huet:
Lizzie A. Freeth published this Guernsey legend in 1872, dedicating it to the Conway boys of HMS Conway at Rockferry. Her brothers had trained aboard the ship under Rev. Henry O'Brien, and gratitude shapes the dedication. The tale itself belongs to Moulin Huet, a mill where old Pierre, his daughter Marguerite, Jacques, and Charlie cross purposes in love and revenge.

A black bargain drives the plot. Jacques promises Father Pierre to put an unwelcome man out of the way, with Marguerite as his reward whether she wills it or not. Alone, he clenches his fist and vows that Pierre shall do the deed himself, since he could not take Marguerite's hand after such foul work. Breakfast, departures, and a bright morning hide restless hearts, while Charlie waits happiest of all for a signal light. Local legend, romance, and village intrigue blend in a short, earnest tale.
14379-elsie-at-nantucket:
Martha Finley wrote this 1884 sequel to Elsie's New Relations, set on Nantucket Island. Finley spent six weeks on the island and used her notes, plus Northrup's 'Sconset Cottage Life, to paint summer life there. Elsie and her kin take rooms in the houses of 'Sconset for the heated term. The tale follows children, parents, and guests at beach and table. Finley writes for young readers who love family stories.

Lulu, a headstrong child, sulks by the beach when she thinks her father loves her less than his other children. She obeys in deed but not in spirit, avoiding her father and nursing unkind thoughts. Her father feels the sting and longs for her old loving ways. A second thread turns on old fears of Rome, as a child asks if persecutors will come to kill them. The book blends seaside fun with lessons on temper, trust, and faith.
14821-a-spray-of-kentucky-pine-placed-at:
George Douglass Sherley, the man from down on the farm, lays a spray of Kentucky pine at the feet of the dead poet James Whitcomb Riley. The small book was printed in Lexington in 1916. Its inscription is twofold, honouring Riley as an Indiana-born, world-wide poet.

A second inscription speaks to the living: Sherley's mother, on the banks of Wolf Run, on her eighty-fifth birthday in August 1916. A prelude explains his reading with Riley some years before. Short, personal and printed in old-style type, the booklet is a tribute from one Kentuckian to another, and a son's gift kept beside a poet's memory.
14843-the-manor-house-of-lacolle-a-descr:
W. D. Lighthall, president of the Antiquarian and Numismatic Society of Montreal, describes the manor house of the seigniory of de Beaujeu, or Lacolle. It stands in a retired place on the New York border, about four miles south-west of Lacolle village and a mile north of Champlain, New York, some forty miles from Montreal.

The highway from Lacolle to Champlain runs through the property, and a traveller from the north enters well-wooded lands before reaching heavy, low stone walls. Privately printed in Montreal, the sketch joins architecture, land and seigneurial history. It suits readers interested in Quebec's old manors, border country and the houses that once governed it.
14848-the-story-of-miss-moppet:
Beatrix Potter's 1906 picture story introduces Miss Moppet, a kitten who thinks she has heard a mouse. The mouse peeps out behind a cupboard, makes fun of her and shows no fear of a kitten at all.

Miss Moppet jumps just too late, misses the mouse and hits her own head on what she calls a very hard cupboard. She ties her head in a duster and sits before the fire, while the mouse watches from the top of the cupboard. Short captions and clear pictures carry the whole joke. It is a tiny tale of pride, a bump and a mouse who knows exactly how safe he is.
14852-the-younger-set:
Robert W. Chambers's novel of New York society follows a younger set through dreams, ashes and afterglow. Its hero begins among his own people, sees a dream end, and lives under the ashes before Mid-Lent brings a new turn.

The unexpected, errands and letters, Silverside, a novice and unwritten law follow, as characters choose their own way and her way in turn. Chambers writes fashionable life with ease: houses, clothes, talk and the quiet costs of keeping up. The book belongs to his society novels, less famous than The King in Yellow, but sharper on money, marriage and the price of belonging.
1513-romeo-and-juliet:
Shakespeare's tragedy of Verona opens with a street brawl between Montagues and Capulets, and a masked ball where Romeo meets Juliet. Their love grows in a garden, a friar marries them in secret, and a duel, a banishment, and a sleeping potion carry the young lovers toward a tomb where both die.

The prologue warns that only their deaths can end the feud, and the play fulfils its promise with lyric beauty and terrible speed. Romeo and Juliet remains the world's great love tragedy. Its poetry, from balcony to tomb, is among the most quoted in English.
15224-with-steyn-and-de-wet:
Philip Pienaar, of the Transvaal telegraph service, wrote this 1902 memoir of war with Presidents Steyn and De Wet. He opens in quiet Thomar, in a Portuguese convent, where faded paintings and falling waters make war seem like a dream. Chapters then return to Colenso, Spion Kop, Pieters' Heights, and Glencoe.

Pienaar taps wires, meets De Wet, slips through cordons, and joins skirmishes from Lindley to Potchefstroom. His account favors the Boer side and reads as a participant's tale. War readers will find it brisk, personal, and valuable for its view from inside the Boer command.
16081-the-anti-slavery-alphabet:
Printed in Philadelphia in 1847 for the Anti-Slavery Fair, this small anonymous book teaches the alphabet through the fight against slavery. Its opening address speaks straight to young readers, urging them to plead for enslaved people and to refuse goods made by slave labor. Each letter then gets a short verse, from A for an Abolitionist to F for the Fugitive who runs away by night.

The verses name plain facts a child could grasp. The cotton field, the driver with his whip, and the brother with darker skin all appear. So does the eagle, which cannot stand for freedom while people are chained. The book is both a primer and a protest, showing how abolitionists tried to win over the next generation one letter at a time.
16256-the-psychology-of-management-the-f:
L. M. Gilbreth's Psychology of Management, published by Macmillan in 1914 and reissued in 1921, applies psychology to scientific management. The opening chapter defines the subject, its importance, and its purpose, then sets out three types of management and a plan for psychological study. Later chapters take individuality in turn, asking how it fares under traditional management and under newer systems.

Gilbreth, a pioneer of motion study, argues that least waste comes not from driving workers harder but from fitting work to minds. Her book speaks to managers, engineers, and students of work. It remains a founding text of industrial psychology, earnest about both efficiency and human nature.
16733-montlivet:
Alice Prescott Smith wrote this 1907 historical romance of New France, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Armand de Montlivet walks the beach at Michillimackinac in May sun as the tale opens. Chapters follow a key, a captive, and the commandant's door. An Ottawa camp, a decision, and a westward trek follow. Mary Starling, compacts, storms, councils, and conquest fill the later pages.

Smith sets love and honor against French, English, and native claims in the Great Lakes country. Montlivet must choose between duty, love, and the price of sleep and conquest. Readers who like old historical romances will find a rich tale of the frontier, with a hero caught between worlds and a heroine who shapes his path.
1680-at-the-sign-of-the-cat-and-racket:
Balzac's tale, dedicated to Mademoiselle Marie de Montheau, opens halfway down the Rue Saint-Denis, near the Rue du Petit-Lion, where a delightful old house stands. At the sign of the cat and racket, a draper's shop, a young artist falls in love with the draper's daughter, and art meets commerce in a Paris of the past.

The house itself, which lets historians reconstruct old Paris by analogy, frames a romance of class, beauty, and ambition. Balzac writes with affection for vanished streets. The tale is a charming early Balzac work, and a love letter to old Paris and its shop signs.
16865-pinocchio-the-tale-of-a-puppet:
C. Collodi wrote this tale of a puppet, here in the Whitman Publishing edition from Racine, Wisconsin, copyright 1916, with pictures by Alice Carsey. Chapters run from a piece of wood that laughed and cried like a child into Master Cherry giving the wood away. Geppetto naming his puppet Pinocchio follows. A talking cricket scolding him, a flying egg, and feet burned to cinders appear. Geppetto giving his own breakfast to Pinocchio closes this part of the tale.

Collodi tells of a wooden boy whose lies, tricks, and good heart carry him through puppet shows, perils, and new feet. The tale mixes fun with moral lessons, in brisk, plain prose. Young readers get a classic story of a puppet who learns to be a real boy, in a lively American edition of a beloved Italian tale.
17275-navajo-silversmiths-second-annual-:
Washington Matthews, a US Army doctor, wrote this short Bureau of Ethnology paper on Navajo silversmiths, with plates of silver objects, a workshop, crucibles, and sandstone molds. Many Navajo smiths forged iron and brass, he notes, but worked chiefly in silver. Tools from American and Mexican traders shaped the craft, and fine files and emery paper lately improved the work.

Matthews traces the art's roots with care, noting Mexican metal skill at the Conquest and the skill of New Mexico tribes. His plates show ornaments worn with pride. The paper gives a clear, respectful early record of a craft that became a hallmark of Navajo art, and it suits readers of Native craft and Southwest history.
17279-the-mormon-prophet:
Lily Dougall's 1899 novel, published in Toronto, takes on the rise of Mormonism and the prophet at its head. Her preface corrects common errors: many readers tie the faith to polygamy alone, name Brigham Young as chief prophet, and see only oppressed women and tyranny. Dougall promises a simpler truth, as far as she can discern it, told in a spirit other than polemic.

The novel follows the prophet's life and the sect's growth with care for motives and belief, not just scandal. Its tone is earnest and fair for its day, though modern readers will judge its views with fresh eyes. Students of religious fiction will find a curious, ambitious attempt to treat a new faith as a human story.
17680-the-title-market:
Emily Post, author of The Flight of a Moth, wrote this novel, published in New York in September 1909 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with pictures by J. H. Gardner Soper. Chapters open with Prince Sansevero diminishing the fortunes of his house and the princess planning to receive an American heiress. Nina follows, then the Duke Scorpa making a deal.

Don Giovanni arrives, love and a garden follow, and Rome sets the scene for opening day at the title market. A door is opened that Giovanni prefers to keep closed. Readers get a society novel of titled Europeans and American money, in Post's polished style. The book suits readers of Edwardian society fiction.
17892-honey-sweet:
Edna Turpin's novel Honey-Sweet, printed by Macmillan with pictures by Alice Beard, opens on the deck of the steamship Caronia, about to sail. Anne, a young girl, stands with her uncle as they watch the dock, and the tale that follows tracks her growth from a shy child to a young woman.

Anne's path runs through homes, schools, and new friends, with kind adults, sharp trials, and the slow bloom of first love. Turpin writes for young readers in a warm, old-fashioned voice, full of home scenes and good manners. It is a sweet, gentle coming-of-age tale, the kind once given to girls as a model of pluck and grace.
18139-rip-foster-in-ride-the-gray-planet:
Blake Savage wrote this Golden Griffon space adventure, first copyrighted in 1952. Its hero is Rip Foster, a young space traveler, and its chapters read like a list of perils: Spacebound, Rake That Radiation, Capture and Drive, Find the Needle, and The Gray World. Later chapters add invaders, a creature called the Scorpion, and a Mercury transit.

The action moves from a rocket crew in space to a strange gray planet that Rip claims as his own. Danger comes from radiation, capture, and enemies who must be driven off. The book aims at young readers who want fast action, clear heroes, and a new world in every chapter, with little pause between escapes.
18280-enter-bridget:
Thomas Cobb, author of Phillida and The Choice of Theodora, wrote this novel, published in a second edition by Mills and Boon in London in 1912. Enter Bridget opens with a difference of opinion about Bridget herself. Mark Driver leans toward more than tolerance, Carrissima Faversham tries to hold the balance even, and her brother Lawrence calls Miss Rosser an adventuress.

Chapters follow late dinners, Mark's explanations, Bridget at Grandison Square, Colonel Faversham, birthdays, an excursion, a proposal, confidences, and Sybil. Later chapters bring the wooing, buying a carpet, hasty words, how it happened, and an appointment. Readers get an Edwardian society comedy of reputation: a new woman in a set household, judged, defended, and slowly understood.
1836-the-case-of-the-golden-bullet:
Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner's Joseph Muller case turns on a golden bullet, a strange object for a murder. The police commissioner is pleased by Muller's work and yet angered by his manner. That mix tells the reader how Muller operates: silent and steady on the calm face he shows his superiors, and unwilling to explain himself before the proof is ready.

The novel follows the bullet back to its owner and its motive, through Vienna society and police routine. It is detection of the patient kind. Its interest lies less in action than in the slow closing of a net around a man who thought a golden bullet would buy him silence.
18510-the-chequers-being-the-natural-his:
James Runciman edited this natural history of a public house, set forth in a loafer's diary, published in London by Ward and Downey. The Chequers is dedicated to Philip and John Wood of South Shields. The diarist says he owes them his gruesome experience and his professional success, with culture, generosity, and admirable relations with the police. The dedication calls the record one of ruined lives.

Contents give an introduction, the wanderer, the pink tom cat, and Teddy. They also give the wanderer again, a robbery, and entertainments. Merry Jerry and his friends, the gentleman, the doctor, and Dicky follow, with poachers, Jim Billings, and the parlour company. The introduction warns that good fellowship is not fostered in a public house, whatever cheerful writers claim. Readers get a dark, comic diary of drink: a pub, its company, and the sad work that goes on behind the jovial glass.
18726-poems-and-ballads-third-series-tak:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Poems and Ballads, Third Series, appears here from his collected poetical works, volume three, in the Heinemann edition of 1917. The series was first printed in 1904 and reprinted several times before this edition.

Its contents run from March: An Ode and The Armada to sea poems, garden pieces, and ballads like A Ballad of Bath and A Jacobite's Exile. Memorial verses honor Sir Henry Taylor and John William Inchbold, while Nell Gwyn and Caliban on Ariel show Swinburne turning old stage figures to new use. The volume gives readers the third series complete, with its odes, ballads, and memorial verses side by side.
18844-the-rebellion-of-margaret:
Geraldine Mockler, author of The Girls of St. Bede's, wrote this girls' story for Jarrold of London, with pictures by Arthur Twidle. It opens at Greystones on a sultry July afternoon, where Margaret Anstruther hides among the elm trees while a voice calls her to tennis.

Margaret dreams, overhears a conversation, and sets out on a journey that brings her together with Eleanor Carson. The two girls change names, meet the Danvers family, and face a detective turn by Hilary and an hour of reckoning when an old man denies that Eleanor is his granddaughter Margaret. The tale mixes schoolgirl fun with a swap of identities and the trouble it brews.
18846-voodoo-planet:
Andre Norton's science-fiction novel, published by Ace Books in 1959, follows Dane Thorson of the spaceship Solar Queen. Dane hopes for a short vacation on the planet Khatka, not the rest of his life, and finds himself matched against Lumbrilo, Khatka's mental wizard.

The book opens on the steamy, water-logged world of Xecho, where Dane, a cargo-master, studies a treacherous sea full of minute organisms hungry for Terran skin. On Khatka, a duel of minds pits his reason against hypnotic witchcraft, with Medic Tau, Chief Ranger Asaki, Captain Jellico, and pilot Nymani at his side. The novel asks whether science and nerve can stand against fear dressed as magic.
18882-the-isles-of-sunset:
Arthur Christopher Benson published this volume of verse in London in 1908, with Sir Isaac Pitman and Sons. Its opening poems speak of twilight gardens, secret wells, clear waters, and an elder pilgrim's tales, setting a mood of quiet reflection. The book's title points to western light over water, a golden stairway trembling on the tide.

Benson, known for essays and for The Hill of Trouble, writes here in a gentle, meditative voice, favoring gardens, evening hours, and thoughts of rest over tales of mighty deeds. Readers get late Victorian and Edwardian lyric poetry at its most contemplative, suitable for slow reading. The volume suits anyone who likes verse that calms rather than excites.
19016-dave-porter-at-star-ranch-or-the-c:
Edward Stratemeyer published this Dave Porter book in Boston in 1910, with Lothrop, Lee and Shepard, illustrated by Lyle T. Hammond. Dave Porter, hero of the Oak Hall series, travels to Star Ranch, where a cowboy's secret waits to be uncovered. An illustration shows Dave urging his horse Hero ahead on the trail.

The story mixes ranch life, riding, and mystery, as Dave and his friends test themselves against western work and a puzzle. Stratemeyer, founder of the famous boys' series factory, writes for young readers who liked school heroes in new settings. Readers get a cheerful ranch adventure, clean in tone and brisk in pace, typical of its popular series.
19224-the-alchemist-s-secret:
Isabel Cecilia Williams wrote this 1910 book of short stories, published in New York by P. J. Kenedy and Sons. The contents list a dozen tales, from The Passing of Tony and The Tramp to A Memorable Christmas Morning, Nancy's Tale, Patsy, and The Story of Julie Benoit. Faith, family, and charity run through the collection.

An old man walks home through cold wind after mail in the village, then braves a Christmas storm again to carry happiness to poor children in a hollow. He keeps first Mass and Communion each Christmas for his late wife Martha and their wandering daughter Sallie. Readers get warm, Catholic tales of duty, sacrifice, and kindness to neighbours in need.
19434-western-worthies-a-gallery-of-biog:
J. Stephen Jeans, editor of Glasgow's Evening Star, wrote this gallery of west of Scotland celebrities, published in Glasgow in the early eighteen seventies. Short lives and critical notes trace how public men rose from struggle to leadership, and what younger readers might learn from them.

One sketch honors an engineer who urged Glasgow to draw its water from Loch Katrine, a plan others later carried out. The book serves both as local pride and as a record of Victorian Scotland's makers, from engineers to men of letters. Other sketches cover shipowner George Burns, whose steamers linked Glasgow with Belfast and Liverpool.
19478-four-day-planet:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science fiction novel of a young reporter on a harsh colony world, published in the early nineteen sixties. The planet's short days, monster hunts, and ship arrivals frame a tale of news, guns, and survival, told in the first person.

A Mayday call opens one tense stretch: a craft lost, its crew curled in cramped quarters, praying or saving oxygen while static crackles on the radio. Piper mixes frontier adventure with press-room grit, and the result is a brisk colony tale for young readers.
19593-the-third-violet:
Stephen Crane wrote this novel of artists and society, issued in New York in the late eighteen hundreds. A train climbs a winding valley past grey crags, then releases its passengers into a summer world of painters, talk, and courtship, where Grace and her friends weigh love and pride.

Crane, famous for The Red Badge of Courage, here turns to lighter ground: studios, flirtation, and the comedy of clever people arguing in clouds of words. The novel shows a young master trying a new tone, with the same sharp eye for color and motive.
1987-the-outlet:
Andy Adams's Outlet follows a trail herd from Texas to the northern ranges, with cowboys, stampedes, and river crossings along the way. Adams, who had himself driven cattle up the trail, writes the work of droving with the care of a man who knew every job on the crew.

The novel's interest lies in its detail: how a herd is bedded down, how a stampede starts, and how men settle disputes on the trail. Adams writes without the romance of later westerns. The book remains a valuable record of the cattle trade in its last great years, told by one who lived it.
19980-a-joy-for-ever-and-its-price-in-th:
John Ruskin delivered A Joy For Ever at Manchester in 1857. Its full theme is the political economy of art. Ruskin finds one trait most notable in the age. We hold poverty in a just and wholesome contempt, he repeats. That contempt, he argues, shapes how art gets bought and valued. Two lectures, given July 10 and 13, make the book. Ruskin asks what beauty costs and who pays.

Ruskin was Victorian England's greatest art critic and a fierce social thinker. These lectures turn criticism toward wages, prices, and public taste. He insists art's value is moral before it is monetary. The talks scandalized Manchester's merchant audience pleasantly little at first. Later readers found them prophetic of arts funding debates. It is Ruskin the reformer in full voice.
20121-lone-star-planet:
Lone Star Planet is a science fiction tale set on a world run much like old Texas. It opens in the office of a Secretary of State on Earth. Ghopal Singh, dark-faced and grey-haired, meets a guest at his desk. Rudolf Klüng, of the Department of Aggression, stands by in black.

From Earth, the action moves to a planet that prizes guns and beef. Diplomats there must learn local ways fast or fail badly. The tale mixes satire, western codes, and space travel in one romp. Readers get a sharp, funny look at power, pride, and frontier law.
20147-rip-foster-rides-the-gray-planet:
Blake Savage wrote Rip Foster Rides the Gray Planet, a space tale for young readers. An officer of the Special Order Squadrons stands his men at ease. He warns that duty calls for a farewell speech from him. He means to make that speech if it kills them all, he jokes.

Rip Foster serves with a space force modeled on old army ways. Rockets, gray planets, and alien worlds fill his missions with risk. Books like this one fed the space dreams of postwar boys. Readers get brisk action, team spirit, and the thrill of early space fiction.
20212-police-your-planet:
Police Your Planet, from 1956, is a science fiction tale set on Mars. A man looks back at his rocket, still pointing skyward behind him. Ahead sprawls Marsport, a mess of slums beyond the air dome. The dome holds breathable air over the city's central part alone.

Law on such a frontier world is rough, bought, and badly bent. An honest man sent to police it faces graft at every turn. The tale mixes crime, politics, and space colony grit. Readers get a hard, fast dose of 1950s pulp science fiction.
20238-the-great-amulet:
Maud Diver wrote The Great Amulet, a novel set among the British in India. All the wedding preliminaries are over as one bright scene opens. A cheerful breakfast of cold chicken, iced cake, and champagne follows. It is served in Maurice's plain rooms over a pastry-cook's shop.

Diver wrote many novels of Anglo-Indian life, love, and duty. Her couples face heat, distance, caste, and the rules of two worlds. The great amulet of the title hints at charm, faith, and fate. Readers get romance rooted in the daily life of British India.
20400-on-the-heels-of-de-wet:
On the Heels of De Wet recounts the hunt for the Boer general Christiaan de Wet during the South African war. The writer, who calls himself the Intelligence Officer, served with the British forces chasing him. De Wet's raids and escapes made him the war's most elusive enemy.

The author admits that a few criticisms crept into his text. He asks readers to recall that regimental officers had suffered in silence for the sins of others. The book mixes campaign narrative with sharp views on how the war was run, from a man who rode in the pursuit.
20737-madge-morton-s-secret:
Amy D. V. Chalmers published Madge Morton's Secret in 1914, opening on a bright September morning. An old Virginia orchard smells of ripe apples, and a press still drips with cider. No one is in sight but one girl, alone among the trees.

That calm start soon gives way to the secret of the title. Madge must guard what she knows while life presses in around her. Chalmers writes for girls who liked feeling, loyalty, and a touch of mystery. The Virginia setting, with its orchards and old homes, gives the tale a warm, rooted feel throughout.
20739-rebels-of-the-red-planet:
Charles L. Fontenay spent his career in newspaper work, starting in 1936 with three papers and the Associated Press. He later worked as rewrite man for The Nashville Tennessean. That newsman's speed shows in Rebels of the Red Planet, his tale of Mars.

Fontenay sets revolt on a harsh red world ruled from Earth. Fast scenes, plain talk, and sudden turns keep the plot moving. The book came from the pulp age of science fiction, when Mars still felt close and strange. Readers get a brisk adventure with a reporter's eye for who holds power and who pays for it.
21270-five-hundred-dollars-or-jacob-marl:
Horatio Alger Jr. opens in the village of Lakeville, where an elderly traveller with bronzed features and a stout cane returns after twenty years away. He wonders aloud whether the two families near to him will welcome him. A polite boy of fifteen, in coarse clothes that show narrow means, stops to answer his questions.

The stranger is Jacob Marlowe, and his secret, tied to five hundred dollars, drives the tale. The boy's family, by contrast, is poor and honest, the usual Alger pattern. Alger wrote dozens of such stories of boys rising by pluck and honesty. A fine house down the street, with two horses and handsome carriages, marks what money looks like in Lakeville.
21556-travels-and-adventures-of-monsieur:
Monsieur Violet's father follows his exiled king to Edinburgh in Captain Marryat's tale of 1843. The boy, then nine, leaves France for good at his father's side. In time the road leads far from Scotland, into the wilds of North America.

Marryat drew much of the book from his own American visit, whose diary appeared in 1839. Trappers, Indigenous peoples, and frontier hunts crowd Violet's travels. The book was Marryat's twentieth, written with his usual speed and invention. Readers get a French hero's view of the prairies, forests, and rivers of the young continent.
22036-recollections-of-forty-years-in-th:
John Sherman spent forty years at the centre of American public life. He served in the House, the Senate, and the Cabinet, and his Recollections of that career appeared in 1895. The book opens with the Sherman family's Saxon roots along the Rhine. It then follows his own rise from Ohio lawyer to national figure.

Sherman helped finance the Union during the Civil War from the Senate. Later he ran the Treasury and gave his name to the Antitrust Act of 1890. His memoir argues his side of old fights over money and trusts. Historians still mine it for an insider's view of Reconstruction-era politics.
2261-romeo-and-juliet:
Two teenagers of warring Veronese houses fall in love at a masked ball and marry in secret within days. Romeo and Juliet races from balcony poetry to street brawls, a banishment, and a desperate plan involving a sleeping potion that goes fatally wrong. Shakespeare makes haste itself the villain, alongside the feud.

The lovers' language lifts the play above its source tale, and Mercutio's wit lights the early acts before darkness falls. Their deaths finally reconcile the Capulets and Montagues. Few stories in any language are so widely known or so often quoted.
2265-hamlet:
A prince of Denmark, urged by his father's ghost to avenge a murder, spends the play thinking instead of acting. Hamlet watches Claudius, who killed the old king and married Gertrude, while Ophelia drowns, Polonius dies behind a curtain, and a troupe of players stages the crime itself. The soliloquies turn revenge into a meditation on death, conscience, and delay.

By the final duel, nearly the whole court lies poisoned, and Fortinbras enters to claim a silent kingdom. The play's language has entered everyday speech more than any other work in English. It remains the central text of Shakespeare's art.
22674-boy-scouts-on-hudson-bay-or-the-di:
G. Harvey Ralphson wrote Boy Scouts on Hudson Bay, or The Disappearing Fleet, a 1914 volume in his Boy Scouts series. Ralphson turned out scout adventures at speed, sending his troop wherever the map looked wildest. Hudson Bay, with its ice, trading posts, and northern waters, gave him a stern setting for this outing.

The sample catches camp talk at rest: one scout admits he sometimes says things that do not come from the heart, and promises to sing a different tune once rested. Ask Ned, he says, whether surrender is his habit when trouble comes. Banter, loyalty, and a mystery of vanishing ships carry the plot. The book mixes northern geography with the era's creed of scout readiness.
2324-a-house-to-let:
Four Victorian masters join forces in A House to Let, a Christmas story built around a mysterious empty house in London. Charles Dickens, Wilkie Collins, Elizabeth Gaskell, and Adelaide Ann Procter each take a section, following an elderly woman's curiosity about the house across the way and the secrets of its former tenants. The tale mixes comedy, melodrama, and a touch of the gothic.

Each author's hand shows in turn, from Dickens's humor to Collins's plotting. The result is a collaborative curiosity that still reads smoothly. Fans of Victorian Christmas stories will enjoy this multi-author entertainment.
23474-the-bishop-s-secret:
Fergus Hume, famed for The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, wrote this nineteen hundred mystery of a bishop with a secret. The preface praises Hume's stirring, ingenious, misleading plots, worked out in vigorous English, and promises no falling off here, with a wider cast of typical men and women.

Rather than long portraits, Hume lets his people reveal themselves in action and speech, so the reader learns them as the plot learns them. A bishop, his household, and a town full of talkers, schemers, and saints drive the tale toward a surprising close. Mystery fans will enjoy the twists, the broad social canvas, and Hume's knack for keeping a secret hidden until the last good moment.
23619-the-royal-picture-alphabet:
Ward and Lock of London printed this royal picture alphabet of humour and droll moral tales, or words and their meanings, with pictures. A poetical preface to preceptors promises learning with laughter, merry and wise, rising higher as subjects turn to matters not thought of before.

Descriptions and pictures combine, so children find truth from error in clear, attractive form. Ablution, the act of cleansing, shows a little sweep who washed his face, but not as advised, for black as soot he stays. Each letter brings a word, a picture, and a droll moral tale. Small readers will learn letters while laughing, and grown readers will enjoy the Victorian blend of instruction, humour, and quaint moralising.
23651-test-rocket:
Jack Douglas published this short science fiction story in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in April 1959. At a rocket testing station, Captain Baird and the aging Doctor Johannsen face a puzzle. The parts of a giant test rocket, dismantled and laid out in careful order, carry their own markings — yet the paint is not their paint.

Six months earlier the rocket had vanished from the observation screen ten minutes after launch, and Baird had cursed the failure. Now something has come back, changed in ways no one can explain, and the two men must work out what happened to it. The story turns on a single eerie idea, told with the clipped dialogue of a military laboratory.
23799-cry-from-a-far-planet:
Tom Godwin's Cry from a Far Planet opens in the control room of an exploration ship, where a man listens to an ominous quiet. No sounds come from the nearby village, though the viewscreen's audio pickups should carry a multitude. Six hours have passed since the native Throon should have come to sit with him and resume their slow attempt to learn each other's language.

Outside, under a dull red sun hidden by thick atmosphere, full day is no more than red-tinged darkness. The ship's handbook warns that a smile of friendship and a snarl of menace both bare the teeth, and that no alien being is ever to be trusted. Godwin builds his tension from that rule, and from a village gone suddenly silent.
24012-the-peter-pan-alphabet:
Oliver Herford published The Peter Pan Alphabet with Charles Scribner's Sons in January 1907, with pictures by the author and a round robin addressed to J. M. Barrie, from his humble and devoted servants, the letters themselves.

The alphabet apologizes for familiarly addressing one of its betters, then recalls the slate where Jamie learned to scrawl his humble letters. Well the letters remember how he drew their shapely features all askew: A lame, B too fat, and C too curly. They loved him dearly all the same, and served him blindly, even through a fearsome Scottish reel. Grand tales, they hint, may still be biding in the ABC, if Jamie will cast his golden net.
24242-broken-bread-from-an-evangelist-s-:
Thomas Champness wrote this book of short devotional pieces, published by the Joyful News Book Depot at Rochdale in 1888. It is dedicated to his wife Eliza M. Champness, his wife and truest friend and his yoke-fellow in the gospel. Champness calls the book a collection of fragments, gathered so that nothing is lost, many of them already printed in Joyful News.

The first piece, Spiritual Farming, takes drainage as its image. Old English moor and fen became good crop land once drained. So, he argues, must the Lord's fields be drained before preaching can bear fruit. Readers get brief, plain gospel talks, crust and crumb alike, meant to feed those who cannot sit to a full meal.
24278-the-green-beret:
Tom Purdom wrote this science fiction story for Analog in January 1961, with pictures by Schoenherr. Corporal Read locks the door and draws his pistol while Sergeant Rashid hands Premier Umluana of Belderkan a warrant from the UN Inspector Corps. The premier must be arrested and brought for trial by the World Court, though he protests that no inspector may arrest a head of state.

In the next room, party guests laugh and glasses clink, while two armed men wait outside the door. Rashid, calling Read a crack shot who likes to shoot, judo chops the premier and swings the inert body over his shoulders. Purdom's theme is the decision a man refrains from making. Readers get a tense tale of arrest, law, and restraint.
244-a-study-in-scarlet:
Dr. Watson, newly returned from Afghanistan, meets a strange young man at St. Bartholomew's Hospital. Arthur Conan Doyle's Study in Scarlet introduces Sherlock Holmes through Watson's eyes, with deduction, chemistry, and a Lauriston Gardens murder. Gregson and Lestrade chase false leads.

Part two shifts to Utah, where John Ferrier and Lucy flee a Mormon prophet's Avenging Angels. The two halves join when the killer's motive surfaces in London. Doyle's first Holmes novel already shows the method and the friendship. It launched the most famous partnership in fiction. Holmes and Watson's first case set a template copied for over a century.
24492-critical-miscellanies-vol-2-of-3-e:
John Morley included this long essay on Condorcet in the second volume of his Critical Miscellanies, published in London in 1905. Condorcet was a French philosopher and mathematician of the Enlightenment, a friend of Voltaire and Turgot, who lived through the French Revolution.

Morley traces Condorcet's birth and education, his principles, and his view of the English revolutions. He follows his political activity to the end of 1792, his election work, and his lack of foresight about the Terror. The essay gives a clear, humane portrait of a thinker who believed reason could improve the world, and who died for that belief.
2451-caught-in-the-net:
Emile Gaboriau, the father of the French detective novel, weaves Caught in the Net around a murder, a blackmail plot, and the patient work of his detective Lecoq's world. The novel follows a young man drawn into a web of crime through love and debt, with Gaboriau's careful plotting and Parisian detail driving the mystery. The net tightens chapter by chapter.

Gaboriau's influence on Conan Doyle and the whole detective genre is clear here. The book's length allows a rich cast and a complex scheme. Mystery fans will find a foundational French classic.
2454-the-silent-bullet:
Arthur B. Reeve's Silent Bullet introduces Craig Kennedy, the scientific detective, in cases solved by chemistry, ballistics, and new inventions. The stories pit Kennedy and his journalist friend against murderers who use science as a weapon, with Reeve explaining the forensic tricks as the plot unfolds. The bullet of the title kills without a sound, and only science can trace it.

Reeve's tales were hugely popular, making Kennedy a rival to Holmes in American fiction. The science, dated now, charms as period ingenuity. Mystery fans will enjoy a founding work of the scientific detective story.
24868-the-cost-of-living-among-wage-earn:
The National Industrial Conference Board published this study in 1919 on the cost of living among wage earners in Fall River, Massachusetts. The Board, a joint body of industrial associations, gathered budgets from mill hands to set fair wages after the war. Its tables break down food, rent, fuel, and sundries for working families.

Details make the figures live. Fuel, heat, and light run to eighty-four dollars and twenty-five cents a year in the more liberal budget. Streetcar fares of ten cents a ride strain poor workers, since few can spare three dollars at once for fifty rides. The report remains a solid source for how mill families lived and spent in 1919.
24909-the-golden-magnet:
George Manville Fenn wrote The Golden Magnet, a boys' adventure that opens at daybreak in the Incas' realm in 1533. Harry, a young Englishman, goes seeking gold in the Golden Americas with Tom, a worker from his father's soap-boiling factory. Tom, down-to-earth and full of commonsense, gets Harry out of scrape after scrape.

Their quest leads through Andean ravines, stone platforms, and dense growth hiding old masonry, toward the gold of El Dorado. Despite foes and hardships, they win the gold, set affairs right, and Harry marries the heroine. Fenn tells a cracking good yarn of the kind late Victorian boys loved, full of dreadful straits and narrow escapes.
25081-the-cricket:
Marjorie Benton Cooke's Cricket, published by Doubleday, Page in 1919, is a novel about a headstrong girl nicknamed for her cheerful, chirping spirit. The story opens with a birthday party the child refuses to attend, hiding rather than face the other children of the colony.

As the summer unfolds, the girl, Isabelle, clashes with her neglectful parents, who let her call them by their first names, and finds steadier guidance from a Quaker household. Cooke mixes humor and sentiment, following a lonely child toward manners, friendship, and a sense of belonging in a world of summer houses and seaside play.
25354-assimilative-memory-or-how-to-atte:
Professor A. Loisette's Assimilative Memory teaches a system for attending and never forgetting, by analytic substitution. Letters hidden in words stand for figures, so a date becomes a phrase the memory can hold.

Harvard's founding in 1636 yields phrases such as Dash a midge and The chum age, while Yale in 1701 gives Took a seat and The quest. Comenius, born in 1592 and dead in 1671, is encoded the same way. Loisette also treats synthetic translation, where the phrase bears no relation to the event itself. Loisette's system promises that attention, rightly trained, need never lose a fact.
25653-conflict-of-northern-and-southern-:
Henry Ward Beecher delivers this great speech in New York City on 14 January 1855, as the eighth lecture of a course before the Anti-Slavery Society at the Tabernacle. Rochester printers Strong and Company issued it the same year.

Beecher sets northern and southern theories of man and society against each other, arguing that slavery degrades both master and slave while free labour honours human worth. The speech belongs to the fierce debate over slavery in the 1850s, and Beecher's pulpit eloquence aims to move listeners from argument to moral action.
25770-the-dragon-s-secret:
Augusta Huiell Seaman, author of The Slipper Point Mystery and The Sapphire Signet, writes The Dragon's Secret, published by the Century Company in 1920 with pictures by C. M. Relyea. Leslie hurrying Phyllis out with seeming haste fronts the book.

Chapters open with the night of a storm, found on the beach, and a mysterious casket. In the sand, an exploring party, and Leslie's next moves follow, as two girls chase a dragon secret through seaside clues, hidden objects, and danger. Seaman writes a girls' mystery of pluck, friendship, and careful detection.
25943-the-tale-of-chirpy-cricket:
A Sleepy Time Tale from Grosset and Dunlap, printed in 1920, follows Chirpy Cricket the fiddler through a summer of music and mishaps. Chapters run from quick and easy tunes and the bumblebee family to too much music, a light in the dark, a plan gone wrong, and Johnnie Green's guest. An interrupted nap, a capture, a queer new cousin, and an underground chat keep the small hero busy.

Chirpy meets a mole cricket whose great forefeet puzzle him, since his own kin have small feet. The mole cricket laughs and explains that big feet dig burrows, and without them he could never tunnel a garden. Later chapters bring Tommy Tree Cricket, a lily pad sit, Mr. Cricket Frog's trick, and a nighthawk's counsel. The tale is short, kind, and full of insect folk.
26113-handbook-of-wool-knitting-and-croc:
Emma Chalmers Monroe's handbook gathers wool knitting and crochet patterns for beginners and experts alike. Step-by-step directions cover edgings, borders, scarf-ends, insertions, yokes, lunch sets, and doilies, with each stage explained and pictured so that plain results follow.

Examples include a helmet, knit front and back with a face opening and joined seams, and a thumbless mitt or wristlet. Rows are given stitch by stitch, with narrowings counted down to a set number of stitches left. Published by Needlecraft in Augusta, Maine, in 1918, the book serves as a working manual rather than a picture book.
26233-the-indifference-of-juliet:
Grace S. Richmond's novel, published in 1905 from serial copyrights of 1902 to 1904, follows Juliet, a young woman famous for indifference to suitors. Its cast lists Horatio Marcy, an elderly New Englander of wealth, Anthony Robeson, a young Kentuckian making his way in Massachusetts, and Wayne Carey, Robeson's former college friend. Chapters promise an audacious proposition, shopping with a chaperon, and the cost of frocks.

Later scenes bring a bishop and a hay-wagon, strawberries, a house party outdoors, and the Robeson will. Anthony plays maid, Roger Barnes proves invaluable, and Juliet proves herself still indifferent, chapter after chapter. The story moves toward a wedding where Anthony, in white clothes, faces the bishop beside Juliet in a simple white gown.
26259-her-mother-s-secret:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth's novel, copyrighted in 1882, opens at Mondreer, where Odalite weeps at her mother's feet. The mother answers that honour must be saved, though hearts be sacrificed, and she presses a match with Colonel Anglesea, a gentleman of the highest social place. Odalite has already declined him, and she protests that she stands on the eve of marriage with the man she loves.

The mother calls her hasty and insists she will think better of it and accept. The clash sets the novel's engine: a daughter's pledged love against a mother's secret and her plan for a grand marriage. Southworth builds the tale from tears, pride, and duty, in the full melodramatic manner her readers loved.
26890-the-rat-racket:
David H. Keller wrote this tale of racketeering with a new weapon: rats. Richard Moyer, senior partner of Moyer and Perkins, importers of high-grade English groceries for over twenty years, reads a letter twice, then hands it silently to Paul Perkins. The firm already pays for protection. Threats hit its trucks, its new building, and its best customers, then a bombing campaign, then the kidnapping of Moyer's son. The police advise them to keep paying.

The new letter looks innocent: the rat menace is growing, rodents have damaged several business houses, and warehouse protection costs five thousand a week. Perkins is not laughing, because the letter was typed on the same damaged typewriter as the gang's earlier threats, all made good. A dozen wealthy men meet at the Manufacturers' Club to weigh a hundred forms of racketeering, and the tale promises that this racket has a flaw.
2691-nan-sherwood-at-pine-camp-or-the-ol:
Annie Roe Carr opens this girls' adventure with a yellow poster spotted on High Street, as Nan Sherwood and Bess Harley leave Tillbury High School. Nan spins about on one foot, full of questions, and the poster points toward Pine Camp and an old lumberman's secret.

Nan's pluck, her friends, and a mystery in the pine woods drive a wholesome tale of camp life, loyalty, and courage. Carr writes in the brisk style of the girls' series books, with cliffhangers and kind hearts. The book delights young readers who like heroines who act first and ask later.
27021-an-explorer-s-adventures-in-tibet:
A. Henry Savage Landor's An Explorer's Adventures in Tibet, published by Harper in 1910 with illustrations by the author, tells of a forbidden country entered at risk. Landor, already known for In the Forbidden Land, traveled roads where brigands drove thousands of sheep and yaks before them.

Later chapters bring disaster at the river, capture, threats of death, a terrible ride, and the executioner, before a charmed life leads him to the frontier and friends at last. The book mixes travel, danger, and firsthand report from a Tibet closed to outsiders.
27116-when-winter-comes-to-main-street:
Grant Overton's When Winter Comes to Main Street, published by Doran in 1922, collects literary essays on the novelists Americans were reading. Chapters take up the courage of Hugh Walpole, Stewart Edward White and adventure, Rebecca West as artist, and the vitality of Mary Roberts Rinehart.

Other chapters cover audacious Mr. Bennett, Cobb's fourth dimension, Frank Swinnerton as analyst of lovers, and the heterogeneous magic of Maugham. Overton writes for the general reader, with an armful of novels and notes on the novelists, closing on books we live by. Overton dedicated the book to George H. Doran, who had the idea. A chapter for children and one on places to go break up the literary essays.
27674-the-boy-volunteers-with-the-submar:
Kenneth Ward's 1917 boys' adventure sends two young Americans under the sea with the submarine fleet during the First World War. It was one volume of his Boy Volunteers series, which followed the same heroes through the Belgian front, French air service, and British artillery.

The book explains submarine machinery and action through clear line drawings, while its heroes face danger, duty, and comradeship aboard. For young readers of the war years, it mixed thrills with a working picture of a new and feared weapon. The publisher advertised the series as the newest boys' books on the European war.
27761-hamlet:
Charles Kean arranged Shakespeare's Hamlet for representation at the Royal Princess's Theatre, as performed on Monday, January 10, 1859, with explanatory notes. Published in London by Bradbury and Evans, the edition lists Kean himself as Hamlet and his wife as Gertrude.

Stage directions explain entrances and the relative positions of performers, and footnotes, originally at the foot of each page, gather at the close of each act. The book is a record of Victorian stage Shakespeare: a heavily edited acting text shaped for a star actor's production. The cast lists Ryder as Claudius, Meadows as Polonius, Graham as Horatio, and Miss Heath as Ophelia.
28189-my-friends-the-savages-notes-and-o:
Captain G. B. Cerruti wrote My Friends the Savages in 1908 from notes kept as a settler in Perak, on the Malay Peninsula. Translated from Italian by I. Stone Sanpietro, the book follows Cerruti from Malacca into the forest, where he meets the Orang Asli peoples, travels by steamer, and learns their ways. His own photographs fill the volume.

Chapters report forest camps, gold, hunting, and village life, with frank notes on Malay settlers and colonial trade. Cerruti writes as a friend, not as a cold observer, and dedicates the book to parents and a sister he never saw again. The text gives a rare, first-hand view of Perak before modern roads.
28457-golden-stars-in-tatting-and-croche:
Mlle. Riego de la Branchardiere's Golden Stars in Tatting and Crochet, published in London in 1861 for one shilling, teaches a simple combination of tatting and crochet. The designs avoid the more elaborate styles of both arts, so any lady with the first rules of each can work the patterns without difficulty.

Stars worked in gold, silk, wool, or cotton trim dresses, cloaks, bonnets, antimacassars, and doyleys, and many designs suit church needlework. The book explains pearl loops, double stitches, and how to commence and join in crochet, then gives patterns such as the octagon star. It is a practical Victorian needlework manual, registered against copying for sale.
28628-devil-crystals-of-arret:
Hal K. Wells's Devil Crystals of Arret, from Astounding Stories of September 1931, gives young Larry a six-hour deadline of death. Benjamin Marlowe and his assistant Larry Powell enter the laboratory to find Joan Marlowe, Benjamin's niece and Larry's fiancée, already belted for travel. A cord joins her wrist to the atomic projector's main switch, and she warns them not to stop her.

Animals sent across the barrier always returned alive within the twelve-hour limit, Joan argues, and Silver Belts already brought back plant and mineral fragments proving Arret exists. She jerks the switch and vanishes in roseate flame before Larry reaches the recall control. Readers get a pulp race against time, among rat-men and tinkling crystals.
28723-susan-and-edward-or-a-visit-to-ful:
Susan and Edward, or A Visit to Fulton Market, published by S. M. Crane of New York in 1847, takes two children marketing. Susan, the elder, is modest, fond of play, sometimes idle, but obedient to her parents. Edward, younger and five years old, is pert, active, lively, observing, and full of sensible questions. Their parents live in Pearl Street, where houses stand close like rows of young peach or apple trees.

One pleasant autumn morning the children, baskets in hand, walk with their mother through Franklin Square, down Pearl Street to Peck-slip, and into Water Street. Fulton Market fills a whole square near the East River, opposite Brooklyn and its ferry. A preface maps New York's markets, from Fulton and Washington to Catherine, Franklin, Centre, Clinton, and Essex.
28848-the-river-prophet:
Raymond S. Spears wrote this 1920 novel about Elijah Rasba, a young mountain preacher who lives by himself in a log cabin on Temple Run. Elijah is the grandson of Old Abe Rasba, who built a stone church called the Temple on a Jackson River tributary and preached the Bible from memory. The old glory has left the ruined church, landslips have wrecked hillside farms, and lightning has destroyed the grist mill, leaving Elijah the last of the congregation.

The story follows Elijah's stern faith as it meets the world beyond the mountains, with a frontispiece showing a woman firing an automatic pistol. Spears writes in the local-color style of his day, mixing religion, romance, and mountain life. Readers get a period novel of Appalachian faith and solitude, centered on a prophet who holds to his grandfather's law while everything around him changes.
28887-the-boy-broker-or-among-the-kings-:
Frank A. Munsey wrote this 1888 boys' novel about Herbert Randolph, a boy broker among the kings of Wall Street. Munsey dedicates it to his father, whose rigid New England discipline once seemed severe and needless, and whose rightness the author now owns with thanks. His preface argues that the best boys' story makes its reader more manly, self-reliant, generous, and noble.

The plot, shown in a frontispiece of Herbert emerging from a cellar prison, mixes finance with adventure and moral trial. Munsey believed boys learn by imitation, not by lectures, and he built his lesson into action. Readers get a lively period tale of youth, money, and character in Gilded Age New York, written by a publisher who knew boys' reading well.
29027-spawn-of-the-comet:
H. Thompson Rich wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Astounding Stories in November 1931. A swarm of huge, fiery ants, spawned by a mystery comet, bursts from shells to threaten the world. The tale opens with a Tokyo dispatch: meteors that pelted Japan as earth passed through the comet's tail are orange, baseball-sized, and too hard to analyze.

Jim Carter, a reporter for the New York Press, reads the news while his city editor Miles Overton grumbles that the things are turning up in New York, Chicago, London, and Rio. The uniformity of size and marking feeds a popular belief that they are seeds. Readers get a brisk pulp tale of alien invasion by insects, with a professor's cannon ray promised against the advancing horde.
29163-the-aural-system-being-the-most-di:
A linguist with nearly forty years of practice, and nearly twenty years living abroad, wrote this 1895 pamphlet from Bradford. His aural system claims to be the most direct, straight-line method for mastering a foreign language. It teaches a student to speak, understand, read, and write at the same time, rather than one skill after another.

The writer urges learners to pick a good grammar, date every lesson in advance, and keep to the plan with steady effort, cutting pleasures if needed until the task is done. He also surveys how modern languages were taught in Belgium. Readers get a Victorian language-learning manual, practical in advice and confident that ear-first study beats slow book study.
29177-the-pygmy-planet:
Jack Williamson wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Stories in February 1932. Larry Manahan, a bored advertising man earning fifty dollars a week, grumbles that nothing ever happens to him. All the adventure he knows comes from movies and magazines, and he longs for a slice of real life.

Larry gets his wish when he journeys down into the infinitely small, to a pygmy planet of tiny beings. Williamson plays the change of scale for wonder and danger alike, as a full-sized man becomes a giant among miniature people. Readers get a brisk early tale of shrinking, exploration, and a desk-bound dreamer finally finding adventure.
29401-the-solar-magnet:
Capt. S. P. Meek's tale, printed in Astounding Stories in October 1931, brings back Dr. Bird in his long scientific duel with Saranoff, his country's arch-enemy. A crowd before the Capitol falls quiet as the President steps to a microphone and tells the nation that Congress has met in extraordinary session to face a grave crisis. The greatest scientists of the country, he says, have gathered in conference, and no step of value will be neglected.

Meek builds his plot on a solar magnet, a device whose pull threatens order itself, and on Bird's race to meet it. The tale mixes Washington ceremony with pulp science and brisk action. Fans of early science fiction will enjoy a period piece where a lone scientist stands between the nation and a strange new force.
29448-pariah-planet:
Murray Leinster's book-length novel, first printed in Amazing Stories in July 1961, opens with a small Med Ship dropping out of overdrive near a strange star. Its hero Calhoun serves a medical service that spans the stars. When the blue plague appears on the planet Dara, fear strikes nearby worlds, and fear hardens into a hate that threatens millions and the peace of the galaxy.

Calhoun must trace the plague, calm the panic, and face a world cut off as a pariah. Small companion beasts called Tormals, charmed when spoken to, add warmth to the tale. Readers get a humane space novel about disease, prejudice, and the hard work of trust across worlds.
29685-submarine-warfare-of-to-day-how-th:
Charles W. Domville-Fife, a lieutenant in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, published this account in London in 1920, with 53 pictures. He tells how the Allied navies met the German submarine threat in the Great War. The tale runs from the first task of guarding sea lanes to the full system that at last held the menace in check. The book covers the training of a vast new force and the building of fleets for a new kind of war.

Hydrophones, depth charges, nets, fast boats, mystery ships, aircraft, and the convoy system each get a chapter, with sea tales to show them in use. Domville-Fife writes from staff work at the naval school of submarine mining, and his tone is plain and sure. The book is both a war record and a guide to the tools that changed sea war.
30015-stopover-planet:
Robert E. Gilbert wrote Stopover Planet, a tale whose headnote reverses a bakery round: early morning deliveries were part of the Honeychile Bakery Service, but on this particular morning the service was reversed. At 2:34 in the morning, Patrolman Louis Whedbee leaves the Zip Cab station, arch supports squeaking and night stick swinging, and walks east to the call box at Sullivan and Cherokee.

Whedbee reaches for the box, then swears softly and steps off the curb, excusing himself. He holds that a policeman must stay courteous always, even arresting a school-zone speeder. This is not a speedster. A huge man stands on top of a truck cutting down the stop light, in what looks like long underwear sewn from unlikely black fur dotted with tiny red spots.
30337-fifty-per-cent-prophet:
Darrel T. Langart tells Fifty Per Cent Prophet in Analog, September 1961, with pictures by Schoenherr. That he was a phony Swami was beyond doubt, the tagline says. That he was a genuine prophet seemed less certain, but then, what is the difference between a dictator and a true prophet? Dr. Joachim sits in a room behind his reception hall, fingers poised above the keys of a creaky electrotyper on his desk.

His long, slender, pale hands hover like two gulls frozen mid-swoop above a tidbit on the sea below. They wait to drop the moment time starts again. All of Dr. Joachim's body seems held in the same stasis, only his lips moving as he frames the next sentence in his mind. A big man, broad-shouldered, he hides beneath a monkish robe, with only his shortness of stature noticeable.
30428-elam-storm-the-wolfer-or-the-lost-:
Harry Castlemon writes Elam Storm, the Wolfer, subtitled The Lost Nugget, copyrighted in 1895 and published in Philadelphia. Contents open with something about the nugget, Tom Mason again, Tom beginning his wanderings, the wrong boat, and Tom's luck.

Tom admires cowboys, hears a temperance lecture, finds a home ranch, and gets lost in the mountains. He reaches the camp of Elam the wolfer, meets unwelcome visitors, and finds something that changes the hunt. Later scenes add Elam under fire, a new expedition, and the nugget found. Castlemon pairs frontier adventure with a boy hero's steady courage.
3045-the-last-chronicle-of-barset:
Anthony Trollope published The Last Chronicle of Barset in monthly installments from December 1866 to July 1867, closing his Barsetshire series. The contents ask how Mr. Crawley got a cheque, follow the archdeacon's threat, Grace Crawley, Miss Prettyman's private room, and Crawley's journey to Silverbridge, then dinner at Framley Court, the bishop's inhibition, and Major Grantly's courtship. The frontispiece shows Crawley before the magistrates.

Grace's family pride runs through the novel, as she insists her father was born and bred a gentleman even when poor, and now disgraced. A suitor argues he is better than the proud people who scorn him. The novel balances the Crawley scandal with the wider Barset world, and it remains Trollope's most moving parish story.
30773-dead-man-s-planet:
William Morrison wrote this science fiction tale about Sam Wilson, a hard, driven father, and his young son Mark, on a ship bound for a cemetery world. Sam snaps at the boy over lessons, then wonders at his own harsh tone, and he thinks of Rhoda, Mark's mother, who was sweet and gentle where he is tough. The tagline frames the planet as both journey's end and the start of a new one.

On the world below, father and son must face grief, duty, and what a fresh start can mean after loss. Morrison keeps the focus on the two of them, not on machines or battles, and the strange planet works as a mirror for Sam's own state. Readers get a quiet, sad story about a father learning, late, how to speak kindly to his son.
31207-where-the-world-is-quiet:
C. H. Liddell's story, printed in Fantastic Universe in May 1954, follows an anthropologist named White on a lone Peruvian odyssey. In a hut below Huascan, the legless priest Fra Rafael tells White of strange, impossible things. After an earthquake, a native girl vanished on the mountain pass toward Huascan, and searchers found the fog grow so thick they were blinded and fled.

A week later another girl vanished the same way, and by the time of the telling seven girls have gone, one after another, all by the same canyon. With the Cordilleras looming through fog along Peru's eastern border, the tale turns field anthropology into quiet horror, where science meets powers not of this earth.
31648-my-fair-planet:
Evelyn E. Smith's My Fair Planet, illustrated by Dillon, appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction for March 1958. Its sidenote says the world is a stage with room even for a bad actor, only this one meant to direct. Paul Lambrequin, climbing the stairs of his rooming house, meets a man whose face is all wrong. The man stops him in a toneless voice with an accent outside the standard repertoire.

Paul says he is a bit near-sighted, which is why he did not shudder at the sight. The stranger demands what is incorrect about him, since he has two eyes, one nose, and one mouth like other people. Paul studies him and answers that somehow they seem put together all wrong. Smith's comedy turns a wrong face into a directing ambition.
3173-essays-on-paul-bourget:
Mark Twain answers the French critic Paul Bourget in these essays. Bourget reports the American joke correctly, Twain allows: Boston asks how much a man knows, New York asks how much he is worth, and Philadelphia asks who his parents were. When an alien observer turns his telescope on America, Twain wants to know the diameter of the reflector first.

The essays then test Bourget's judgments one by one, with wit as the main weapon. A little note to Bourget himself sharpens the reply. Twain defends American manners without denying American faults, and the book remains a model of how to answer a foreign critic: laugh, quote him fairly, and hit back harder.
31792-an-old-chester-secret:
Margaret Deland's 1920 novel returns to Old Chester, the small town of her earlier tales, and centers on Miss Lydia Sampson, a woman less tainted by secretiveness than anyone in town. Lydia has no reticence about her own affairs because they are inherently public: she had broken her engagement to Mr. William Rives a fortnight before the wedding, and everybody knew it.

Years later her renewed engagement ends when Rives flees some ten minutes before the marriage ceremony, again before invited guests. Readers get a novel of small-town manners, poverty, hospitality, and pride, told with Deland's close attention to what a whole town knows and says.
32257-malplaquet:
Hilaire Belloc's Malplaquet, published in London by Stephen Swift and Company in 1911, is a short battle history with sketch maps. Its five chapters run from The Political Meaning of Malplaquet and The Siege of Tournai through The Manoeuvring for Position and The Preliminaries of the Battle to The Action. A frontispiece shows Malplaquet itself, and the maps trace the campaign in detail.

One map shows how the lines of La Bassee blocked the Allies' advance on Paris, and Marlborough's scheme to outflank them by taking Tournai, then Mons. Another shows the Allies, holding Lille, thrusting the French back onto the defensive line from St. Venant to Valenciennes, cutting off the garrisons of Ypres, Tournai, and Mons. Readers get a compact, map-driven account of the battle of September 11, 1709, and the manoeuvres that led to it.
32316-the-honored-prophet:
William E. Bentley's science-fiction tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1954, is set on a planet ruled from beneath a black dwarf sun. Its ruler calls a council after a prognosticator warns of a distant planet. People there will one day reach space flight and use a weapon made by one person to destroy his world.

The council moves from disbelief to fear, anger, and plans for self-preservation. To erase the threat, the ruler sends an assassin on a mission meant to stop the future before it happens. Yet prophecy in this story follows strange patterns, and an act meant to evade fate may instead help bring it about. Bentley builds a compact tale of prediction, power, and irony, where trying to outrun a warning becomes the surest way to fulfil it.
32785-once-upon-a-planet:
J. J. Allerton tells of Miotis, the mightiest warlord on his planet, in this story from Amazing Stories of December 1948. Miotis has given his whole life to the art of destruction. He controls the lives of his subjects through war.

One day his people weary of the sport, and in the middle of his last campaign both his men and his enemies lay down their arms. Bored and restless, Miotis turns to his vizier Kannot for counsel. He then comes down to Earth to recover his lost appetite for war, but what he sees there makes him feel differently.
32889-cue-for-quiet:
T. L. Sherred's science fiction story, from Space Science Fiction in 1953, begins with a factory worker tormented by constant noise. Presses grind, cranes wail, and steel sheets snap overhead while he works the roof line, and his headache grows until it seems permanent. Then he finds a cure for it, and the cure gives him a power no ordinary person could expect.

The story turns on what a man does once the din stops and a strange new strength takes its place.
