Sherred keeps the focus tight on one worker's body and temper, letting the factory's roar stand for a world that never lets up. It is a short, vivid tale about noise, relief, and the danger of a gift that arrives without a warning label.
32938-first-annual-report-of-the-bureau-:
J. W. Powell, director of the Bureau of Ethnology, sent this first yearly report to the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution for the year 1879-80. It reached print in Washington in 1881. The main report sets out the new bureau's field work, its collections, and its plans for study of the native peoples of North America. It frames a young federal science agency at the point where survey work, language notes, and museum objects began to be kept as one body of record.

Ten accompanying papers carry most of the volume's weight. Powell himself treats the growth of language and sketches the mythology of North American Indians. Other papers take up mortuary customs, a catalogue of linguistic manuscripts, and research among the Klamath Indians. Read together, they show how early ethnology mixed word lists, myths, burial practice, and material culture into a single program of inquiry.
33513-the-frightened-planet:
Sidney Austen's Frightened Planet opens with Karn, a savage who knows a thing or two about justice, hurling a giant idol to the floor. Its tale follows a huge ball tracing an arc of flame across the early morning sky, slowing in descent and landing where Karn might have seen it. Austen writes of a planet frightened by a visitor from the sky, in a pulp tale of wonder and law.

The story's appeal lies in its brisk, imaginative action, as a primitive hero meets a cosmic event with his own rough justice. Its tone is pulpy and vivid, suited to fans of early science fiction. For readers who enjoy lost-world tales, The Frightened Planet offers a short, thrilling glimpse of a world shaken by the heavens.
33644-the-secret-of-the-ninth-planet:
Donald A. Wollheim writes a 1959 science fiction novel of a voyage around the solar system. It is built on the assumption that researchers then at work on anti-gravitational control would succeed within a decade. Once gravity can be negated, reversed, or otherwise used, Wollheim argues, circumnavigation of the solar system becomes plausible. Nineteen chapters carry his travelers by guided missile, rope of space, and rocket through a hidden skyport and a valley of stolen sunlight.

Stops include a hot spot on Mercury, the veil of Venus, a primeval ocean, a dying planet, Martians who do not care, the pole of Callisto, and ice cold on Oberon. Stops also include orbit around Pluto, a stronghold of the lost planet, and ending in a museum of galactic life. Wollheim dedicates the book to three denizens of this minor planet. Young readers will enjoy its grand tour and its sense of wonder.
33810-on-the-magnet-magnetick-bodies-als:
William Gilbert of Colchester, physician of London, wrote this landmark work on the magnet, printed here in a 1900 Chiswick Press edition. Gilbert argues, from many trials, that the earth itself is a great magnet, and he treats lodestones, magnetized bodies, and the compass with fresh care. Edward Wright's praise prefaces the text.

The book sets out experiments in plain, forceful prose and draws a new picture of how magnets act. Sailors, makers of instruments, and natural philosophers all found matter here. It stands as a founding text of the study of magnetism, written before modern physics yet full of close observation.
3411-the-stokesley-secret:
Charlotte Yonge writes a family story for young readers about the Merrifield children at home. The book opens on a comic domestic problem, when five year old David wonders aloud how a pig can pay the rent. His older sister Susan, a dark eyed young lady making tea, tries to keep order while the boys at the table grumble and ignore her.

The secret of the title grows out of the children's efforts to manage money, animals, and their own quarrels without troubling the grown ups. Yonge keeps the tone gentle and moral, praising patience, honesty, and care for younger siblings. The novel gives a warm view of a large Victorian family, where small sums and small duties feel very large to children.
34402-phases-of-an-inferior-planet:
Phases of an Inferior Planet is a novel by Ellen Glasgow, issued at New York and London in 1898. It was her second book, after The Descendant, and the publisher's page quotes praise for that first novel at length. One Boston paper praised its sure touch and its hold on its theme. A New York paper found its drama novel and strong, wrought with truths of modern science.

Glasgow dedicated the book to a friend named in initials only. The astronomical title hints at her matter: a life seen in phases, like a planet that circles closer to the sun than our own. She became one of the leading American novelists of the South. This early work shows the cool eye and the irony that marked her later, famous books.
3484-o-flaherty-v-c-a-recruiting-pamphle:
George Bernard Shaw writes a short play from the First World War that calls itself a recruiting pamphlet in dramatic form. Its hero, O'Flaherty, is an Irish soldier home on leave, proud of his Victoria Cross yet plain spoken about army life. Shaw's long preface argues that British officers often liked Irish soldiers for their bravery while failing to understand them.

The play mixes comedy with sharp comment on Ireland, empire, and the war. Shaw notes that recruiting in Ireland ended in rebellion, with Dublin's center ruined and rebel prisoners shot, a bitter backdrop to any call for Irish recruits. The piece suits readers interested in Shaw's wartime politics and in Irish voices on the Western Front.
34854-handicraft-for-girls-a-tentative-c:
Handicraft for Girls is a school course in hand work for young girls. Idabelle McGlauflin drew the course from her post in Denver schools. Needle work and basket craft lead the list of skills in the title. The book bears a rights line of the year nineteen ten.

The course runs five years at one hour a week in its first stretch. School boards give the stuff for all but the big dress tasks. Paper work, cloth lore, and home care and trim fill later terms. Drawings show each stitch and weave in step by step form. The book served teachers who made hand skill a part of school life.
35582-the-new-guide-to-knitting-crochet:
The New Guide to Knitting and Crochet is a pattern book by Marie Jane Cooper. In her preface, dated at Hastings in January 1847, she says she is well versed in these arts in practice. She warrants her patterns correct and trusts the book will prove a useful addition to every work-table.

The index lists patterns for Siberian cuffs, a leaf pattern for a pincushion, twisted knitting, and a Vandyke border. There are open-knitted lace cuffs, a Prudence cap, a cardinal cape, and a shell-pattern purse. Later pages give a Shetland shawl, a star-pattern shawl, a knitted muff, and long sleeves for under a dress. The frontispiece shows under sleeves, a baby's hood, and a crochet collar. The guide is a working handbook of Victorian fancy work for ladies. Its patterns mix dress trimmings, caps, purses, and shawls.
35686-mississippi-outlaws-and-the-detect:
Mississippi Outlaws and the Detectives is one of Allan Pinkerton's detective books, issued in the series that bore his agency's name. The publisher's list of fifteen titles stands at the front. Mollie Maguires and the Detectives heads it, with Strikers, Communists, and Detectives beside it.

This volume is the ninth of the set. Its title joins river outlaws to the detectives who hunted them, with Don Pedro among the figures named. Pinkerton's books mixed case record, advertisement, and melodrama in equal parts. They sold the agency's fame as boldly as any broadside. The list at the front boasts an unprecedented success for the series. Whatever their polish, these volumes built the American myth of the private detective: tireless, disguised, and always on the outlaw's trail.
35918-dry-fish-and-wet:
Dry Fish and Wet, by Elias Kræmmer, tells tales from a Norwegian seaport. Worster translated it; Gyldendal issued the English text in 1922 at London. The town holds near twenty thousand souls by the last count given. Old men there still brag of coffee fleets direct from Rio in past days.

Timber, corn ships, and merchant princes fill the town store of tales. Clerics of bright name add a second glow to its past in memory. Chapters follow Knut Holm, Bramsen, and Hermansen of the Bank in turn. The Rantzau story, a royal visit, and ships coming home fill the set. Nils Petter legacy and The Admiral close the port chronicle.
3639-diary-of-a-pedestrian-in-cashmere-a:
Captain Knight of the Forty eighth Regiment writes a diary of a walking tour through Cashmere and Thibet, published in 1863. Knight walked rather than rode, so his account notes roads, villages, and people at foot pace. His preface thanks Captain Cunningham for an essay on Cashmere architecture and a French writer, Klaproth, for help on Thibet.

The diary describes mountain passes, temples, bazaars, and the daily work of travel in the Himalayas. Knight writes as a soldier on leave, curious and practical, with an eye for scenery and for local custom. The book suits readers interested in Victorian travel, Kashmir, and Tibet before railways and modern roads changed them.
36892-a-cabinet-secret:
Guy Boothby wrote a novel of a state secret and a first hand teller. The book came out in London in 1901. Wallis Mills drew its plates, a woman bent low at page 118. Boothby wrote Dr Nikola and Pharos the Egyptian. A front talk sets the teller's long tie to Paris in plain words.

Paris and De Belleville are both old friends, he says at once. Twenty years of that tie stand back of the tale's first page. De Belleville is a fine mate with one fault hid in him. Few would own that fault, but the teller must print it plain. State plots and gay Paris mix in Boothby's hand. Each part turns the screw.
3797-in-the-days-of-the-comet:
H G Wells imagines a comet whose green vapors change human nature itself in this novel of the future. The narrator, an old man writing in a tower above a changed world, recalls his youth as a jealous lover bent on murder. He meant to kill Nettie, who had given herself to another, and Verrall, who stood for the injustice of the social order, then take his own life under the towering comet.

The vapors intervene, and the second book shows the awakening, a cabinet council facing a new humanity, and love after the change. Wells uses the comet as a device to ask whether mankind can outgrow greed, war, and spite. Readers who like utopian fiction will find a strange and earnest book, half romance and half prophecy.
3817-to-let:
John Galsworthy closes the Forsyte Saga with this novel, set in the London of 1920 after the Great War. Soames Forsyte, emerging from his Knightsbridge hotel on a May afternoon, walks to a picture gallery instead of taking a cab, as he has done since the war. Around him gather the next generation, Fleur, Jon, and June, with old Jolyon walking in memory and Irene returning to unsettle every plan.

The contents promise encounters at Robin Hill, a mausoleum, an idyll on grass, and at last Fleur's wedding and the last of the Forsytes. Galsworthy writes with his usual cool irony about property, beauty, and possession. Readers who followed the saga from The Man of Property will find a fitting close, with the old order letting its house to strangers.
38252-fairies-i-have-met:
Fairies I Have Met is a book of fairy tales by Mrs. Rodolph Stawell, with colour pictures by Edmund Dulac. It was published by Hodder and Stoughton in London and New York. The dedication tells of Penelope, a little girl who lived among the oleanders before she could toddle. Three sunbeams hid in her hair, her eyelashes, and her heart to travel with her to England.

The tales grow out of that fancy: small meetings between children and the fairy world. One story, named in a picture caption, has a girl asking to be a nightingale. Dulac's colour plates place the book among the rich gift books of the early nineteen hundreds.
3859-memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-a:
This complete text gathers the secret memoirs of Madame Elizabeth-Charlotte of Bavaria in full, from her first letters to her last judgments on the Regency. The preface traces nearly eight hundred letters found among Brunswick papers in 1767, and a French edition of 1788 that cut the piquant traits and softened the bold German. The complete version restores the duchess's voice, frank, funny, and furious by turns.

Later passages show Liselotte watching her son's unfortunate marriage, which she never doubted, and blaming Maintenon's insistence for it. Talk of millions on all sides marks the Regency's moneyed air. Readers who want one Liselotte rather than a volume at a time will find the whole arc here, from Sun King evenings to a son's troubled rule.
38727-a-vindication-of-natural-diet:
A Vindication of Natural Diet is an essay by Percy Bysshe Shelley, reprinted in 1884. Pitman of London and the Vegetarian Society of Manchester issued this edition. Shelley first wrote the piece among the notes to Queen Mab in 1813. Later that year it appeared alone as a pamphlet. The prefatory notice calls the original pamphlet exceedingly scarce. Only two copies were known to survive, one in the British Museum.

Shelley's object was to show a vegetable diet the most natural for mankind. He argues from health and morality, not from pity for animals. His materials came avowedly from the writings of Newton. The style, the notice insists, is Shelley's own throughout. The essay became a founding text of English vegetarian argument. Its 1884 reprint served a growing vegetarian movement.
38791-the-bushranger-s-secret:
Mrs Henry Clarke wrote The Bushranger’s Secret, a tale of risk in Australia for young readers. Blackie and Son issued the book in Glasgow and Bombay. W S Stacey drew the pictures. Clarke had written The Ravensworth Scholarship and other school tales.

Two men share a bare hut on a sheep farm in South Australia. The floor is packed earth and the bunks hang on a log wall. Twelve chapters move from a fugitive to a hunt for lost wealth. A place called Deadman’s Gully holds the key prize. Later chapters strand men in the bush to face thirst and death. A cruel foe makes the hunt worse. Readers get bush craft, greed, and grit in quick turns.
39018-mr-marx-s-secret:
Mr Marx's Secret is a mystery novel by Oppenheim, printed at Boston by Little, Brown in 1916. Oppenheim also wrote Mr Grex of Monte Carlo and The Illustrious Prince. The book was reprinted twice within its first month. A frontispiece by Vaux Wilson dresses the volume. News from the Pacific opens the tale.

The chapters quicken at once. Mr Francis appears, then a murder at the slate-pits. A mother's warning and Ravenor of Ravenor follow, with a doubtful visitor. A meeting brings a metamorphosis, and an abode of mystery houses Mr Marx himself. Lady Silchester, a cry in the avenue, and a startling discovery build the middle. Forestalled, a gleam of light, and a doctor's opinion wind the skein tighter. Oppenheim, the prince of storytellers to his fans, deals his secrets card by card.
39063-the-motor-girls-in-the-mountains-o:
Margaret Penrose wrote The Motor Girls in the Mountains, or The Gypsy Girl's Secret, copyrighted by Cupples and Leon in 1919. Cora Kimball drives the car in the opening chapter, breaking the speed limit on a sun-flecked country road. Belle Robinson and her twin sister Bess ride behind her. Bess asks to be pinched to be sure the ride is real. The chapters promise a missing purse and a group of vagabonds.

A mountain camp, a drifting boat, and help from the sky follow. The girls reach the gypsy camp, and Falsely Accused and Waylaid raise the stakes. A knocking at midnight and a council of war close the run. The gypsy girl's secret gives this outing its mystery, and the series sold motor freedom to girl readers.
39715-the-argentine-as-a-market:
Argentine as a Market is a trade report in the publications of the University of Manchester. It is number nine of the university economic series and number six of the Gartside reports. Sherratt and Hughes, publishers to the Victoria University of Manchester, issued the report. 

The report rests on a tour in the Argentine in 1906 and 1907 by its maker. The Gartside reports sent Manchester men to study the markets where British goods might sell in those years. Argentina, rich from beef, wheat, and railways, was then a prize market of the world. The report weighs its ports, railways, credit, and tastes for the Manchester merchant in plain terms. Such reports are the paperwork of the informal empire of trade. They show British industry, still confident in 1907, sending scholars to learn how a young republic bought, borrowed, and built with the money of its harvests.
40037-fort-duquesne-and-fort-pitt-early-:
Fort Duquesne and Fort Pitt, with early names of Pittsburgh streets, is a short local history. The Fort Pitt Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution issued it in nineteen hundred twenty one. The Allegheny County group put out this sixth edition. Its sketch is drawn from Parkman and older local works.

A dated list runs from seventeen hundred fifty three onward. Washington came to Fort Le Boeuf in December of that year. He urged a fort at the Forks of the Ohio soon after. French troops seized the half built post in spring next. Braddock fell in seventeen hundred fifty five on his march. Forbes took the burnt fort in November seventeen hundred fifty eight. Stanwix began Fort Pitt, and Bouquet built its block house in seventeen hundred sixty four.
40134-a-moral-alphabet:
A Moral Alphabet is a comic verse alphabet signed only with the initials H B, with pictures by B B. Edward Arnold published it in London in 1899. The pair had already made The Bad Child's Book of Beasts and More Beasts for Worse Children.

Each letter gets a short poem and a moral that rarely behaves. A stands for Archibald, who told no lies and won this very book as a prize, so the moral bids children brush hair and teeth and tell the truth. B is a bear that eats the man who fights and outruns the man who flees. C is a cobra whose bite gives an Indian judge restless nights, with no moral worth recalling. D falls to the dreadful Dinotherium, a beast with a saw-like back.
40491-the-red-lottery-ticket:
Fortuné du Boisgobey wrote a Paris tale that Vizetelly of London sold in a sixpenny series in 1887. It opens on a fine April day, with a cab crossing the bridge by the Louvre. Two young men smoke cigars inside and chat in high spirits. Both are students in name and idlers in fact.

George Caumont is the son of a Norman cattle breeder, sent to Paris to study law on three thousand francs a year. His friend Adhémar de Puymirol lives on a small sum from an aunt and is meant to become a doctor. The pair skip lectures, pass an exam now and then, and dream of a rich marriage. Creditors press and kin grumble, yet this spring morning all seems rose bright. The tale is a light French novel of debts, hopes, and young men on the make.
40782-smithsonian-institution-united-sta:
Bulletin 240 of the United States National Museum gathers eleven papers from the Museum of History and Technology. Each paper treats one object or theme in the Smithsonian store. The first, by Don Berkebile, tells of the 1893 Duryea automobile, an early American motor car. Silvio Bedini writes on the Borghesi astronomical clock. Robert Vogel treats the engineering work of Wendel Bollman, a bridge builder. Edwin Battison traces screw-thread cutting by the master-screw method since 1480.

Later papers take up the earliest electrical instruments that work by magnetism. Howard Chapelle writes on Fulton's steam battery, a blockship and catamaran of the war age. Eduard Farber gives a history of phosphorus. The set shows the museum's way of study: one thing at a time, told whole. The papers serve the student of the history of technology.
41187-this-house-to-let:
This House to Let is a mystery novel by William Le Queux, in an edition dated nineteen twenty one. It was published in London by Hodder and Stoughton in that year. A prologue opens early on a July morning in nineteen nineteen. Constable Brown walks his beat in Cathcart Square, a quiet Kensington backwater.

The square mixes small narrow houses with near mansions around an old dairy. Brown, an easy going young policeman, is content and friendly with the cooks. He pauses at Number Ten, the square's one big empty house to let. It has stood vacant for over three months, though such houses seldom wait. Brown blames the caretaker Miles, too cosy in his quarters to let it go. Miles, he thinks, scares off viewers with talk of damp and ghosts.
41468-the-widow-in-the-bye-street:
The Widow in the Bye Street is a poem in narrative verse by John Masefield. It was printed in London by Sidgwick and Jackson in 1912. The book is inscribed to the poet's wife. The poem tells of a widow in a small Shropshire town and of her only son. It is written in short rhymed stanzas that carry the tale plainly and with pity.

The widow has no wealth and no title to renown. She rises from a ragged mattress before the sun and stitches all day until her eyes are red. She must stitch, because her man is dead. Mostly she makes her bread by hemming shrouds for a rich undertaker in the High Street. Hungry cats steal in from the yard of the poor house, and mangy chickens peck about the door. They find nothing there.
41558-dorothy-dale-s-great-secret:
Margaret Penrose wrote this Dorothy Dale tale of a great secret. Cupples and Leon printed it in New York in 1909. Past books took Dorothy to Glenwood School as a girl of today. Chapter one gives the girls an automobile ride at term end.

Tavia praises boarding school for the leave it grants at close. Bologna from Daly's shop sets the friends laughing on the road. Tavia plans, an apparition, and an untimely letter follow in contents. Leaving Glenwood, a runaway, Buffalo, and a play fill the middle. Behind the scenes at the play and a clue found mark the tale turning point.
41811-life-of-thomas-a-becket:
Milman's life of Thomas à Becket was lifted from his history of Latin Christianity and issued on its own. Sheldon and Company printed it in New York in eighteen sixty. Milman, Dean of Saint Paul's in London, tells the dramatic church and state story in English history: the quarrel between Becket and Henry the Second.

The preface calls that struggle a contest between genius and sovereign power, between religion and the sword. It notes that Becket's life begins in oriental legend and ends in heroic tragedy. Becket rose from the king's chancellor to Archbishop of Canterbury, and defied his old friend over the rights of the Church. Murdered in his cathedral, he drew pilgrims to his tomb by the hundred thousand. The volume closes with footnotes, and its front matter sketches Milman's life, from Eton and Oxford to the deanery.
42100-the-bride-of-the-tomb-and-queenie-:
Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller wrote The Bride of the Tomb and Queenie Terrible Secret, issued by Street and Smith in New York as Eagle Series number four hundred twenty six. Two long tales fill the book, with elegant coloured covers as the series boasted. The first tale is called The Bride of the Tomb, or Lancelot Darling Betrothed. It runs to forty chapters. The second tale runs to forty three chapters.

Queenie Terrible Secret is subtitled A Young Girl Strange Fate. Miller was a famed writer of sensational tales for cheap series sale. Brides, tombs, secrets, and strange fates promise love, peril, and hidden guilt in full measure. Chapter lists alone show the scale of incident the tales pack in. Readers of dime and series fiction get two full melodramas in one volume. The book shows how popular tales were sold to eager readers of the age.
42601-the-expositor-s-bible-the-propheci:
The Prophecies of Jeremiah, in the Expositor's Bible, pairs the prophet's book with a sketch of his life and times. Ball, chaplain of Lincoln's Inn, wrote the commentary, issued in New York in 1890. He had contributed to other large commentaries of the day.

The sketch fills the first fifty-odd pages before the chapters begin. Ball notes that Jeremiah, a priest by birth, was fitted by training for his call. The priesthood formed part of the land's nobility, and its schooling was the best of the age. The chapters then take up the call and consecration, the trust in Egypt's shadow, and a contrast of Israel and Judah. The Scythians as scourge, the broken covenant, and the fall of pride follow. The divine potter and the broken vessel close the main line.
4287-the-red-planet:
William J. Locke set this novel in England during the First World War. Mars, the red planet of war, hangs over sheltered homes as well as battlefields. Its narrator is a paralyzed veteran of the South African War. He shares his house and memories with his old comrade Sergeant Marigold.

Both men were wounded by the same Boer shell. Through visits from Lady Fenimore and Sir Anthony, the novel meditates on grief, duty, and mourning families. Its reflections draw on the Latin tag Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori. Locke writes from inside a household touched by war, rather than from the trenches, and the story's force lies in that quiet viewpoint.
42987-nightmare-planet:
Nightmare Planet is a science fiction story by Murray Leinster, written for Science Fiction Plus and printed in its June 1953 issue. The magazine text is the source of this edition.

An opening note places the story in a famous series. Leinster's The Mad Planet and Red Dust, first printed in 1923, had been reprinted for thirty years. Nightmare Planet is the closing tale, written for this magazine, and brings back Burl for new adventures. The story opens as the directory ship Tethys lands first on a rich world of seas and cloud. The planet seems perfect in every way but one: no living thing, not even bacteria, exists there. It could not be settled, Leinster writes, because it had never been settled before.
43565-thomas-hardy-s-dorset:
R Thurston Hopkins wrote a guide to the Dorset places tied to novelist Thomas Hardy. D Appleton and Company brought it out in New York in 1922, with art by E Harries and with photographs. Chapters move town by town through the county Hardy knew well. Folk tales, inns, churches, and old customs fill the route.

Readers meet Dorchester, Blandford, Shaftesbury, and the Vale of Blackmoor along the way. Each stop ties a real place to a scene or name in Hardy books such as Jude the Obscure. Local speech, cider making, and poet William Barnes get close care too. The book suits fans who want to walk the ground behind the novels.
4359-lombard-street-a-description-of-the:
Walter Bagehot wrote this essay on the money market under the title Lombard Street, the London street of bankers. He chose a concrete name on purpose, to show that the money market is not an impalpable mystery but a real place, describable in plain words. Books on it are difficult, he argues, only when writers make them so.

Bagehot explains banks, reserves, panics, and the Bank of England's part in them, with the Act of 1844 in the background. His aim is clarity for practical readers. Lombard Street remains a classic of financial writing, praised for turning an abstract system into streets, firms, and decisions.
44828-wild-margaret:
The title page names Geraldine Fleming as author, but a transcriber's note at the front corrects the record. The novel is His Guardian Angel, or, Wild Margaret, by Charles Garvice. Fleming was a house pseudonym of the publisher Street and Smith. Thirty-three chapters follow, with no titles given.

Chapter one brings two travelers down at the small station of Leyton Ferrers on the Great South-Northern Railway. A young girl drags her own bag and parcel from a third-class carriage while the porter chats with the guard. A young man from first class, cigar in lips and cap at an angle, orders the porter to see to the young lady first. She asks the way to Leyton Court and learns it is little better than two miles and a half, which she reckons means three.
45734-the-chaplain-of-the-fleet:
Walter Besant and James Rice wrote a joint novel set in old London. A library form came out in London in 1888. Its heroine is Kitty, and the Fleet is its key ground. Part heads all start with the word How, like a tale told by a friend. The South Sea Bubble crash plays a part in the plot.

Kitty loses her father and friends at the start. She makes vows, rides to London by coach, and meets the Doctor. A Fleet wed rite and Fleet free ways fill her days. Two women are jailed when the Bubble bursts. Love, debt, and pride drive the long tale.
45741-smithsonian-institution-united-sta:
Bulletin 249 from the Smithsonian Institution in Washington came out in 1968. It holds papers fifty two to fifty four from the Museum of History and Technology. All three papers deal with archeology. A front note explains the two series in which the national museum issues its research.

The Proceedings, begun in 1878, carry shorter papers in a compact form. The Bulletin series holds longer monographs on the collections and work of the museums. Copies go to libraries, cultural bodies, and specialists round the world. Readers get new facts from museum study in fields from anthropology to technology, set out in a sober record meant to last.
46388-the-story-of-the-alphabet:
Edward Clodd wrote a small history of the alphabet, with ninety pictures. George Newnes issued The Story of the Alphabet in London in 1900. Clodd had written The Story of Primitive Man and Pioneers of Evolution. He gave the book to Dorothy Day, his grandchild, with love.

Chapters trace picture writing, memory aids, and scripts of China and Egypt. Wedge writing, the Rosetta Stone, Cretan signs, and Greek papyri each get a part. Runes and ogams close the survey of how signs spread. General readers gain a clear, short path from cave marks to the letters in daily use.
47087-motor-matt-s-race-or-the-last-flig:
Motor Matt's Race, or The Last Flight of the Comet, is a dime novel by Stanley Matthews. Street and Smith published it in New York on March 20, 1909. The price was five cents, by subscription two dollars fifty a year. An illustration shows Chub snatching a letter from Motor Matt's fingers. I've got it, pard, the caption has him shout. The contents list sixteen chapters of road adventure. Trouble on the Road and The Stampede open the tale.

Clip's Note and a tip from McKibben move the plot along. A Victim of Circumstances and the pride of Tom Clipperton follow. The Rifled Cache and The Break in the Road raise danger. The Old Hopewell Tunnel and Steam versus Gasoline give the race. In Court and a conclusion close the story. Motor Matt was a boy inventor hero of early motor fiction.
47391-john-brown-confessions-of-a-new-ar:
John Brown, Confessions of a New Army Cadet, is a comic war school tale. The title page names Campbell as its author in full. Campbell had won laughs with his Private Spud Tamson books before. Chambers put the book out in London and Edinburgh in 1919. It is given to the officers of two Scots divisions of the war.

Chapter heads run from the cadet school to the commandant's farewell. A sergeant-major from the Guards drills the raw young gentlemen cadets. Talk turns to the modern girl, sport, and the mind in war. John Brown's letters home fill a chapter in the mid part. A Canadian newspaper, a jolly rag, and mother on a visit appear. The new army officer is weighed at the end of the course.
47744-sekhet:
Irene Miller wrote Sekhet, a long novel issued by John Lane in London and New York in nineteen hundred twelve. Sekhet was an old Egyptian goddess of love and its cruelty. Her name hangs over the whole cast. Forty two chapters trace one young woman through work and want.

Evarne Stornway is the heroine, born to great beauty. Scenes move from deep country to London, Italy, Paris, and Egypt. Evarne joins a touring stage troupe that plays a Scots bard piece. Managers, models, and landladies crowd her path. Work at a needle fills one bleak stretch. Love and pride clash as Sekhet smiles, in the book’s phrase. The cast list alone runs to more than twenty named folk.
47960-romeo-and-juliet:
William J Rolfe edited Shakespeare’s Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet with notes for school and study. The American Book Company issued the book in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. Rolfe had led the high school at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Print rights run back to eighteen hundred seventy nine in the front leaves.

A history of the play opens Rolfe’s long groundwork here. The first quarto came out in fifteen hundred ninety seven, he notes. It holds two thousand two hundred thirty two lines in all. The second quarto of fifteen hundred ninety nine runs far longer. Three thousand seven lines fill that fuller, truer text. Most critics call the first a pirated, short cut text. One long scene in act two shows the rewrite at work. Notes fill more pages than the play in this rich school book.
489-one-basket:
Edna Ferber gathers thirty-one short stories in this volume, though only the first set is fully printed here. The Woman Who Tried to Be Good opens the book, following Blanche Devine, a fallen woman in a small town who seeks respect and finds only higher prices and cold stares. The Gay Old Dog, That's Marriage, and Farmer in the Dell follow.

Ferber writes with sharp humor and sympathy for women boxed in by town talk. Her heroines fight for decency, work, and a fair hearing. The book shows Ferber's early gift for town life in miniature, where a single shop or street can hold a whole moral drama.
4985-ruth-fielding-of-the-red-mill-or-ja:
Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill opens on a long train journey, as Ruth rides the afternoon Limited from the West toward Cheslow through the fertile valleys of upper New York State. The drumming wheels roar in her ears for hours, stations fly by, and dusk falls as she spells their names with quick eyes.

At journey's end waits the Red Mill, and Jasper Parloe's secret, which will shape Ruth's new life among strangers who may become family. The record names no author for this work. Readers get a girls' series novel about an orphan's fresh start, where work, friendship, and a mystery unfold around an old mill.
50217-dave-dawson-with-the-pacific-fleet:
R Sidney Bowen wrote a Dave Dawson war novel copyrighted in 1942 by Crown Publishers of New York. Bowen's other Dawson books are listed: at Dunkirk, with the air force, in Libya, on convoy patrol, and at Singapore. Contents open with Order for Eagles. Center of the world and special assignment follow. Death in the Pacific and silent wings come next.

A midnight menace, pilot's luck, and nobody's airport build the middle. Rescue wings and a vulture's nest precede a little bit of England. Dave Dawson was a favorite of wartime boy readers. Bowen flew in the first war and wrote flying fiction between wars. The Pacific fleet volume followed Pearl Harbor swiftly.
50405-uncle-wiggily-s-auto-sled-or-how-m:
Uncle Wiggily's Auto Sled is a picture story book for children by Howard R Garis, published by Charles E Graham and Company in 1919. Lang Campbell drew the pictures. Uncle Wiggily is the bunny rabbit gentleman of Garis's long running series of bedtime stories.

The long title tells the whole plot in advance. Mr Hedgehog helps Uncle Wiggily get up the slippery hill. Uncle Wiggily makes snow pudding. Something happens in the snow fort as well. The publisher's note promises that readers who like this funny little picture book may be glad to know there are others. Garis built a small industry on the rabbit's adventures, one mishap and one animal friend at a time. The book's tall, slim format and big pictures suit reading aloud at the nursery table.
5099-heart-of-the-sunset:
Rex Beach's Western novel is set in the ranch country of southern Texas, around Las Palmas and the border lands. Its chapters follow water-hole ambushes, a rodeo, and a judge's promise. Luis Longorio grows bolder, and his raids threaten ranchers on both sides of the line.

Against that violent border world, Beach sets a Texas Ranger, Dave Law. The ranch people must choose between law, loyalty, and revenge. The novel mixes romance, gunplay, and range life, and it gives a vivid picture of the Texas frontier as railroads. Rangers, and rival claims closed in on it.
51307-this-house-to-let:
This House to Let, by William Le Queux, was published in London in 1921 by Hodder and Stoughton. The prologue opens very early on a July morning in 1919. Constable Brown is on his beat in Kensington, in the neighbourhood of Cathcart Square, an old-fashioned backwater of the respectable suburb.

The square was built on no regular lines round a very old dairy. Small, narrow houses nestle beside what might be called mansions. A narrow-fronted milk-shop stands next door to a palatial residence. Brown, a tall, strapping young fellow friendly with all the cooks on his beat, takes his duties easily and is content with his lot. The bright morning is quiet, the square sleeping, only market-carts rumbling far off toward Covent Garden. Le Queux sets his mystery in the still streets.
51585-bohemian-days-in-fleet-street:
An unnamed journalist recalls his Bohemian days in Fleet Street here. Long printed the memoir in London in the year 1913. Contents open with the street of adventure and drifting into it. Learning to swim and into the maelstrom follow in the tale.

Society journalism, odd fish, and Bohemian clubs fill the middle chapters. The joker, Ansdel afternoons, and friends the players come next. Bookies, the press in transition, and an olla podrida close it. A Gibbs novel, The Street of Adventure, sparked the book, he owns. Mine ease at mine inn stands among the later chapters of the Fleet Street memories.
51597-gourmet:
Gourmet is a science fiction story by Allen Kim Lang. It ran in Galaxy Magazine in April 1962. Its problem is the endless one of all spaceship cooks. A cook must feed the men tomorrow on what they ate today. Men on ships, Lang writes, think and talk endlessly about food. A history of seafaring can be read from a commissary list, he claims.

Old sailors named themselves for their hash, the Lobscousers. The limey took his name from the citrus in his diet. Marsmen of Lang's day are called Slimeheads for their algae fare. Chlorella and other algae fill the ship's spaces and open the road to space. The narrator cites the beef and cheese chapter of Moby Dick as proof. Gourmet humour runs on menus through the whole tale.
52245-where-science-and-religion-meet:
William Scott Palmer wrote Where Science and Religion Meet, for Hodder and Stoughton. A French line from Boutroux stands at the front, naming life as the link of science and religion. A long quote from Jowett, on Plato, sets the method of the book. Men still grope, Jowett says, for a method wider than any now in use. The method of idealized experience is the promise held out at a distance.

That method joins what men split: past and present, part and whole, theory and fact. It joins the divine and the human, and one science to an other, in its aim. Palmer gives no names of authorities and no references in the text. In their place, an appendix lists short sets of books that back the case. The book seeks a road where lab and faith need not war.
52300-william-blake-painter-and-poet:
William Blake, Painter and Poet, is a short life and study by Richard Garnett. Garnett was keeper of the printed books in the British Museum. The London and New York edition is dated eighteen ninety five. A list of illustrations opens the book. A design from the Book of Job, the Sons of God, serves as frontispiece. Plates from the Songs of Innocence and of Experience face early pages.

Pages from The Book of Thel and from America stand among the plates. The position of William Blake among artists is exceptional, the text begins. Of no other painter of like distinction, save Rossetti, can it be said that his fame as a poet fully rivalled his fame as a painter, it argues. In some opinion his fame as a seer goes higher still.
52326-the-radio-planet:
The Radio Planet is a tale of the far worlds by Ralph Milne Farley. It first ran as a set tale in a sheet of tales in nineteen twenty six. The host print is a cheap form from a New York house. A next tale of the same set, of the beasts of the wave craft, is named at the front. The first words of the hand set a hard ask.

Could you make a wave set, that ask says. Do not give your word in haste. We do not ask if you could put a set in one piece from parts made by more hands. We ask if you could build the whole set your self, from the ground up.
52574-third-planet:
Third Planet, a science fiction story by Murray Leinster, ran in Worlds of Tomorrow in April 1963. It opens in a cold war deadlock. The Council of the Western Defense Alliance has yielded once more on a border shift in south east Asia, rather than risk atomic war. The Coordinator must break the news to the Com Ambassador.

The Ambassador stuns him by reciting the secret decision in full detail, stage by stage. Their spies, it seems, know every move before it is made. He grants three days for clearing out citizens marked for death. The head note hints at the turn ahead: aliens who lost their lives to nuclear war may yet hold the means to save Earth.
52594-three-years-in-tibet:
Three Years in Tibet is the travel record of Ekai Kawaguchi, a Japanese Buddhist monk. It was published at Adyar, Madras, in 1909, with the Japanese pictures kept. Kawaguchi had been rector of a monastery in Tokyo.

His preface tells how the journey began in study. Reading the Lotus Sutra in Chinese set him on the road. He gave up his post in 1891 and spent three years as a hermit at Kyoto, deep in Chinese Buddhist books. He found that the Chinese texts alone would not do. The Sanskrit originals and the Tibetan versions, held to be more exact, lay in Tibet and Nepal. The book tells of his years in that closed land, and of the texts and teachings he found there.
52684-cricket: Steel and Lyttelton wrote the cricket volume of the Badminton Library of Sports and Pastimes, a set of twenty eight books on field sports. The Duke of Beaufort edited the series, with Watson to help him. The cricket book carries sixty five pictures. Notes in the text speak of diagrams that map where balls pitch and how off breaks move. The hints mark it as a full handbook of the game for players and fans of its day.
53192-a-texas-blue-bonnet:
Caroline Emilia Jacobs, writing as Emilia Elliott, published this girls' novel with the Page Company of Boston in nineteen ten. It stayed in print through many impressions into the nineteen thirties. Its heroine is Blue Bonnet Ashe, a Texas ranch girl. She lives on a ranch with her Uncle Cliff and her collie Don.

The opening chapter finds Blue Bonnet suddenly afraid of riding, a shameful thing in an Ashe, and unwilling to explain herself. The contents promise the cure. She is sent east to school, meets the Boston relatives, faces a dare and a class affair, and spends Christmas among new friends. Illustrations by John Goss show the heroine in her happiest scenes. The book began a popular series built on a simple contrast: free Texas ranch life against the manners of an eastern girls' school.
54403-where-the-twain-meet:
Where the Twain Meet is a travel book by Mary Gaunt, the author of Alone in West Africa. It was published in London by John Murray in 1922. A letter at the front thanks the friend who taught Gaunt her art and passed on each of her books for twelve years.

The first chapter is named Britain's First Tropical Colony. Gaunt sails for Jamaica. She recalls that Jamaica was an old slave colony. That fact links the trip to her West African years. As a girl she had longed to go to West Africa since she was twelve. In Liverpool she stayed with shipowning friends whose people had traded with Africa for hundreds of years. In those days, she notes, such trade meant the slave trade. The book weighs east and west, and past and present, against each other.
54788-the-memoirs-of-franc-ois-rene-vico:
The Memoirs of François René, Vicomte de Chateaubriand, volume two, is part of the English version by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos of the Mémoires d'Outre-Tombe, published at London in 1902. Six volumes carry the life, with pictures from sources of the time. This volume opens as the young Chateaubriand goes to see his mother at Saint-Malo while the Revolution grows.

Book seven follows his marriage, the clubs and theatres of Paris, and his emigration to fight with the army of the Princes, ending wounded and exiled in Jersey. Book eight sinks into his poor London years, a garret in Holborn and nights in Westminster Abbey. Few memoirs mix history and self so richly.
54807-the-memoirs-of-franc-ois-rene-vico:
The Memoirs of Francois Rene, Vicomte de Chateaubriand, volume three of six, was published in London in nineteen two by Freemantle and Company. Alexander Teixeira de Mattos translated the Memoires d'Outre-Tombe. Illustrations came from contemporary sources. Chateaubriand had been ambassador to England, as the title page notes.

The contents of this volume cover the years eighteen seven to eighteen thirty. Book five recalls the purchase of the Vallee-aux-Loups and the writing of The Martyrs. Part three opens with the last days of the Empire in eighteen fourteen. The Allies enter Paris, Bonaparte abdicates at Fontainebleau, and Louis the Eighteenth returns. The Hundred Days follow, with Chateaubriand attending the exiled king at Ghent. Few memoirs place their author so near the fall and return of thrones.
55070-the-memoirs-of-franc-ois-rene-vico:
Alexander Teixeira de Mattos translated The Memoirs of Francois Rene, Vicomte de Chateaubriand, from the Memoires d'Outre-Tombe. Freemantle and Company published the six volumes at London in 1902. This fifth volume carries books thirteen and fourteen. Book thirteen continues the Roman embassy. Dispatches to the Comte Portalis alternate with letters to Madame Recamier. Conclaves, a fete at the Villa Medici, and Monte Cavallo fill the Roman pages.

His relations with the Bonaparte family get a section. He returns to Paris, then leaves again for Rome by the Pyrenees. The Polignac ministry fills him with consternation, and he resigns his embassy. Book fourteen covers the Algerian expedition and the opening of the session of 1830. The chamber is dissolved, and the Ordinances of July 25 follow. Chateaubriand's memoirs, written for posthumous fame, mix high office with high self-regard.
55511-the-silver-bullet:
The Silver Bullet is a novel by Fergus Hume, published in London by John Long. Hume lists many earlier books on its title pages, most of them tales of mystery. The opening chapter is called The House in the Pine Wood. It begins on a treeless moor at night, far from any town. Two walkers, Robin Joyce and his friend Herrick, have tramped since eight in the morning.

Robin is worn out, peevish, and close to tears on the moor. Herrick, stronger in body, knows his friend's frail health and weak nerves. He waits while Robin rests and smokes, then talks of plain things to brace him. Robin protests that he is no Hercules and feels things more keenly. He also notes that he came back only the night before from London. The pair hope to reach a village within a few miles.
55964-the-sapphire-signet:
The Sapphire Signet is a mystery story for girls by Augusta Huiell Seaman. The Century Company published the book at New York in 1916, with pictures by Relyea. Seaman had written The Boarded-Up House. The tale is also called The Lass of Richmond Hill in its first chapter head.

Charlton Street lies dull and dark at five on a winter afternoon. One house alone keeps its parlour unlit while a face peers from behind the curtains. A find in an attic and a trunk with a false bottom open the puzzle. A boy named Alexander takes hold and digs into old records. A Mrs Mortier warns a girl against talk with rebels, hinting at a wartime past. A sapphire signet ring stands at the secret's heart. Seaman built many such house mysteries for young readers.
56087-in-queer-street:
Fergus Hume wrote In Queer Street, a novel for White of London in 1913. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and other tales. Chapter one is set in a boarding-house, where a landlady holds forth. Mrs Tesk tells a new boarder, Spruce, that her house is not wildly gay. Each inmate, she says, is devoted to an ideal: gaining wealth in virtuous ways. Spruce, a twinkling little man, cuts in with dry wit.

Drop the word virtuous, he says, and most folk share that ideal. He wants money himself, or he would not come to a Bethnal Green lodging-house. Boarding-house, if you please, says the landlady, drawing up her thin figure. Contents promise old school-fellows, blackmail, and an amazing discovery.
56101-sweet-rocket:
Sweet Rocket is a novel by Mary Johnston, printed at New York in October 1920. Johnston also wrote Sir Mortimer, Michael Forth, and To Have and to Hold. The tale opens on a country road in autumn. A woman driving turns her phaeton off the highway into a narrow lane, and the forest deepens.

The passenger, new to the countryside, breathes its scent with delight and takes off her hat. Maples have lighted fires, and hickories make gold along the way. Dogwood and sumac dye crimson at the roadside. The gray horse crosses a brown streamlet where mint fills the air. Johnston sets her tale in a rich woodland that feels far away, yet right at hand.
56324-the-city-of-the-discreet:
The City of the Discreet is a novel by Pio Baroja, rendered from the Spanish by Jacob S. Fassett, Jr. It came out in New York in 1917 from Alfred A. Knopf. It is the second volume of the Borzoi Spanish Translations. The first of that set is The Cabin by V. Blasco Ibanez, and the third Martin Rivas by Alberto Blest-Gana.

The front pages list the other works of Baroja in Spanish, with glosses in English. Labraz and Zalacain the Adventurer stand there, and a group called Life Fantastic. A set called Race holds The Errant Lady, The City of Mist, and The Tree of Knowledge. A set called The Struggle for Life stands in the list as well. The volume is an English rendering of a Spanish novel of town life, by its title: a city of discreet folk.
56470-the-great-pearl-secret:
C N Williamson and A M Williamson wrote The Great Pearl Secret, a novel of plot and hidden wealth. Doubleday, Page and Company issued it in nineteen hundred twenty one. Julian de Miskey drew the front picture. Chapters carry names such as Behind the Bookshelf and The Grey Room.

Juliet Phayre waits in a grand hotel suite for her wedding day. Her maid Simone guards her and runs her errands. A widow in black, Lady West, slips in to view the gifts. She sits in the dark by the fire till the maid finds her. A letter sealed by a Russian queen enters the tale soon after. Love, jewels, and a spy ring pull the plot tight from there.
5722-the-shewing-up-of-blanco-posnet:
Bernard Shaw's Shewing Up of Blanco Posnet, dated 1909, is a short play Shaw himself calls a religious tract in dramatic form. His preface attacks censorship, arguing that a silly censorship blocks serious religious drama while permitting lesser fare. The play that follows tests a horse thief's conscience, pitting law, scripture, and human mercy against one another.

Readers and theatre groups will find Shaw at his most provocative in miniature: sharp talk, a moral reversal, and a hero who refuses easy judgment. The edition preserves period spelling, including shew for show and missing contractions, as printed. It suits those who enjoy Shaw's debates on stage, and anyone curious about how censorship shaped what playwrights could say.
5748-in-secret:
Robert Chambers builds the spy novel In Secret around a letter in a yellow envelope. The letter is dumped with thousands of others onto long tables. Hundreds of women and scores of men open mail there for a bureau known only by initials. A girl picks up the letter, slits it open, and sets a case in motion that the first chapter, called Cup and Lip, only begins to reveal. Chambers writes in the brisk style of wartime intrigue.

Readers follow codes, watchers, and hidden loyalties through a world where a single envelope can endanger lives. The novel suits fans of early spy fiction and First World War thrillers, with romance and danger kept in balance. Its opening in a mail-censoring room gives the book a distinctive, modern feel, since the war itself becomes the machinery of the plot.
57646-through-unknown-tibet:
M S Wellby, Captain of the 18th Hussars, told of a journey across Tibet and China. T Fisher Unwin issued Through Unknown Tibet in London in 1898, with pictures. Wellby wrote the book at Lucknow, Simla, and in the wilds of Waziristan. He calls it a plain story plainly told, begun in November 1897.

Lieutenant Malcolm shared the road, with three faithful men named in thanks. Shahzad Mir, Lassoo, and Esa Tsareng stuck through thick and thin. One chapter treats a rising in China from a mission friend's notes. Travelers gain frank lessons in what to do and what to shun.
57867-robin-linnet:
Robin Linnet is a novel by Benson, author of Dodo. Hutchinson published it in London. The first chapter opens at a university, where two friends read Plato's Apology together. The pair, known as Day and Pie, sit side by side in Damon's room in the great quadrangle. A candle gutters in the draught between them.

Propped against the candle stands a firmly literal translation, to which both constantly refer. Beneath the candlestick, much less consulted, lies a Greek lexicon. Benson opens his tale with this fond picture of undergraduate shortcuts. The novel follows its hero from college into the world, in Benson's light and witty manner.
58304-falling-in-with-fortune-or-the-exp:
Horatio Alger began a boys tale finished by Arthur Winfield and printed in 1900. The tale stands complete in itself, the preface says, but forms the second of two companion volumes, the first being Out for Business. Robert Frost, who figured in the other book, is the hero here. Driven from home by a harsh step father, he had gone out for business in the first tale.

By a curious turn of chance he becomes private secretary to a rich lady and travels with her to England and other places. The lady has a nephew whose character is none of the best. Is this your ring, aunt, a pictured scene asks. These two stories give readers the last tales begun by Alger, the famous writer of boys' books. Rags, luck, and honesty win the day as ever.
59172-willie-s-planet:
Mike Ellis wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in April 1955. The most fitting place for a man to die is where he dies for man, the blurb says. Yet Willie chose a sterile, alien world that would not even see a man for millions of years. Tom stands at the filtered porthole of a tiny cabin and soaks up sunlight.

After ten months of deep space blackness the sun feels good. By golly, Willie, this is luck, Tom says, our hundredth and last star, and it is an Earth type sun. Willie holds a color chart to the spectrum screen and finds it almost on, a couple of degrees off. Then his thin face tenses with a hunch about this star that he cannot shake.
59259-the-outer-quiet:
Herbert Kastle wrote The Outer Quiet for Worlds of If Science Fiction in May 1955. The tale opens on a conquered Earth. Its unnamed hero shares a Brooklyn room with six other men. He has survived the destruction of New York and eight months in prison.

Punishment by the Conquerors' beam is ruining his sight. A first offense left a slight blur in his vision. A second has nearly blinded him, leaving the world a watery haze. A third offense means death. He must find Adele before death finds him, the story says. Each morning a whistle starts the prisoners' aimless wandering. They stroll in silence between the five buildings of a former housing project. Fear, the epigraph warns, is often man's greatest enemy.
59403-jekyll-hyde-planet:
Jack Lewis set this tale on Centauri IV for Worlds of If in February 1956. Its blurb names the pair: Centifor was a paradise planet, another Garden of Eden. And Leon Stubbs was the serpent of the lure.

The ship comes in low, slowing against dense air. Passengers talk, laugh, and press their faces to the ports. A speaker crackles in the lounge: twenty minutes to landing on Centauri IV. Transfers for Orion, Antares, Cygni, and Polaris should stand ready, the voice jokes. Young Billy grips Claude Marshall's arm: do we really have to change? No, Billy, his father smiles. This is as far as anyone is going.
59970-the-life-of-joseph-smith-the-proph:
The Life of Joseph Smith the Prophet is a biography by George Cannon, in a second edition printed at Salt Lake City in 1907. The Mormon Texts Project prepared this copy. Cannon's preface opens with the deaths of Joseph and Hyrum. Like the first martyr, he says, they yet speak, in testimony, admonition, and warning.

No men suffered greater persecution, and none were less understood by their generation, he holds. The Saints, he hopes, will find joy in the book, and the world will judge more fairly. Cannon finished the closing chapters in prison, for holding to the principles the brothers taught. That fact, he says, makes the Life dearer to him. He sends the work away like parting from a beloved companion.
60162-solario-the-tailor-his-tales-of-th:
Solario the Tailor is a book of fairy tales by William Bowen, published by Macmillan in 1922. Its subtitle names the hero's stock in trade: tales of the magic doublet. Solario tells his stories night by night to his listeners. Detailed chapter summaries at the front spell out each night's wonders.

The first night tells of the old man in the spangled coat. A doublet with a missing button stands at the tale's dark heart. A tall black man and his fair daughter keep a mansion in a walled park. Eight tailors before Solario could not sew on that single button. A hideous old woman visits him, and a jolly mule driver sings. The quest leads to Alb the Unicorn, whose hair sews the button fast. The second night gives Alb his own story with a princess.
60967-a-change-in-the-cabinet:
H Belloc wrote A Change in the Cabinet, first issued by Methuen and Company in London in nineteen oh nine. A saw heads the book, Strive, strive, howeer we strive, youth declines at fifty five. Belloc gave the book to Miss Alice Beardsley. Sir T Charles Repton is the chief figure. He is Warden of the Court of Dowry, a post that carried Cabinet rank.

Chapter one opens with Repton at breakfast in a large house overlooking Hyde Park from the north. The time is March nineteen fifteen in the telling. Repton sat for Pailton in Parliament, after earlier seats in Merionethshire, Kirkby, Bruton, and Dorset. His constrained, cold manner had hurt him with voters, the teller notes. It was not his first office, but he had never stood so high in the councils of the nation. A tale of politics, place, and age follows in Belloc crisp, comic prose.
61072-our-street:
Our Street is a book of sketches by Thackeray, writing under a pen name. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1848. The narrator observes his street from a little nook in it. A fellow lodger and friend joins him in cynical watching. The street presents a strange motley scene, he writes. We are in a state of transition, he observes. They are not yet in the town and have left the country. He took rooms at number seventeen Waddilove Street years before.

He has never moved, yet finds himself at number forty six Pocklington Gardens. New stucco and Doric porticoes absorb the old district, he says. Rents rise from fifteen to eighteen shillings with the new name. A plate calls one neighbour the siren of our street. Thackeray sketches a London street being genteelly rebuilt.
61097-the-frozen-planet:
The Frozen Planet is a science fiction story by Keith Laumer, taken from Worlds of If for September 1961. It is one of his Retief tales, about a diplomat of the space age. The story opens with an unusual briefing. Magnan tells Retief that an officer of his rank is seldom assigned to courier duty, but this mission is unusual.

Four planets called Jorgensen's Worlds lie deep in a sector where the alien Soetti have been pushing forward. The worlds are of no importance in themselves. But the Soetti, meeting no resistance so far, mean to seize them by force. That is open aggression on Terrestrial-held ground, Magnan stresses. A show of resistance is needed at this point. Retief, relaxed and silent over his cigar, is sent as courier with secret plans, including the Soetti war plan in detail and a battle plan for the local people.
61203-baum-s-complete-stamp-dealers-dire:
Baum's Complete Stamp Dealers Directory is a trade list compiled and published by Baum, Norris and Company. It was printed at Syracuse, New York, in 1873. Its title promises a complete list of dealers in stamps. All dealers in the United States are covered, it claims. The principal dealers of Europe are included as well. A list of philatelic publications is added at the back. A preface explains that many directories had been commenced before. None had ever been published, the compilers say.

Great care was taken to procure every prominent dealer's address. Few have been omitted, the preface holds, though perfection is impossible. Dealers are constantly starting and retiring, it notes. Names marked with a star are explained in a key. The young compiler Frank Baum later wrote the Oz books. This directory shows his start in the stamp trade.
61919-dead-man-s-planet:
Dead Man's Planet, a novelette by Winterbotham printed in Planet Stories in the fall of nineteen forty-one, begins with a landing. Mick Conner brings his space freighter down with a gentle bump on a shapeless mass of rock and iron floating between Mars and Jupiter. The asteroid measures scarcely ten miles thick, and Mick calls the landing a life-saver as he seals his fur-lined suit.

Alf Rankin calls up from the charting room with a surprise. The rock is not barren, since stuff grows on it. Mick stays cool, citing moss on Eros and the many plant kinds on Juno. The story's blurb promises the real marvel: for unmarked ages, a dead man kept ghostly vigil on that frozen asteroid.
62374-the-story-of-the-alphabet:
Otto Ege of the Cleveland School of Art told the story of the alphabet in a book printed at Baltimore in 1921. A verse thanks old Cadmus, who made us his debtors by inventing capital letters one day. A chart shows various alphabets in the fuller illustrated edition. Ege asks if the reader knows his ABCs and has ever questioned their origin.

Each letter character has a history and a reason for its present form, he says. Our passage from barbarism to civilization can be credited to the alphabet, he argues. Folk nearer its birth held its invention a wonder, before long use dulled the marvel. Ege traces signs from early marks to modern letters for students of art and print.
62600-the-russian-ballet:
A E Johnson wrote The Russian Ballet, a book put out at Boston and New York in 1913. Rene Bull drew the plates that fill the book. Johnson calls the book a keepsake of shows that had thrilled crowds in four lands. He first sketches the long past of dance as an art.

Each famed dance work then gets its own part, told in short form. Petrouchka, Thamar, and the tale of Scheherazade all appear. The Firebird, the Rite of Spring, and Swan Lake close the list of works. A last part honors Anna Pavlova, the star of the troupe. Dance fans of that age could hold the shows in mind long after the stage went dark.
62756-margaret-and-her-friends-or-ten-co:
Margaret and Her Friends records ten conversations with Margaret Fuller on the mythology of the Greeks and its life in art. The talks were held at a Boston house beginning March 1, 1841, the title page says. Caroline Healey reported them, and the book was issued at Boston in 1895. A preface and a list of the members of the class stand at the front.

The contents open with a general statement of mythology, continued in the second talk with Emerson present. A story from Novalis and Apollo fill the third. Minerva and the serpent, then Venus and Psyche with Emerson present again, follow in the heads. Fuller's Boston conversations for women were a famous seed bed of American thought. These pages keep the talk of that circle, half a century on, for readers who never sat in the room.
63049-up-in-the-garret:
Up in the Garret is a children's story by Robin Ranger. Carlton and Porter issued it in 1862 for the Sunday school trade. The scene is the large house of a Mr. Bondy, set on a knoll. Grass, flowers, and fruit trees surround it. The narrator insists the garret, not the house, is the story's true stage. He teases the reader who thinks rats and mice make it a poor subject.

Bondy's garret is large, with four small windows. Old bedsteads and chairs wait there to be mended. Trunks, carpet bags, and rolls of spare carpet fill the floor. Stoves stand put away out of sight. Six chapters move from how the garret looked to coming down from it. The little Bondies and a swallow story fill the middle. Fine times upstairs is the promise the book keeps.
63107-mrs-dalloway-in-bond-street:
Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street is a short story by Virginia Woolf, printed in The Dial, volume seventy five, in 1923. Clarissa Dalloway steps out on a June morning in Westminster to buy gloves herself, while Big Ben strikes eleven above the traffic.

In a few pages Woolf braids street sights with floods of memory: a girlhood home, old friends, a dead young soldier, and the weight of other people's pain. Hugh Whitbread bows by the china shop, and the errand turns into a whole life. The story became the seed of her novel Mrs Dalloway two years later.
63550-the-art-of-ballet:
The Art of Ballet is a history of ballet by Mark Perugini, first printed at London in 1915. A photograph of Adolph Bolm in Carnival stands at the front. Perugini splits his history into eras, and the first book runs from an overture on the art itself through Egypt, Greece, and Rome.

Chapters treat mime and pantomime, the church's thunder and compliance, and a banquet ball of 1489. The Ballet Comique de la Reine of 1581 and Arbeau's dance book of 1588 get their own studies. The first era closes at the turning point: Louis the Sun King and his academy of dancing, from 1651 to 1675. Stars, theatres of the fair, and great dancers fill the second era.
63568-buffalo-bill-s-best-bet:
Buffalo Bill's Best Bet, or A Sure Thing Well Won, is a dime novel by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham, the best known writer of Buffalo Bill tales. The Project Gutenberg text follows the issue of Street and Smith of New York, with copyright in 1914. The book opens with a warm sketch of William Cody himself.

That sketch recalls the Rose Street office where Ingraham, Ned Buntline, and Josh Billings met with the publisher. The tale then runs through twenty-nine short chapters. Heads promise a bet, a double reward, an ambush, and a foe's gratitude. Parson Bristow holds trumps in one chapter. Mary Hale stands at the heart of a woman in another. The plot mixes scouts, outlaws, and red and white chiefs in the usual border style.
6379-the-net:
Rex Beach, author of The Spoilers and The Barrier, opens The Net with a train from Palermo, late, its long shadowy fingers reaching down as passengers wait. A confession and a promise, a golden girl, and a feast at Terranova follow, with what waited at the roadside, a new resolve, and a search beginning. Old trails, one who knows, Myra Nell Warren, and a kidnapping lead to La Mafia, the blood of ancestors, and the net tightening.

A later talk dismisses duels at dawn with shotguns of scrap iron, glad the war is over and such fashions past. It turns to antiques, where Jean Lafitte's original sword has just been sold, though good stuff pays poorly. Beach writes a Sicilian American tale of crime, honour, and quest, where a train delay opens a net that tightens chapter by chapter toward trial, verdict, and appeal.
63828-the-burnt-planet:
William Brittain wrote The Burnt Planet, a tale from Planet Stories in winter 1948. A front note sets the grim theme in one breath. Mad with despair, the folk fought back from the ruins. The foe should not have a world its own folk had destroyed, the note says. Rain and dusk open the tale.

A crew unloads a great silver space ship by a broad river. Stark ruins sprawl a mile off across flat land. In a metal hut the commander checks his clock with nerves. His star man smiles and says the scouts will be fine. No life but small beasts that fled has been seen. The commander feels death in the ruins and fears he sent too weak a party. The tale turns on that dread.
64125-joe-leslie-s-wife-or-a-skeleton-in:
Joe Leslie's Wife, or A Skeleton in the Closet, is a tale of crime and search by Alexander Robertson, a man of the heal craft. Its host print came from a Chicago house on a famed ave of that town. The same hand's past tales are list on the title leaf, with names of gold make, sweet hearts, smuggle ghosts, and froze hearts. The list of parts runs to four and twenty.

The tale opens in the dim room of a New York man of search. A small clock in that room points to the hour of four when a knock comes at the door. The man of the room sits lone, his feet high on the desk, his thoughts far off.
64171-on-board-the-rocket:
Robert Adams wrote this account of his own voyages, copyrighted by him in 1879. Lothrop published it at Boston, with a motto from The Merchant of Venice: ships are but boards, sailors but men. His preface states that all the incidents are facts from his own experience, names altered only to spare the living and the dead.

Adams issues the book not as literature but as a needed exposure of abuses on shipboard, too common and too little known. He points to his own methods of discipline as promoting the merchant marine. The contents follow the Rocket out through gales, doldrums, and sharks. Then comes the Dublin to Gibraltar and the Mediterranean, with flogging, brass knuckles, and three kinds of discipline weighed. Later voyages reach Java, Singapore, and Penang, with three months' extra pay in the East Indies, near wreck, and Padang thieves.
64480-amour-amour-dear-planet:
Amour, Amour, Dear Planet is a science fiction tale by Mark Clutter. It ran in Planet Stories in March of the year 1953. A blurb tells of anti pleasure Mohcans who seek a new, sinless world. They depend on their hostage, Spacecaptain Jan Obrien, to find it. Obrien, the blurb adds, is an amorous imp from way back.

Obrien comes home drunk to a Terra wrecked by its worst war. Ten years without Earth liquor have left him unfit to fly an aircar. All the same he whizzes down a Rocky Mountain canyon at dawn. A young woman in a sheer evening gown begs him to slow down. He had started the night in a Chicago nightclub in the tale.
645-the-figure-in-the-carpet:
Henry James writes of a writer's secret in this short novel, published in 1916 in Martin Secker's edition. A young critic, asked to write on Hugh Vereker's new novel for The Middle, learns that Vereker's work holds a hidden figure in the carpet, a pattern no reader has yet found. George Corvick, breathless and worried, sets the quest in motion.

James writes with urbane, teasing prose, letting the search pass from critic to friend to widow without ever naming the secret. The tale turns on whether art can be solved like a riddle. It endures as a classic James puzzle, where meaning hides in plain sight and escapes every seeker.
64873-ice-planet:
Ice Planet is a science fiction story by Carl Selwyn. It appeared in Comet magazine in May 1941. A head line shows Neptune circling below like a green light bulb. Bill Ricker lounges in a red leather chair as the story opens. He peers from the port of a sleek space ship. If it is going to happen, it has got to be quick, he thinks. His own reflection and the pale green globe are all he sees. The great planet hangs like a ghostly emerald in the void.

Five passengers ride in twelve seats on that ship. A whiskery old fellow asks if Neptune is not pretty. Further down sits a tubercular looking Martian in the cabin. A fat man chewing a dead cigar sits handcuffed to a woman. She is beautiful and dangerous as orchids, Ricker thinks. Selwyn sets a trap among the stars near Neptune.
65076-pastorals-of-dorset:
Pastorals of Dorset, by Francis, writing as Mrs Francis Blundell, is a tale set. Longmans issued this new impression in 1915 at London and New York. Some tales first ran in the Cornhill, Longman Magazine, Temple Bar, and Punch. Shepherd Robbins leads, with Farmer Joyce climbing to his sheep in smock frock.

Joyce at seventy still works a hard day with the best of his juniors. Private Griggs, Up at the Lotments, and The Only Soldier follow in the set. A rustic argus, the rosy plate, and Becky and Bithey fill the middle. Johnny at Shroton Fair and how Granfer volunteered close eleven tales. Dorset dialect and farm folk fill these village pastorals.
65343-the-ambassador-s-pet:
Alexander Blade wrote The Ambassador’s Pet, a short science fiction tale. It ran in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in October nineteen hundred fifty seven. Captain Johnny Martin flies the spaceship 13-XV-1 for Space Service. His sealed orders send him far from Earth on short notice.

Martin must fetch an envoy from Aldebaran VII and bring him to Earth for talks. Peace between Earth and that world hangs by a thread. The envoy plans to bring a pet along for the trip. Martin may not land on the planet at all. A side ship must hand the pair over in space. The pet, and the care it needs, drive the strain of the run.
65520-the-sunny-side-of-the-street:
The Sunny Side of the Street is a jest book by Marshall Wilder, out in nineteen five. Wilder was known past a past book on the folk he has smiled with. Plates of text draws fill this book. It is writ with love to his sire. Parts treat fun and jest men, grave men of sunny mood, and days at the chiefs house and near it.

Heads tell of the force of a joke, of kings and their joke men, and of jest ways in far lands. A part on tale craft weighs the slow hand, the great chiefs tales, and three famed jest pens of the age. Stage mens jokes, a sunny old city, and the press take heads. A part past the chiefs house tells of a guess made to a war man who rose to that post.
65550-the-mosquito-fleet:
The Mosquito Fleet is a war history of small torpedo boats by Bern Keating. A school book house print kept the work in reach of the young. Rights date the text to the year nineteen sixty three. The gift page names two boat chiefs who died in the great war.

Parts first sort fact from myth on the first of these swift small craft. Then come the grind at Guadalcanal and blows at twin gates of a strait. The war in Europe seas and far isle seas fill the back of the book. Photos from the navy dress the tale of night runs and gun fights. Small crews in wood hulls earn a proud page in the sea war.
65726-day-of-the-comet:
Ivar Jorgensen wrote Day of the Comet, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in October 1956. The premise is blunt: a comet will destroy the earth within days. The magazine's blurb says that with the world ending in hours, petty squabbles stop mattering, and only time and regret remain.

The announcement reaches Frank and Dee Allison in the middle of their bitterest quarrel. Dee has just said she never knew she could hate a person as she hates him. Then the radio music cuts off, and a calm announcer states that the earth is doomed. The end is set for Sunday afternoon, after days of storms and tidal disasters. Frank calls it a gag; Dee knows the commentator would join no hoax. The story watches a marriage under the shadow of the end.
65978-champions-of-the-fleet:
Edward Fraser wrote this naval history for John Lane, who printed it at London and New York in 1908. Champions of the Fleet bears the subhead: captains and men-of-war, and days that helped to make the empire. Nineteen plates fill the book.

A plate sets the Victory and the Dreadnought side by side, to one scale, with a submarine by the old ship. Our Dreadnoughts, their name and battle record, open the text. Kent claims the first blow in chapter two. What the navy did for Clive, in the days of the Black Hole, follows. Boscawen's taking of the Téméraire and Hawke's great prize fill the middle. The Victory's building at Chatham gets a chapter of love and fact.
66065-doily-bouquet:
Doily Bouquet is Star Book number 71, a crochet pattern booklet put out by the American Thread Company under a 1950 copyright. It sold for ten cents and was printed in the United States. Four doily designs share two basic centers.

The designs are the Grape Doily, the Violet Doily, the Butterfly Doily, and the Holly Doily. The front calls the plan the very newest, the very smartest scheme for delightful table settings. A set of doilies with the same centers in different gay flower borders adds a decorator touch to a luncheon table. All four designs fit either of the two basic centers. A table ensemble note bids the maker work the other doilies for a service of eight, in white and bright flower colors. Craft fans get mid century table lace.
66091-eunice-and-cricket:
Eunice and Cricket, by Elizabeth Westyn Timlow, copyright 1897 from Estes and Lauriat of Boston, is a story for girls and a sequel to her Cricket books. Harriet Richards drew the pictures. The dedication runs to Elma and Sylvia, and the goat, and the goat earns his place in chapter sixteen.

The book opens with Eunice and Cricket learning a new camera, posing small sisters and the family goat Johnnie on the doorsteps. Chapters bring a party, a quarantine, a lost baby scare, a diamond ring, and school theatricals. Timlow writes the cheerful, busy world of well loved children at home.
66125-impromptu-or-how-to-think-on-your-:
Grenville Kleiser wrote Impromptu, or How to Think on Your Feet, issued in New York and London by Funk and Wagnalls Company in nineteen ten. It was printed for the exclusive use of his mail course students. An essay on the study of forensic eloquence by Isaac Grant Thompson closes the book. A letter to the student states the method. Three short rules head it: think clearly, express yourself clearly, be yourself.

In hundreds of instances the results of this simple exercise have been little less than wonderful, Kleiser claims. Daily practise in impromptu speaking is the whole prescription, he says. The book lists subjects and gives specimen one minute speeches. Lincoln as a speaker, salesmanship, Providence, Bismarck, and George Washington stand among them. A dedication, government by the people, brevity, and votes for women follow. Speakers get a drill book for quick thinking on their feet.
66271-bulkies-sweaters-to-knit-and-croch:
Bulkies: Sweaters to Knit and Crochet is a pattern booklet priced at thirty-five cents. It is Book Number 006 in its line, with Play Time as its cover name. The patterns call for American Thread yarns, Dawn Knitting Worsted or Dawn Sayelle.

The first pattern is a boy's hooded jacket for sizes seven, eight, ten, and twelve. It takes seven or eight four-ounce skeins, size ten needles, and a size G crochet hook. A separating zipper, fourteen to sixteen inches long, closes the front. The gauge is set at four stitches to the inch and six rows to the inch.
