Full directions shape the back from the hem up, then cut the raglan armhole by steady decreases. Chest sizes and back lengths are given for each size.
66588-a-man-sized-pet:
A Man-Sized Pet, a western tale by Tuttle, opens round a rough pine table in a cabin on Sleeping Creek. Three men play pitch by the light of a smoky kerosene lamp. Magpie Simpkins, tall and thin with a scholar face and a walrus moustache, peers at his cards. He wears the only pair of glasses on Sleeping Creek, bought in Missoula.

Tellurium Woods, fat and bald with a rich brown beard, sits as the second of the trio. Bantie Weyman makes the third man at the table that night. The tale builds its humour from such outsized frontier types in close quarters. Tuttle wrote many tales of Magpie and his crew for magazine readers of the West. A pet of man size, as the title teases, drives the fun of the plot.
66590-problem-planet:
Russ Winterbotham wrote Problem Planet, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in June 1955. The narrator is a space pilot of twenty-four. Senator Clive Littlebrook, eleven years older and brilliant to the point of stupidity, is his passenger. Their ship, bound for a committee meeting on Arcturus Three, meets the second planet of an unimportant sun in hyperspace. The pilot must dump the fuel to dodge a collision.

Marooned on a lonely world they thought uninhabited, the two men face years before any message could bring rescue. The senator curses the pilot for three hours, then turns philosophical. The magazine's tag line promises the turn: a spacewreck brings complications not in the rule book. Survival is a basic instinct, but to some men, so is politics. Winterbotham builds a two-man castaway tale in which rank and argument matter as much as air and food.
6683-the-little-nugget:
P. G. Wodehouse opens at the Hotel Guelph in London, where Mrs. Elmer Ford of New York sits restless in a fine suite one January afternoon. The hotel has housed her well, fed her well, and set servants to guess her needs, yet she fumes with impatience. Philosophers, Wodehouse jokes, might ponder the limits of human effort.

The little nugget himself, a boy prized by several parties, soon draws plots, kidnappers, and a fateful phone call. Wodehouse keeps the farce light, with a future Mr. Peter Burns in the wings. The Little Nugget is a gay, clever comedy of a rich boy, bold schemers, and a very English sense of fun.
67380-a-lucky-deal-or-the-cutest-boy-in-:
Lucky Deal, or the Cutest Boy in Wall Street, is a dime novel tale. It ran as number one of Fame and Fortune Weekly in 1905. Frank Tousey published that weekly at Union Square in New York. Each issue cost five cents, or two dollars fifty a year by post. A Self Made Man signs as author of the tale of luck.

Chapter one, The Wolf at the Door, opens in the Hazard home. Mrs Hazard gasps that she has been robbed of the rent money. Two fives and five ones had waited in a bureau corner for the agent. Her daughter Annie, fifteen, sits feather stitching an infant's jacket in silk. Rent, theft, and a bright boy's rise drive the weekly's plot.
67842-an-oberland-cha-let:
An Oberland Châlet, by Edith Elmer Wood and published in New York in 1910, recounts a stay in the Swiss Oberland. The book is dedicated to the fellow occupants of the Châlet Edelweiss. A long list of plates sets the scene before the tale starts. Grindelwald and its lower glacier lead that list of views.

Other plates show the Wetterhorn, the Mönch and Jungfrau, the Grimsel Hospice, and the Matterhorn above Zermatt. Mont Blanc, Brienz, Lucerne, and the Saint Gotthard Pass all appear as well. Readers get a house based tour of high Alpine ground. The mix of home life at the châlet and famed peaks gives the book its charm for armchair travellers.
68128-memorials-of-old-dorset:
Memorials of Old Dorset, edited by Thomas Perkins and Herbert Pentin, was published in London in 1907 in the Memorials of the Counties of England set. Perkins, late rector of Turnworth, wrote on Wimborne Minster and Christchurch Priory. The book is dedicated to Lord Eustace Cecil, past president of the county field club, and carries many pictures.

Contents open with Historic Dorset by Perkins himself, then the barrows of Dorset, the Roman occupation, and the churches of the county. A front caption praises the downs above the Channel, where one may walk mile after mile on natural lawn and meet no soul, only birds, scenery, and God. The volume mixes hard archaeology with fond local pride, parish by parish.
68369-illustrated-history-of-the-united-:
The Illustrated History of the United States Mint is a large reference work on American coinage, published in Philadelphia by George G Evans in a new revised edition edited by the publisher. Its title promises a complete description of American coinage from the earliest period to the present time. The processes of melting, refining, assaying, and coining gold and silver are fully described.

Biographical sketches honour the mint's founders and officers. Thomas Jefferson, Alexander Hamilton, and Robert Morris stand among them. John Jay Knox, James P Kimball, and Daniel M Fox represent the later service. A glossary of mint terms serves the beginner. Official tables give the annual products of gold and silver by state and country. Photographic plates reproduce rare American coins, with a price list of their numismatic value. The book is part history, part dealer's catalogue.
68546-the-house-on-henry-street:
The House on Henry Street, by Lillian Wald, tells the story of a settlement house in New York. Henry Holt printed the book in 1915, and this copy is a printing of November 1938. Wald gives the work to the comrades who built the house with her.

The contents open with the East Side two decades back, then the founding of the nursing service. The nurse and the community, children and play, and schooling follow in order. Handicapped children, children who work, and the nation's children each get a chapter. Later parts treat youth, trade unions, weddings, and social halls. A front plate is an etching of the house itself. Wald's own start, told in the text, was a sick woman in a squalid rear tenement who moved her to settle on the East Side.
68898-journey-to-lhasa-and-central-tibet:
Sarat Chandra Das, a Bengali scholar in British service, made two secret journeys into closed Tibet. John Murray printed his Journey to Lhasa at London in 1902. Rockhill, the American scholar of Tibet, edited the book for English readers.

Das was born at Chittagong in 1849, in a Hindu family of the medical caste. He read at Presidency College, Calcutta, and caught the eye of Sir Alfred Croft. In 1874 he took charge of the Bhutia Boarding School at Darjeeling. There he threw himself into the Tibetan tongue and made friends with the Raja of Sikkim's men. From that base he crossed the passes in disguise, a pundit spy with prayer wheel and hidden compass.
69503-looking-toward-sunset:
Looking Toward Sunset is an anthology for older readers compiled by Maria Child. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston; this copy is the twelfth edition. Child drew the pieces from sources old and new, original and selected. A saying of Jean Paul Richter stands at the front. When the sun sets, he wrote, all shadows point toward the morning. Goethe's words on the indestructible soul follow as a second motto.

Child dedicates the book to two honoured friends. Their active usefulness gave beauty and dignity to declining years. Her preface recalls readers who met her Juvenile Miscellany in childhood. Those readers now share her books with their own children. Child, travelling down the hill of life, offers cheer to companions on the way. The anthology means to console rather than instruct.
69547-never-the-twain-shall-meet:
Never the Twain Shall Meet is a South Seas novel by Peter Kyne, published in nineteen twenty three. Grosset and Dunlap issued the New York edition of Kyne's tale that year. Kyne had written Cappy Ricks Retires and Kindred of the Dust before it. Chapter one opens aboard the trading schooner Moorea on a morning at sea.

Tamea, a girl of Riva, sings a song never sung before from the jib's belly. Her chant tells how she left her mother's people in her father's great canoe. She sails to the white man's country, glad and curious at the change. Yet she fears the hearts there may prove as cold as the morning fog. Captain Larrieau hears her and knows his charge is homesick already. He puts the helm down to shake her out of her sad mood.
70067-cheese-and-its-economical-uses-in-:
Cheese and Its Economical Uses in the Diet is a farm guide from the state. Two food staff of the farm branch wrote the guide in 1912. It was put out fresh, with small shifts, in June 1916. Cheese is a chief farm good and a food in most homes, they say.

Folk held that cheese sat hard on the gut and did harm. Tests made by the branch found no truth in that old claim. Cheese was found to be well used by the body in those tests. It stood with the best foods in how full its use was. The guide then gives ways to cook cheese for the home table. The aim is cheap meals where cheese stands in for dear foods.
70077-beyond-the-sunset:
Beyond the Sunset is a frontier novel by Howden Smith, author of The Doom Trail, published by Brentano's in 1923. The narrator is a Jacobite exile whose estates were forfeited for loyalty to the Pretender. In New York he found a wife, Marjory, and a fortune in trade, and settled as sedately as any Dutch burgher.

The first chapter is called I Am Saved from Myself, and it opens in grief. A fever brought north by a Portuguese snow ship killed Marjory within two years of their happiness, and the narrator sits bowed at his counting-room desk while spring sings outside. The contents promise the remedy: a wilderness trail west, scalp-hunters, and the crossing of the great river. The novel is a first-person frontier romance in the old confessional manner.
70377-fifty-years-in-wall-street:
Henry Clews wrote Fifty Years in Wall Street. The Irving Publishing Company of New York issued it in 1908. The book grows from his Twenty-Eight Years in Wall Street. A fresh sketch adds the past twenty-two years. Clews signs himself with a doctor of laws degree. His portrait fronts the volume.

Clews means to shed light on little-known events, his preface says. Wall Street deals and trades fill the record. The state and growth of the country get a money man's view. Fifty years in the great money center shape the whole. Readers keen on old finance get a broker's own memory of panics, booms, and big names. Few trade books span so long a run on the Street.
70459-to-let:
To Let is a book of tales of India by B M Croker, published at Philadelphia by Lippincott in 1906. Eight tales fill the book. Mrs Raymond, The Khitmatgar, and The Dâk Bungalow at Dakor stand in the list. The title tale opens with a quote from Hamlet: List, list, O list. Its teller is a woman who came out to India as a slim young spinster. She went to live with her brother Tom and his wife Aggie. Her mother, with four grown daughters, was not sorry to spare one.

Aggie is the ruling force of the house, trim, orderly, and feverish with energy. Tom, big and fair and easy-going, worships the sole of her small slipper. Croker writes of Anglo-Indian homes, servants, and stations with a fond, sharp eye. Her tales mix comedy with the strange and sad.
70728-tafilet:
Tafilet is a travel narrative by Walter Harris, printed by Blackwood in 1895. Harris, a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, had written on Yemen and Morocco before. His route crossed the Atlas Mountains into the oases of the north west Sahara. Maurice Romberg drew the pictures from the author's sketches and photographs. The book is dedicated to Clements Markham, president of the Society.

Thirteen chapters trace the journey stage by stage. Marakesh opens the account, then the ascent of the Atlas. Berber life in the high valleys gets its own chapter. The road runs through Dads to the arrival at Tafilet. Harris spent time with the Sultan there, a rare chance for a European traveller. The return journey and the accession of a new Sultan of Morocco close the book. An index of 381 pages of text ends the volume.
71301-the-wishing-carpet:
The Wishing Carpet is a novel by Ruth Comfort Mitchell, author of A White Stone and Corduroy. Appleton published the book at New York and London in 1926. Mitchell dedicates the work to her sisters Barbara and Jane. Long chapter heads in the old style sketch each step of the tale.

The heroine, Glenwood Darrow, buys a fine Persian rug that outshines her golden oak chairs. Her mother hunts gentility while Glen dreams over the carpet. A mill town, a young mountaineer, and a suitor named Luke Manders fill the middle. A curse from Granny Mander hangs over the Darrow house. Glen works for a living and refits her rooms to match the rug. Mitchell writes of class pride, first love, and small town pride with a light hand.
72131-fairyland-planet:
John Silletto wrote Fairyland Planet, a science fiction tale in Infinity in October nineteen hundred fifty eight. Richard Kluga drew its plates. One world holds a Daddy, a Mommy, and one hundred thirty seven Kids. All live in joy there till one plain question lands.

Mike-One, thirty eight by Earth count, comes to Daddy’s office. Ice Cream Recess runs, yet his face stays grave and still. His chess friend Adam-Two, just twenty three, wonders much. That wonder has now caught Mike-One in its pull as well. Is there really a Santa Claus, he blurts out at last. Daddy’s grin froze where it sat on his face, he owns. Twenty years he had waited for some Kid to ask it. The whole Fairyland plan could burst on his reply.
72275-the-sign-of-the-prophet:
The Sign of the Prophet is a historical novel by James Ball Naylor. Saalfield published it at Akron, Ohio, in 1901. Its subtitle calls it a tale of Tecumseh and Tippecanoe. Naylor dedicates it to Samuel McClure of the Ohio State Journal, who backed his early writing. The first chapter opens on a sultry August morning in 1811. Two men paddle a dugout canoe down the Scioto river.

Columbus now stands near the spot where the scene begins. The water runs clear and green in the shade of overhanging trees. Sun rays turn the slow tide to burnished copper. Wild flowers and singing birds line the shores. The paddlers heed none of it, driving their craft swiftly on. The prophet of the title is Tecumseh's brother, the Shawnee prophet. The road to Tippecanoe runs through the tale.
72926-the-murders-in-praed-street:
Murders in Praed Street is a detective novel by John Rhode, set in a London street of shops. Contents divide the book into two parts, The Crimes and The Criminal, for the reader. Part one runs from The Street and The Herbalist to The Inquest and The Poisoned Pipe Stem. Inspector Whyland, a middle aged poet, a black sailor, and a house in Praed Street fill the chapters.

Part two opens with the entrance of Doctor Priestly, the author reasoning detective, at chapter thirteen. The Morlandson trial, the bone counter, Corfe Castle, and a clay pit follow in that part. A discovery, an invitation, an explanation, and a death chamber close the list of chapters. Rhode wrote many such puzzles of poison and counters, in which a chain of small objects carries the guilt home to the killer at last.
73148-pogo-planet:
Martin Pearson wrote this space tale for Future combined with Science Fiction, where it ran in October 1941. Pearson had earlier written Cosmos Eye and The Unfinished City. His hero is Ajax Calkins, billed as a modest little superman and a shrinking violet of fate.

Ajax flies to Midplanet, a world long known from the pull it exerts on Saturn and Uranus yet never seen by glass. His ship bounces on green soil and lands upside down in a thick swamp. Ajax climbs out among ropes, guns, spare shoes, and cans of food, thrilled to hold a major planet. On this world, the head note says, one had to hop in some way to get anywhere.
73172-the-pardoner-s-wallet:
Samuel McChord Crothers's Pardoner's Wallet was published by Houghton Mifflin in November 1905. A publisher's list of Crothers's earlier books, with prices, fronts the volume: The Endless Life at eighty-five cents, The Gentle Reader at a dollar twenty-five. The essays are dedicated to Katharine, with whom these things have been talked over. The title essay opens with Chaucer's pardoner, wallet stuffed full of pardons, fresh from the court of Rome.

Crothers calls the pardoner an impudent vagabond who lived on the credulity of country people. Yet he admits a wish to see the merry knave come down the road again. Later essays treat unseasonable virtues, an hour with our prejudices, and how to know the fallacies. The difficulties of the peacemakers, a community of humorists, and the cruelty of good people fill the back half. Crothers writes as a gentle essayist, turning old figures to present morals.
74876-lady-lucy-s-secret:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote a tale for young readers, issued by the American Sunday-School Union in 1869. It belongs to a series on the children of Stanton-Corbet, set in the year 1704. The full title adds a second name, The Gold Thimble. Lady Lucy is first seen at her work on a warm August morning.

The narrator dwells on how girls then were trained to sit, stand, and hold themselves. Lucy looks pretty and calm, yet the tale hints she is not to be envied. Aunt Bernard appears in the front picture in shock and anger. The story mixes home life, duty, and a hidden matter kept from view.
75000-folk-tales-from-tibet:
Captain O'Connor, secretary and interpreter to the mission to Lhasa in 1904, collected and translated folk tales from Tibet. His book came out in London in 1906 with pictures by a Tibetan artist and verses from Tibetan love songs. O'Connor spent two years in Tibet, at Gyantse and Lhasa and elsewhere, and made friends in all ranks of life.

He found a wealth of folk lore hid from the outside world. Some tales had come whole from India or China, he notes, and some fine tales could not be printed at all. Patience and growing trust won him the rest. The tales give English readers a rare first hand taste of Tibetan story craft.
75547-beauvallet:
Beauvallet is a historical romance by Georgette Heyer, first published by Heinemann in London in 1929. Heyer sets her tale in the Elizabethan sea war. Its hero is El Beauvallet, the freebooter whom every Spanish admiral dreams of capturing, the mocker of Spain.

The novel opens in mid-battle. The English ship Venture has held off beyond the Spanish guns for an hour, raking the great galleon Santa Maria with her longer-reached cannon. Now she bears down to grapple, and Don Juan de Narvaez rallies his soldiers in the waist for the hand-to-hand fight they welcome. The galleon is riddled and groaning, but Don Juan counts the loss cheap if Beauvallet is taken aboard her. Heyer writes the sea fight with a landsman's relish for rigging, broadsides and boarding, and the swashbuckling never lets up from that first page.
75570-psychology-of-the-stock-market:
Psychology of the Stock Market is a short book by G C Selden, author of Trade Cycles, published in New York in 1912 by the Ticker Publishing Company. Selden argues that the smaller swings in stock prices come less from business facts than from the shifting state of mind of the people trading.

Chapters take up the speculative cycle, inverted reasoning, the mysterious They blamed for market moves, and the habit of confusing the present with the future. Others treat the panic and the boom, scale orders, and the mental attitude of the single trader. Experienced professionals, he notes, already admit that minor fluctuations are chiefly psychological. The book is an early, plain-spoken study of crowd feeling in finance.
76293-the-magnet:
Henry Rowland wrote The Magnet, a romance first printed in serial form as The Pilot-Fish and issued in book form at New York in 1911. Clarence Underwood drew the pictures. The tale opens aboard the schooner yacht Shark, at anchor in Shoal Harbour, Maine. She has served as a floating home for fifteen years under Captain Eliphalet Bell, a retired navy man.

Rowland gives the old yacht a full portrait before the plot stirs. She is square jawed, plain in her gear, and kept clean past all need. The crew is small for her size, and winches do much of the work. From that snug start a sea romance grows, in the mode Rowland's magazine readers knew well.
76919-the-magic-casket:
The Magic Casket is a collection of detective tales by R Austin Freeman, published in London by Hodder and Stoughton. Nine tales are listed, from the title story to Gleanings from the Wreckage. The hero is Doctor Thorndyke, Freeman's forensic detective, whose sharp eyes open the first case. The narrator is his companion, in the usual manner.

Near the King's Road in Chelsea, chance and Thorndyke's observation draw them into the casket affair, the opening states. Other tales turn on an alibi, a stalking horse, and a pathologist to the rescue. Freeman built his fame on sound science in crime stories. Each puzzle here is solved by traces, tests, and close reading of things.
77664-young-man-with-a-trumpet:
Young Man with a Trumpet is a fable by Frank Belknap Long, written for Fantastic Universe. Its editor's note ranks it with Animal Farm and the animal fantasies of Dal Stivens. When Man left Earth forever, the animals still carried on proudly. They knew they could never equal the Great One's shining deeds.

What they missed most of all was music. Animals have an excellent idea of pitch, the tale insists, and can sway to nature's rhythms. So they huddled and asked: why not try? The ass, their leading spirit, stood on his hind legs and brayed tremendously. A bray is not music, the tale rules. The fox and the wart-hog held their ears, and the search for a true musician went on.
78138-pink-grass-planet:
Sam Merwin Jr. wrote this tale of the worlds of space. A note from the man who prints it warns of its sting. A man may grieve his heart out for a lost Eden, the tag line says. But five short years of the folly of men may make that world a dread dream. The tale opens as a starship lands at night. Ricardo Webb steps out on the ramp and takes a deep breath of the air of Earth.

The air is sharp, strange, and yet known to him. In the glow of the field lamps his breath makes a small cloud in the brisk night of November. He swears he will never curse a cold season of Earth once more. Five years in the damp, tepid air of a far world have taught him its worth.
78198-kismet:
Kismet is a play in three acts by Edward Knoblauch. Methuen first published it in London in 1912. Its subtitle calls it an Arabian night. The book is dedicated to the memory of Richard Burton. Without Burton, Knoblauch says, it could never have been written. The cast is large and rich in Eastern titles. Hajj the beggar stands at its head. The Caliph Abdallah and two wazirs drive the plot.

Marsinah, Hajj's daughter, leads the women of the piece. The acts run through a single day of fate. Morning scenes fill the bazaar and the wazir's hall. Afternoon brings the palace and the prison. Evening closes in the harim baths and the streets. Kismet means fate, and fate rules every turn. The play was a stage hit in London and New York.
78890-spanish-bayonet:
Stephen Vincent Benet wrote Spanish Bayonet, published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. George H Doran held the copyright of 1926. Benet dedicated the book, his brightly-painted arrow, to his mother and father. A prelude, The Barbary Ape, opens the tale. Four parts follow: The Pride of the Colonies, The Dazzling Net, The Pit of Oppression, and The Fire on the Beach.

The scene is Port Mahon in Minorca, shortly after Easter in 1769. The crops have failed for the third straight season, and the sweetmeats of Easter Eve are few and poor. Ships wait in the harbor to carry families over the ocean. In the Floridas, under the British flag, a man may claim fifty acres after four years of labor. Sebastian Zafortezas looks down on the town as dancing fills the streets.
79291-the-mysterious-locket:
The Mysterious Locket, a tale by Ruth Lynn, was published at London for young readers. The Religious Tract Society issued it with coloured illustrations in the volume. Lynn also wrote City Sparrows, and Who Cared for Them, the title page notes. A plate cries come to grandad, my beauty, at the front of the book.

No Lifeboat opens the contents as chapter one of the tale. Miss Silexa and the locket set in pearls follow in the chapter list. The desired haven, the mysterious letter, and a light in the tunnel come next. A parable from nature and a shadow on the threshold mark the middle turns. The golden shore and the sainted well close the listed heads in the contents. A seaside orphan tale of faith and a lost treasure fills these pages.
79565-spawn-of-the-comet:
Spawn of the Comet is a science fiction novelette by Otis Adelbert Kline, complete in one issue of a weekly story magazine of September 1930. Its head note gives the menace in one breath. Out of the sky came the living clouds that threatened mankind, it says. They swooped down thirstily to drink the blood of all earth life.

The tale opens with fake news clippings in the manner of its day. A citizen of Tampico was badly hurt by a falling skull, the first headline cries. The skull was believed to be that of a missing airman, one Jackson. It struck the man on the shoulder as he walked the main street, and knocked him down. Broken bones were found beneath the bruise. Near the skull lay the metal frames and broken glass of an airman's goggles.
8155-colonel-thorndyke-s-secret:
Adventure and family inheritance drive G. A. Henty's story, which moves from imperial India to an English country home. A British soldier steals a valuable diamond bracelet from a Hindu idol, and the jewel eventually reaches Colonel Thorndyke. Wounded in service, Thorndyke returns to England. He confides the bracelet's secret to his brother, a country squire, and leaves the treasure for younger Thorndykes, whose adventures carry the tale forward.

Henty, famous for boys' adventure tales, here mixes imperial India with English country life, and a stolen idol's curse with a family inheritance. The publisher's introduction promises a story out of the ordinary, and the plot delivers pursuit, mystery, and danger. For young readers, it is a classic Henty tale of honour, treasure, and adventure.
836-the-phoenix-and-the-carpet:
E. Nesbit wrote this fantasy about children who find a wishing carpet and, rolled inside it, the egg of a phoenix. The phoenix hatches, talks, and joins their travels, while the carpet bears them to magic countries and strange courts. Gifts, wishes, and mishaps follow, as the children's plans go comically wrong.

Nesbit writes with humour and warmth, letting the children argue, boast, and make amends. The phoenix, vain and kind by turns, steals many scenes. The book, dedicated to Hubert Griffith, is a beloved sequel to Five Children and It, and a classic of Edwardian children's fantasy.
837-the-story-of-the-amulet:
E. Nesbit wrote this sequel to Five Children and It, in which the children find half of a magic amulet and seek its other half through time. The Psammead, the sand-fairy, guides them to ancient Egypt, Babylon, and Atlantis, and to a queen who visits London and to Julius Caesar's Britain.

The children learn that the amulet's power brings peril as well as wonder, and that history is full of real people, not just pictures. Nesbit blends time travel with humour and heart, and the tale ends with the amulet made whole. The book is a classic of children's fantasy, rich in past worlds and in family fun.
8954-lady-audley-s-secret:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon opens Lady Audley's Secret with Lucy, Lady Audley, and the approach to Audley Court through a hollow rich with fine old timber and luxuriant pastures. An avenue of limes, bordered by meadows where cattle look inquisitively over high hedges, leads to an old arch and a clock tower with a stupid. Bewildering clock that has only one hand and jumps straight from hour to hour, always in extremes. Through the arch lie the gardens, with a smooth lawn before the house.

Beneath that pretty surface sits the sensation novel's famous secret: Lady Audley's past, her hidden husband, and the nephew who investigates her. Braddon's 1862 bestseller made bigamy, madness, and murder drawing-room topics, and it founded the sensation genre. Readers still enjoy its pace, its villain-heroine, and its portrait of a Victorian household where beauty and respectability hide a desperate past.
9398-gloria-and-treeless-street:
Annie Hamilton Donnell wrote Gloria and Treeless Street in 1910, a short novel of youth, wealth, and a change of heart. Gloria, rich and idle at seventeen, watches life from a wide porch on a treeless street. Across the way, a small, neat girl goes out each day with a bag, on some errand Gloria cannot guess. Curiosity soon pulls Gloria out of her own ease.

Gloria sets out to learn where the girl goes, and what work fills her days. The search leads her past her guardians, Aunt Em and Uncle Em, toward a wider view of need and use. Donnell keeps the tone light but the point firm: comfort means little till it is shared. A reader gets a sweet, old-style tale of a girl who grows up by looking outward.
9780-fair-margaret:
H. Rider Haggard, famed for King Solomon's Mines and She, wrote Fair Margaret in 1907, a romance of Tudor England and Spain. Peter meets a Spaniard, gathers violets, and loves Margaret, while John Castell guards a secret. Chapters follow news from Spain, a snare, a chase, and a meeting on the sea. Father Henriques, Inez and her garden, and the Holy Hermandad darken the plot.

Later chapters bring Isabella of Spain, the doom of John Castell, and a falcon's stoop, till the Margaret wins out to sea. Haggard writes with swift, adventurous verve. A reader gets a swashbuckling historical romance, rich in ships, plots, and star-crossed love.
9872-the-great-secret:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Secret, a spy romance of rooms, raids, and international plots. Chapters open in room 317, with a midnight raid, Miss Van Hoyt, and a match at Lord's. Mr. Guest, a tête-à-tête dinner, and Wortley Foote the spy follow. A legacy of danger, gathering jackals, and a dying man deepen the case.

Later chapters bring a cable from Europe, double dealing, and a change of nationality, with a waiters' union and an enemy camp. A reunion of hearts closes the chase. A reader gets a brisk Oppenheim thriller, full of spies, legacies, and a secret worth killing for.
a-house-to-let:
Charles Dickens, Wilkie Collins, Elizabeth Gaskell, and Adelaide Ann Procter share the writing of this Christmas book, as the title page states. An elderly lady, Sophonisba — Sophy — has moved to London for her health, and the empty house across the way will not leave her mind. It is to let, yet never let, and strange signs appear in its windows.

Her servant Trottle investigates, and the tales told along the way — a Manchester marriage, going into society, three evenings in the house — fill in the house's sad history. Trottle's report and the final section, Let at Last, untie the knot. The pieces differ in tone, and the frame holds them together neatly.
a-perilous-secret: Charles Reade builds this melodrama around two children, one poor and one rich, and the two fathers whose lives entwine them. The chapter titles trace the arc: a clandestine marriage, a secret in danger, lovers parted and quarrelling, a woman outwitting two men, calamity, burial alive, and retribution. Through sharp practice and a serpent let loose, the secret threatens everyone who guards or pursues it.
a-spray-of-kentucky-pine-placed-at-the-f: George Douglass Sherley lays a spray of Kentucky pine at the feet of James Whitcomb Riley in this tribute. Printed at Lexington in a second edition in 1916, it honours the dead poet. The inscription is two-fold: reverently to the Indiana-born, world-wide poet, and lovingly to the author's mother on her eighty-fifth birthday. A prelude recalls a reading tour over more than half the republic, taking in Canada's finest provinces, made with Riley years before.
a-study-in-scarlet:
Arthur Conan Doyle's novel introduces Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson. Part One, told as Watson's reminiscences, opens with the wounded army doctor back from Afghanistan and looking for lodgings in London. He is introduced to Holmes, who is beating corpses in a hospital laboratory and has just found a test for blood. The contents name the early chapters plainly, from Mr. Sherlock Holmes through The Science of Deduction to a murder in Lauriston Gardens.

A man is found dead in an empty house, with the word RACHE written in blood and no wound to explain the death. Scotland Yard detectives Gregson and Lestrade compete while Holmes reads the scene. Part Two, The Country of the Saints, jumps to a Mormon pioneer story in Utah that supplies the motive, before Watson resumes for the conclusion.
at-the-sign-of-the-cat-and-racket:
Honore de Balzac opens At the Sign of the Cat and Racket halfway down the Rue Saint-Denis. Clara Bell translated the tale. Its old draper's house has a timbered front tracing Xs and Vs like hieroglyphics. The draper Guillaume guards his shop, his apprentice Theodore de Sommervieux, and his daughter Augustine with equal suspicion. The painter Theodore falls for the girl in the window.

Their marriage joins art to trade and tests both: Augustine's father cries that they wish to kill his daughter when the couple's worlds collide. Balzac placed this tale first in his Comedie humaine's private-life scenes in later editions. Its shop talk, dowries, and quiet marital tragedy announce the whole vast design in miniature.
avat-ras-four-lectures-delivered-at-the-:
Annie Besant delivered these four lectures at the twenty-fourth anniversary meeting of the Theosophical Society at Adyar, Madras, in December 1899. The English edition followed from the Theosophical Publishing Society in 1900. Besant opens by calling her hearers brothers, gathered to study the fundamental truths of all religions. Her subject is the avatara: a divine descent into human form.

Lecture one asks what an avatara is; lecture two treats the source of avataras and the need for them. Special avataras fill the third, and Shri Krishna the fourth. Besant reads the Puranas as facts of a higher plane described in lower-plane terms, warning that separateness itself is illusion born of limited faculties. The lectures present Hindu doctrine through Theosophy's lens of planes, cycles, and hidden unity.
bartleby-the-scrivener-a-story-of-wall-s:
Herman Melville published this tale of Wall Street as a story of a law-copyist unlike any other. Its narrator, an elderly lawyer, waives the biographies of all scriveners he has known for a few passages in the life of Bartleby, the strangest of them. Of Bartleby, he warns, no materials exist for a full biography; it is an irreparable loss to literature.

Bartleby copies steadily, then begins to refuse: he would prefer not to. Charity curdles as the lawyer watches pity turn, past a certain point of hopeless misery, into repulsion. Melville anatomises that turn without excusing it, in prose of terrible calm. The office on Wall Street empties around one motionless man, and the story closes over the dead-letter office rumour that explains, and does not explain, him.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-02-jewis:
John Lord devotes the second volume of his Beacon Lights lectures to Jewish heroes and prophets. Abraham leads, under the heading Religious Faith. His contents read like a sermon outline: the call of Abram, his migrations, Melchizedek, and the covenant. Last comes the sacrifice of Isaac, with the hard question faced squarely. Had Abram a right to sacrifice his son?

Prophets and kings follow in order, Elijah among them in the ninth century before Christ. Evil days fell on Israel after Solomon's death: the country rent by division, disorder, and civil war, ten tribes gone. Lord treats the Preacher of Ecclesiastes with sympathy, sustained at last by the holy fear that is the beginning of wisdom. The volume is Bible history retold as character study for general readers.
britannica-1911-aali-mehemet:
Mehemet Aali Pasha receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Aali, born at Constantinople in 1815, rose through the Turkish diplomatic service: embassy secretary at Vienna, minister in London, then foreign minister under Reshid Pasha. Grand vizier in 1852, he soon retired.

The Crimean War recalled him to foreign affairs, and he sat for Turkey at Vienna in 1855 and at the Paris congress in 1856. He held the grand vizier's post five times in all. In 1867 he served as regent while the sultan visited the Paris Exhibition. Aali backed Western reforms under two sultans and matched Christian diplomats point for point, the entry holds. He died in Asia Minor in September 1871.
britannica-1911-ackermann-louise-victori:
Louise Victorine Choquet Ackermann (1813-1890) was a French poet born in Paris and educated by her father in the philosophy of the Encyclopaedists. She went to Berlin to study German and there married Paul Ackermann, an Alsatian philologist, in 1843. His death after little more than two happy years sent her to Nice to live with a sister. Early verse tales appeared in 1855 and 1862.

Reputation rests on sterner work. Her Poesies of 1874 are sombre and powerful verse expressing revolt against human suffering, praised for vigour and form even by critics who deplored their desperate impiety. A prose volume of a solitary's thoughts, with a short autobiography, followed in 1883.
britannica-1911-afranius-lucius-roman-po: Lucius Afranius was a Roman comic poet who flourished about 94 B.C., as recorded in a brief 1911 Britannica article. His plays dealt chiefly with everyday subjects from Roman middle-class life. He said himself that he borrowed freely from Menander and others. The article describes his style as vigorous and correct, and his moral tone as that of his period. About four hundred lines of his work survive as fragments, printed in Ribbeck's collection of Roman stage poetry.
britannica-1911-albret:
Albret, a lordship in the Landes of France, is traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the seat of a great feudal house. The family of Albret ranked among France's most powerful in the middle ages. Its members fought in the local wars of the age. During the fourteenth century they backed the English cause for a time, then transferred their support to France.

Arnaud Amanieu of Albret helped take Guienne from the English, and his son Charles became constable of France and died at Agincourt in 1415. Alain the Great failed to marry Anne of Brittany and surrendered Nantes to the French in 1486. Royal grants had meanwhile built the house's lands up greatly. John of Albret became king of Navarre by marrying Catherine of Foix. Their granddaughter Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre, married Anthony de Bourbon and became the mother of Henry IV of France.
britannica-1911-alkanet: Alkanet is a plant of the borage family, named Alkanna or Anchusa tinctoria in the entry, and also called orchanet, dyer's bugloss, Spanish bugloss, or bugloss of Languedoc. Its name is a diminutive from the Spanish and Arabic words for henna. The plant grows in the south of France and along the shores of the Levant, the eastern Mediterranean coastlands. Its root yields a fine red colouring matter, and that dye was used to tint tinctures, oils, wines, and varnishes.
britannica-1911-alphabet:
Alphabet, a series of signs each standing for a single sound, is defined in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The word comes from alpha and beta, the Greek names of the first two letters. The ideal alphabet would give one sound to one symbol, and never two sounds to the same symbol. Signs for combined sounds are not needed, the article says. They survive only as handy short forms.

In some writing, such as Sanskrit, those short forms are carried to an extreme. Early printers cast type for Greek contractions, but they have since been dropped. The letter x is a mere short form for ks or gz. No alphabet matches the ideal exactly, nor could one stay exact, since the sounds of most languages keep changing.
britannica-1911-amulet:
Stones, metals, and strips of parchment are the stuff of most amulets, often cut or written with signs and legends. Gems did double duty as jewels and charms, and some herbs and animal parts served the same end. Makers took great care over timing, seeking kind stars and fair influences so the charm kept its strength.

An amulet is just such a charm, worn — usually hung at the neck — to guard its bearer against witchcraft, sickness, and accidents. Belief in hidden evil powers is traced among Eastern peoples from the earliest ages. From there the account weighs Moses' rules on binding the law to hand and forehead. Egyptian practice and later Jewish phylacteries follow, with the question of where such things tip into superstition. Famous healing stones and other authorities end it.
britannica-1911-bagdad-vilayet:
Bagdad, or Baghdad, is a vilayet of Asiatic Turkey between Persia and the Syrian desert, covering most of ancient Babylonia. From the mid-1600s to the mid-1800s it was the Turkish empire's largest province, at times almost an independent principality under its governors.

Since then it has shrunk: a western piece went to a new sanjak in 1857, Mosul was cut away in 1878, and Basra in 1884. It stays the empire's largest province in area, holding some of the most fertile lands of the Tigris and Euphrates valleys. Yet most of it is desert today, since the irrigation canals its fertility depends on were neglected. North of Bagdad lies arid limestone steppe; south, flat flood land of enormous yield wherever water reaches.
britannica-1911-baphomet:
Baphomet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on an imaginary symbol or idol. The Knights Templars were accused of worshipping it in their secret rites. The word is thought to be a corruption of the name Mahomet, the entry says. In several medieval Latin poems that name seems to appear in this very form.

A later writer revived the old charge against the Templars in works on the mystery of Baphomet. In his reading, the word means the baptism of wisdom, or of fire. He linked it to the rites of an early sect and to carving on Templar churches. An elaborate attack on his claims appeared in a French journal in 1819. Its author was a well known defender of the Templars, the article notes.
britannica-1911-barnet:
Barnet is a residential district in Hertfordshire, England, ten miles north of London, served by the Great Northern railway. It falls into three chief parts. Chipping or High Barnet is a market town of 7,876 people in 1901, set on a hill. Its first name recalls the market granted to the abbots of St Albans by Henry II.

Near High Barnet, at a point marked by an obelisk, the decisive battle of 1471 was fought between York and Lancaster, where the earl of Warwick fell. The town stood on the Great North Road as a great coaching station. East Barnet, with an ancient church holding Norman work, and New Barnet complete the group named in the 1911 Britannica entry.
britannica-1911-baronet:
Baronet is the title of a new dignity between barons and knights, created by James I of England. Why that name was chosen is not known for certain, the entry admits. The object was plain, though: to raise money for the crown, professedly to support troops in Ulster. Each grantee paid for thirty men at eight pence a day for three years. The sum came to £1,095 in all.

At its founding in May 1611 the king promised no more than two hundred baronets. Each was to hold £1,000 a year in land, with a grandfather who had borne arms. Those limits soon fell away. The honour carried the prefix Sir and precedence above knights. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, goes on to the Irish baronetage of 1619 and the order's later history and rules.
britannica-1911-basinet:
Basinet, a word that is a diminutive of basin, names a form of helmet described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The original small basinet was a light, open cap with a peaked crown. Soldiers used it as an alternative to the large, heavy heaume, the great helm, and sometimes wore the two together. Its peaked crown, the entry stresses, is the feature by which a basinet can always be recognized in pictures and surviving examples.

Development made the basinet a full war helmet. In the later half of the thirteenth century it grew larger and heavier and replaced the heaume altogether. This form had a vizor, though not always a pivoted one. It joined the gorget, the neck armour, by a camail or mail hood, so head and neck were entirely covered. Spellings varied widely, and the form bassinet was also used for a baby's hooded wicker cradle.
britannica-1911-basset:
Basset, or bassette, was a French card game explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Five persons played it with a pack of fifty-two cards. The entry calls it once very popular but by then practically obsolete, a game whose fashion had passed. It was said to be Venetian in origin. Justiniani, Venice's ambassador, brought it to France in the later seventeenth century.

Play resembled lansquenet in its general shape. A banker faced several punters, the ordinary players betting against the bank. Players won or lost according as the cards turned up matched those already exposed on the table, or failed to match them. That matching mechanism, with money riding on each turn, is the game's whole substance. Readers are sent to lansquenet for more on this family of games.
britannica-1911-bayonet:
Bayonet names a short thrusting weapon fixed to the muzzle or fore-end of a rifle or musket. The word may come from Bayonne in France, where a dagger called the bayonnette was made by the late 1400s. Early bayonets were plain daggers on wooden hafts that plugged into the muzzle.

Plug bayonets stopped a soldier from firing once they were fixed, so ring and socket forms soon replaced them. French fusiliers got plug bayonets in 1671, and English regiments followed within a few years. Later pages compare the lengths of British, German, Russian and Japanese rifles with bayonets fixed, ending with a longer British pattern approved in 1908.
britannica-1911-beet:
Beet is the subject of a plant entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a grown form of Beta vulgaris, a plant found wild on the coasts of Europe, North Africa, and Asia. The plant lives for two years. In the first year it forms a thick fleshy root.

In the second year it sends up a branched leafy stem with small green blooms in clusters. Many kinds are grown for their large roots. They go by names such as mangel wurzel, field beet, and garden beet. The garden kind has long been grown as a salad plant and table food. Sugar beet is treated under the entry on sugar.
britannica-1911-belle-isle-charles-louis:
Charles Louis Auguste Fouquet, comte and later duc de Belle-Isle (1684–1761), was a French soldier and statesman. Grandson of Louis XIV’s disgraced finance chief Nicholas Fouquet, he was born at Villefranche de Rouergue. He joined the army young and held a dragoon regiment of his own by 1708.

Belle-Isle rose through the wars of the Spanish and Polish Successions, though the Bastille and exile checked him for a time under the duke of Bourbon. Cardinal Fleury restored him, and in 1736 the king gave him the government of Metz, Toul and Verdun, which he kept for life. His power in war and policy then stood at its height, and his brother the Chevalier also served as soldier and envoy.
britannica-1911-billet:
Billet covers two word families in this 1911 Britannica entry, one about paper and one about wood. The first billet, from the French for a small note, was an invitation card in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Its special military sense is an order giving a soldier quarters with a named householder. From that order the word slid to mean the quarters themselves. A good billet thus came to mean a comfortable post or job.

William III's saying that every bullet has its billet uses the word for an allotted destination. A voting paper sense appears in 17th-century Scotland, tied to the Act of Billets of 1662. The second billet is a piece of wood cut round for fuel. Its name passed to gold ingots, iron bars, and a heraldic rectangle. In Norman building it names a moulding of small wood-like blocks.
britannica-1911-bion-poet:
Bion was a Greek bucolic, or pastoral, poet, born at Phlossa near Smyrna. He flourished about 100 BC, the 1911 Britannica article holds. Older accounts made him a friend of Theocritus and tutor of Moschus, around 280 BC. That dating is now generally judged wrong, the article says. Stein's metrical study puts Bion in the first half of the 1st century BC. Nothing is known of his life except that he lived in Sicily.

The tale that jealous rivals poisoned him is called a likely invention. His remains show little of Theocritus's vigour and truth to nature, the entry judges. An overdone sentimentality marks them instead. The longest and best piece is the Lament for Adonis. It treats the first day of that god's festival. Editions and translations close the piece, including Andrew Lang's English version of 1889. Oxford's classical series issued a text in 1905.
britannica-1911-bonnet:
Bonnet is a word entry tracing a head covering from a cloth name to many later uses. It comes from Latin bonetum, a kind of stuff, then the cap made of that stuff. Bonnet was the common English word for a soft head covering until the late 1600s, and the sense lives on in Scotland for caps like the glengarry.

On a ship, a bonnet is an extra piece of sail laced to the foot of a sail, though it once meant a piece laced to the top. In the entry's own day the word chiefly named a woman's close-fitting head covering, set apart from a hat by its grip on the head and often by having no brim. The term also spread to guard pieces on engines and safety lamps, and in slang to a gambler's decoy.
britannica-1911-bracket:
Bracket, in building and carpentry, is a projecting piece of wood or metal that holds parts together or carries a shelf. In stone the same feature is called a console. In furniture the word names a small fancy shelf for a wall or corner, made to hold knick-knacks, china, and other small ornaments.

The word's past is odd. It was often linked to brace, a clamp, from the Latin word for arm. But the earliest form, bragget, in 1580, points instead to the French braguette or Spanish bragueta, from the Latin for breeches. That word served both for the front of a pair of breeches and for the building feature. How the sense travelled is not clear, the entry admits, though the supposed link to brace surely helped it along.
britannica-1911-brevet:
Brevet is a short official paper, its name a small form of the French bref, and papal indulgences were among its early uses. By the time of this entry the word clings chiefly to army life. A brevet gives an officer a lasting rank above the one he truly holds in his own corps, as opposed to a local or passing step up.

Rules differ by army. In British service brevet rank starts only above captain, while in the United States army even a first lieutenant may hold one. French use runs apart again: brevete marks a staff officer who has passed staff college, matching the English letters p.s.c. placed after a name. The piece is brief, but it sorts out three national habits in a few lines.
britannica-1911-budget:
A budget is an account of how income and outlay for a set time are to be made to balance. A finance minister draws one up for his state, and smaller bodies use the term by likeness. The word comes from a Gallic term for a sack, by way of a Latin word for a leather bag. The term came into use in England about 1760.

In the United Kingdom the chancellor of the exchequer lays the budget before the House of Commons, as a rule in April. He shows the true results of the past finance year, which now ends on 31 March. He states how far his past guesses held good and what surplus or shortfall arose. He then gives a fresh guess at the yield of taxes in the new year. He also sets out what the state is like to spend.
britannica-1911-cabinet:
Cabinet is a word with two chief senses, traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One sense is a small private room, and the other is a piece of furniture with drawers and shelves. The word is a small form of cabin, so it first meant a small hut or shelter. That first sense is now out of use.

From the use of a room or a case to keep fine prints, pictures, and medals safe, the word came to mean the set of things so kept. The text gives the Cabinet du Roi as a case in point. Louis the Fourteenth had that set of prints made from 1667 to mark the chief acts of his reign. A cabinet edition of a book is then a small, fine form of that book, fit to be kept in such a case.
britannica-1911-capet:
Capet is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Capet is the name of a family that gave France its kings for near nine centuries. Rulers of great fiefs in France also bore the name. The house mixed with other royal houses of Europe. The sense of the name itself is still in dispute. Hugh, elected king of the Franks in 987, first bore it.

The article names Robert the Strong as the true founder of the house. He gained countships from King Charles the Bald. His sons ruled as dukes, and one was chosen king in 887. When the last Carolingian king died in 987, the Franks passed over his brother. They elected Hugh Capet and crowned him at Reims. The direct line then ruled France until 1328. A younger branch, the Valois line, followed it.
britannica-1911-chateau-renault-francois:
François Louis de Rousselet, Marquis de Château-Renault (1637–1716), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French admiral. He was the fourth son of the third marquis. The family was Breton in origin and long settled near Blois. He entered the army in 1658. In 1661 he moved to the navy, which Louis XIV was eager to build up. He was made captain in 1666.

His early service was mostly cruises against the Barbary pirates. He was wounded in action with them. He rose to chef d'escadre in 1673 and to lieutenant general in 1687. When war with England broke out after 1688, he commanded at Brest. He carried the troops and stores sent to aid James II in Ireland. Admiral Herbert watched him, and they fought an indecisive action in Bantry Bay. He later fought under Tourville at Beachy Head in 1690.
britannica-1911-chatelet:
Châtelet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French word for a small defensive building, from the medieval Latin castella. A châtelet guarded an outwork or a gate. Some were very strong and large. It differed from the château in being purely defensive and not a residence. In Paris, before the Revolution, the word named both a building and the jurisdiction seated in it.

The Paris Châtelet had first been a castle defending the approach to the Cité. Tradition traced it to Roman times. Its jurisdiction was the provostship and viscountship of Paris, of feudal origin. Under Saint Louis the provostship became a public office, no longer sold. The provost heard appeals from the city's lesser judges, like a bailli. Under Henry II the court became a presidial court, judging some cases without appeal, while keeping its old name.
britannica-1911-civet:
Civet, or civet-cat, designates the more typical members of the mammalian family Viverridae, and the entry centres on the scent that gives them their name. A deep pouch near the genital organs holds civet, a fatty substance poured in from glands. At first semifluid and yellow, it hardens to a pomade and darkens. Its strong musky odour, properly diluted, gives a floral fragrance that musk cannot match, the entry says.

The African civet runs two to three feet long, stands ten to twelve inches high, and hunts birds and small beasts by night, climbing trees in pursuit. Captive civets are kept only for perfume, scraped from the pouch twice a week, most from the male. The zibeth, a smaller species without the dorsal crest, ranges from Arabia to Malabar and the Indian islands. In the wild it does great damage among poultry and other stock.
britannica-1911-cloquet:
Cloquet is a city of Carlton county, Minnesota, on the St Louis river, 28 miles west by south of Duluth, with 7,031 people in 1910. Foreign-born residents numbered 2,755 in 1905, among them Swedes, Finns, Canadians and Norwegians in large groups. Four railways serve the city, the Northern Pacific, the Great Northern, the Duluth and North-Eastern and, for freight only, the Chicago, Milwaukee and St Paul. The river furnishes good water power for its mills.

Manufactures include lumber, paper, wood pulp, match blocks and boxes, all tied to the northern forests around it. The first mill was built in 1878, and the village was named from the French word claquet, the sound of the mill. That naming tale is given as fact in the entry's short history. Cloquet was incorporated as a village in 1883 and was chartered as a city in 1903.
britannica-1911-collins-william-poet:
William Collins (1721–1759) was an English poet born on 25 December 1721. The entry ranks him with Gray as the greatest English lyrist of his century. His father was a rich hatter and mayor of Chichester. The boy went to Winchester College in January 1733. Whitehead and Joseph Warton were among his school fellows there.

Pope visited the school nine months after Collins came. He set a prize subject for verse, and the entry muses that the boy's face may have caught his eye. Collins printed his first verses in 1734, on the royal nuptials. No copy of that pamphlet survives. A second early poem is lost as well. The heart of the entry is his Odes, twelve in count. They appeared in December 1746. The small book fell flat at first. Yet it won him the praise and friendship of sharp judges.
britannica-1911-coquet:
To coquet is to act the arts of love making, most often from vanity, or to flirt. In a wider sense it means to trifle or dally with a thing. The word comes from a French verb that first meant to strut like a cock bird. That bird struts when it seeks to draw the hens to it. The French noun once served in English for a beau.

The female form, coquette, is now the one form that still survives in common use. It names a woman who feeds her vanity by brief use of her charms. From that use comes the verb form now often spelt with more letters. The word can also serve for a manner or a hat. A group of crested humming birds bears the same name.
britannica-1911-crotchet:
Crotchet, from the French croche, a hook, is properly a small hook. The word names the hook-like bristles of certain sand-burrowing worms. In music a crotchet is a note worth half a minim and twice a quaver. It is drawn as a round black head on a stem without a tail. The French croche, by contrast, names the tailed quaver.

From an old French saying, or from a sense of twist or turn like the word crank, comes the last sense in the entry. A crotchet can mean a whim, a fancy, or a perverse fixed idea. The adjective crotchety, for a fussy and unreasonable person, grows from that sense. One hooked shape thus links worms, music paper, and a bent of mind. The entry keeps all three uses side by side.
britannica-1911-crown-and-coronet:
Crown and coronet name head ornaments worn as signs of honor or rank. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses that a crown first held no royal sense. It began as a wreath of leaves or blooms for game winners. Gold forms later marked brave or useful service in Rome in many types.

A grass crown honored a general who took a city by siege. An oak crown honored a soldier who saved a citizen in battle. Wall and ship forms marked first scaling and sea wins in turn. The entry draws a sharp line between crown and diadem. A diadem was a bound cloth band from the east, not a crown.
britannica-1911-dame-s-violet:
Dame's violet is the English name of Hesperis matronalis, a herbaceous plant of the order Cruciferae, close kin to the wallflower and the stock. It grows on an erect, stout, leafy stem two to three feet high. Its leaves are short-stalked and unevenly toothed. The flowers, white or lilac and three-quarters of an inch across, open above them. Slender pods, pinched in between the seeds, follow the blooms.

The flowers give their scent in the evening, and that habit names the genus, from the Greek word for evening. The plant is native to Europe and temperate Asia. In Britain it is found as an escape from gardens, growing in meadows and plantations. Form, scent, range, and garden origin make up the whole entry. No use of the plant, in medicine or cookery, is recorded in it. The short account stays with what the eye and nose can check.
britannica-1911-ermine-street:
Ermine Street is named by writers from the 11th century onward as one of four “royal roads” in Britain, with Icknield Street, Watling Street, and the Foss Way. Those roads were said to stand apart from all others under the king's special protection. The entry doubts the category itself. The authorities disagree on the roads' exact courses, and no legal practice shows them specially favoured. The set of Four Roads, it judges, is likely a lawyer's or antiquary's invention.

Early charters still prove the roads existed in Saxon and Norman days, naming them as boundaries. Ermine Street matches part of a Roman line north from London through Huntingdon to Lincoln. The entry warns, though, that the Four Roads were not the chief highways of Roman Britain.
britannica-1911-eros-planet: Eros is a minor planet, and the hosted entry is a single short notice rather than a full article. Witt discovered it at Berlin on 14 August 1898. The entry says that, so far as was yet known, it is unique in one respect. Its perihelion, the point of its orbit nearest the sun, lies far within the orbit of Mars. No size, orbit figures, or later observations are given.
britannica-1911-eubulus-poet:
Eubulus was an Athenian poet of the Middle Comedy who flourished about 370 B.C. Some 104 plays are credited to him. Fragments of about fifty survive in Athenaeus. The remains show little interest in politics. He kept mainly to mythological subjects instead. When chance offered, he mocked the swollen style of the tragedians, above all Euripides.

The entry praises his pure language and correct versification. It is a very short notice, closing with a pointer to Kock's Comicorum Atticorum fragmenta of 1884. Nothing is said of his life, family or rivals. The two Eubulus entries stand back to back in the volume, one for the statesman and one for the poet. Only the fragments, gathered by Athenaeus, let this poet be judged at all.
britannica-1911-fleet:
Fleet takes all its meanings from the verb to fleet, from Old English fleotan, to float or flow. The root is Indo-European, seen in Greek words for sailing and Latin for rain. It survives in place names such as Byfleet and Northfleet. It also names the Fleet, a London stream that once ran to the Thames by Fleet Street. From floating comes the word's great use: ships in company, above all warships under one commander.

A fleet's parts sail under their own subordinate officers, and the line between fleet and squadron is often one of name only. Fishing uses the word too, for a company of fishing vessels and for a row of drift-nets tied together. From flowing comes the adjective fleet, swift, and fleeting, for what fades fast like running time. The hosted file goes on to the separate Fleet Prison article after this word study.
britannica-1911-foster-myles-birket:
Myles Birket Foster (1825-1899), English painter, was born at North Shields. At sixteen he entered the workshop of Ebenezer Landells, a wood engraver, and worked six years as an illustrative draughtsman, mainly on landscape. During the next fifteen years he became famous as a prolific and skilled illustrator. About 1861 he gave up illustration for painting. He won wide popularity with his pictures, chiefly water colours, of landscapes and rustic subjects, with figures mainly of children at work and play.

Foster was elected associate of the Royal Society of Painters in Water Colours in 1860 and full member in 1862. His work is remembered for its delicacy and minute finish, and for its dainty, pleasant feeling. The notice is short and stands in a shared file between the entries for Sir Michael Foster and Stephen Collins Foster. Two lives of Birket Foster are named at the end for readers who want the full story.
britannica-1911-fret:
Fret is treated here in two senses. The first comes from the Old English fretan, to devour or gnaw. It covers the slow eating action of chemicals or water, and in figure the chafing of the mind. Linked with it is the fret as a bar across the fingerboard of a banjo or guitar. The bar marks where the fingers stop the strings.

The second fret, of doubtful origin, is a network ornament. Heraldry uses it for an interlaced figure. It is best known as the Greek fret: bands of set lengths laid at right angles on temples and vases. The pattern was born from woven cloth. Egypt used it on tomb ceilings, Rome carved it, and Mexican temples at Mitla carried it. In France the pattern is called the meander. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-fuller-margaret:
Fuller, Margaret (1810–1850), afterwards Marchioness Ossoli, was an American writer born at Cambridgeport, Massachusetts, on the 23rd of May 1810. Her father educated her himself, and she was reading Latin at six years old. From 1840 to 1842 she edited The Dial, the journal of the Transcendentalists, and she held conversation classes. In 1844 she joined the New York Tribune under Horace Greeley as literary critic.

She sailed for Europe in 1846, and in December 1847 she married the Marquis Ossoli in Italy. During the Roman revolution she worked in a hospital in Rome through 1848 and 1849. Returning to America, she was drowned with her husband and son in the wreck of their ship on Fire Island on the 16th of June 1850.
britannica-1911-garnet:
Garnet is the name of a group of closely linked minerals, many used as gem stones, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. The name may come from a Latin word tied to the pulp of the pomegranate in colour, or to its seeds in shape. Old writers grouped garnet with other red stones under names such as anthrax and carbunculus.

The modern carbuncle is a deep red garnet cut with a smooth, rounded top, often hollowed at the back because of its depth of colour. Garnets were used as beads in ancient Egypt and much used by the Romans for cut gems. The article then turns to their makeup, noting that all are a kind of silicate stone with a shared general form, in six main types.
britannica-1911-garret: Garret came from an old French word for a watch tower, tied in root to guard and ward, as the short 1911 Britannica entry explains. In its first sense it named a small look-out turret built on a wall. From that post high on a building, the name slid to a room on the top storey. Such a room takes its sloped ceiling from the roof above it, and the word now lives in that sense alone.
britannica-1911-gatty-margaret:
Margaret Gatty (1809-1873) was an English writer, born at Burnham in Essex in 1809. The 1911 Britannica entry makes her the daughter of the Rev. Alexander Scott, chaplain to Lord Nelson. From age ten she drew and etched at the British Museum print-room. In 1839 she married the Rev. Alfred Gatty, vicar of Ecclesfield near Sheffield.

She is best known as 'Aunt Judy', a pen name taken from her daughter's nickname for her. Her Parables from Nature ran to five volumes between 1855 and 1871, and Aunt Judy's Magazine began in May 1866. The entry praises her sympathy with children and the wholesome cheer of her books. It also lists her life of her father, her book on British seaweeds of 1862, and later works on emblems and sun-dials. She died at Ecclesfield on 4 October 1873.
britannica-1911-gauntlet:
Gauntlet, in the 1911 Britannica, is first a glove, and above all the steel-plated glove of medieval armour. The word is a diminutive of the French gant, glove. Most of the short entry, though, goes on the punishment of running the gauntlet.

To run the gauntlet was to pass between two rows of men who beat the runner with sticks, rope-ends or other weapons. It was once a punishment for military and naval offences, and the Prussian army gave it up under Scharnhorst. North American Indians used it to torture prisoners, the entry adds. The word in this sense is a corruption of gantlope, from Swedish words for a lane and a course. It became familiar in England, the entry says, in the Thirty Years' War.
britannica-1911-geoffrey-plantagenet:
Geoffrey Plantagenet, count of Anjou, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 1113 to 1151. He was the son of Count Fulk the Young and of Eremburge of La Flèche. He was born in August 1113. He was also called le bel, the handsome.

The surname Plantagenet came from a habit of his. He is said to have worn a sprig of broom in his cap. The broom plant in French is genêt. In 1127 he was made a knight. In June 1129 he married Matilda. She was the daughter of Henry the First of England. She was also the widow of the emperor Henry the Fifth. Some months later Geoffrey succeeded his father. His father gave up the countship and went for good to the kingdom of Jerusalem. Geoffrey's years of rule went to two tasks. He subdued the Angevin barons and conquered Normandy.
britannica-1911-geoffrin-marie-therese-r:
Marie Thérèse Rodet Geoffrin, a Frenchwoman who lived from 1699 to 1777, played a noted part in the literary and artistic life of Paris, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica profiles her salon. Born in Paris, she wed Pierre François Geoffrin, a rich maker and officer, in 1713, when she was still in her teens. He died in 1750.

Not till she was near fifty did Madame Geoffrin emerge as a power in Paris society. Taught much by Madame de Tencin, she began about 1748 to gather a circle of artists and men of letters. Each week she gave two dinners, one on Monday for artists and one on Wednesday for the Encyclopaedists and other writers. Guests of note from abroad, Hume and Horace Walpole among them, came to her table. Walpole praised her common sense in his letters, though the entry calls her a small tyrant in her circle.
britannica-1911-gimlet: A gimlet is a tool used to bore small holes. The word comes from an Old French term, most likely a small form of an Old English word for a bore. The tool is made of steel. Its shaft has a hollow side, and a screw at the end does the boring of the wood. A handle of wood is fixed across the shaft at the top. A gimlet is always a small tool. A tool of the same kind at a large size is called an auger.
britannica-1911-givet:
Givet is a town of northern France, in the department of Ardennes, on the Meuse about a mile from the Belgian frontier. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the town 5,110 people in 1906, and the commune 7,468. It was once a fortress of considerable importance.

The town falls into three parts. Charlemont citadel and Grand Givet stand on the left bank, Petit Givet on the right, joined by a stone bridge of five arches. Charles V founded Charlemont in the 16th century on a rock 705 feet high, and Vauban strengthened it; it alone survives of the fortifications, the rest destroyed in 1892. Grand Givet has a church and town-hall built by Vauban and a statue of the composer Mehul. Petit Givet is the working quarter, with tanneries, glue factories, pencils and tobacco-pipes, and the town carries a busy river trade.
britannica-1911-goblet:
Goblet is a large type of drinking vessel, shaped like a cup without handles and set on a stem with a foot. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a very short entry. The piece is a word study as much as a description of the vessel itself. 

The word comes from an old French form, a diminutive of a word for a cup. That French word was itself formed from a low Latin word for a small cup. That Latin word in turn came from the word for a tub or cask. The entry points the reader to the article on drinking vessels for more.
britannica-1911-gorget:
Gorget is an armour article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the collar piece of a suit of armour. The name comes from an Old French word for throat. The term came into use near the year 1480. The piece was most often made of small overlapping rings of plate, fixed to the body armour or to the helmet.

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries men wore it with half armour, with the plain breastplate, and at times with no body armour at all. In those years it slowly became a badge of officers. As such it outlived armour itself. It survived as a small metal plate worn at the front of the collar of a uniform coat, lasting past the Napoleonic wars. In the German army of the article's day such a plate marks the military police.
britannica-1911-graaff-reinet:
Graaff Reinet, a town of South Africa, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies 185 miles by rail north west of Port Elizabeth, at 2,463 feet above the sea. Its count in 1904 was 10,083, of whom 4,055 were whites. The town stands on the banks of the Sunday river, below the Sneeuwberg hills. Its Dutch church, built in stone, seats 1,500 souls.

Graaff Reinet is a busy market for farm goods, famed for mohair, orchards, and vineyards. Cape Dutch settlers founded it in 1786 and named it for the governor of Cape Colony and his wife. In 1795 its burghers rose against the Dutch East India Company and set up a republic. British troops took the Cape before order could be restored by force. A fresh revolt in 1799, led by Marthinus Prinsloo, also failed and ended in trials at Cape Town.
britannica-1911-greenough-james-bradstre:
James Bradstreet Greenough, an American classical scholar who lived from 1833 to 1901, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Portland, Maine, he left Harvard in 1856 and spent a year at its law school. He was called to the bar in Michigan and practised at Marshall till 1865. That year he went back to Harvard as a tutor in Latin.

He rose to assistant professor in 1873 and full professor of Latin in 1883, a post he held till near his death. His study of Latin syntax led to an Analysis of the Latin Subjunctive in 1870. With Joseph Allen he wrote a Latin grammar for schools in 1872, a work of great care. He gave the first Harvard courses in Sanskrit and comparative philology in the 1870s. He also helped found Radcliffe College.
britannica-1911-grivet:
The grivet is a monkey, Cercopithecus sabaeus, belonging to the guenon group and closely allied to the green monkey. It is common throughout equatorial Africa. White fur marks its chin, whiskers and under-parts, along with a broad band across the forehead, while the head and back are olive-green.

That colour pattern is the entry's main means of telling the animal apart from its near relatives. Grivets were very commonly seen in menageries, so captive animals, as much as wild ones in Africa, shaped what European readers knew of the species. The entry is a short one, giving the grivet's scientific name, family group, range, markings and familiarity in collections.
britannica-1911-harte-francis-bret:
Francis Bret Harte is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American writer born in New York in eighteen thirty nine. He went west to California as a teen with his mother. There he worked as a teacher, a miner, a printer, and an editor.

The entry credits him as an early master of the short tale. He ran the first strong magazine of the Pacific coast. His tales of gold camps mixed wit, pathos, and sharp drawn folk. Two famed tales and one famed poem are named in the entry. His work gave the rough new west a voice that the east and Europe prized.
britannica-1911-hugh-capet:
Hugh Capet (about 938-996) was king of France and founder of the Capetian line, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He was the eldest son of Hugh the Great, and when his father died in 956 he succeeded to many fiefs round Paris and Orleans. That made him one of the strongest lords under his cousin, the Frankish king Lothair, who owned him, though grudgingly, as duke of the Franks.

Many counts of northern France did homage to Hugh as their overlord, and Richard I of Normandy was both his vassal and his brother-in-law. His power reached into some districts south of the Loire. He backed his king when Lothair and the emperor Otto II fought over Lorraine. Stung by the king's conduct in making peace in 980, he went to Rome to conclude an alliance with Otto instead.
britannica-1911-hugh-de-puiset:
Hugh de Puiset is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was bishop of Durham from about 1125 to 1195. He was nephew to King Stephen and to Henry of Blois. Henry brought him to England and raised him in rank. He became an officer of the see of Winchester. He later held posts at York as well in church. In 1153 he was chosen bishop of Durham.

That choice faced the ill will of the York chief. Hugh won his blessing by a trip to Rome in person. He took small part in state acts under Henry the Second. He stayed in the north at work on his see. He was present at a crowning in 1170 and was barred. He stayed neutral in the clash of king and Becket. He had to yield three strong towns to the king.
britannica-1911-hughes-john-poet:
John Hughes (1677-1720) was an English poet and writer on many subjects, born at Marlborough in Wiltshire, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. His grandfather had been ejected from the living of Marlborough in 1662 for Nonconformist views. Hughes was educated at a dissenting academy in London, where Isaac Watts was a fellow scholar, and became a clerk in the Ordnance Office.

In 1717 Lord Chancellor Cowper made him secretary to the commissions of the peace. He died on the night his most famed work, The Siege of Damascus, was first played, in February 1720. His poems include pieces in honour of William III and a rendering of part of Lucan. He wrote words for cantatas set by Pepusch and others, added pieces to the Tatler, Spectator, and Guardian, and persuaded Addison to stage Cato.
britannica-1911-jennet:
Jennet is the subject of a short word and horse entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word names a small Spanish horse. In English it is at times used for a mule, the offspring of a female ass and a stallion. The word reached English through French from Spanish.

In Spanish the source word first meant a light horseman who rode with his legs tucked up. That name is traced to a Berber tribe famed for its horsemen. English and French shifted the word from the rider to his horse. In Spain itself that horse sense arose only in modern times, the entry notes. The short text is a neat case of a word on the move.
britannica-1911-king-william-poet:
William King, who lived from 1663 to 1712, was an English poet and wit. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth to a small estate. Westminster school and Christ Church, Oxford, formed his schooling. His first work defended Wycliffe against a French history of heresy. He soon won fame as a comic writer on the Tory side. A ballad on a church dispute shows his manner.
