In 1694 he pleased Princess Anne with a defence of Denmark. That service made him her secretary. He then backed Charles Boyle in the fight over the letters of Phalaris. His account of Bentley's clash with a bookseller drew fire. Bentley struck back, and King answered with satires in dialogue form. In 1700 he mocked the credulity of Hans Sloane in print. The entry shows a pamphlet fighter of the age.
britannica-1911-kuwet:
Kuwet, also spelled Kuweit or Koweit, is a port in Arabia at the north-west angle of the Persian Gulf. It stands about 80 miles due S. of Basra and 60 miles S.W. of the mouth of the Shat el Arab. The town lies on the south side of a bay 20 miles long and 5 miles wide, its mouth guarded by two islands. The bay forms a fine natural harbour, with good anchorage in 4 to 9 fathoms. The town has 15,000 inhabitants.

The land round Kuwet is near desert, so the town lives by the sea and its trade. Its sailors are held the most skilful and trustworthy on the Gulf. As the port nearest to Upper Nejd it takes in rice and piece goods and sends out horses, sheep and wool. In 1899 Sheikh Mubarak placed his interests under British protection. The trade through the port in 1904–1905 was £160,000.
britannica-1911-lansquenet:
Lansquenet carries two senses in the 1911 Britannica. One is the French worn-down form of Landsknecht. That word named the German hired foot-soldier of the 1500s. The other sense is a card game. The game is said to have come into France with those soldiers. The word thus links the gaming table to the camp.

Play uses a pack of 52 cards. The dealer lays two cards face up at his left. One card goes before himself. A fourth card sits in the middle. Other players stake on that middle card within a set limit. Fresh cards are then turned. A card that matches one already shown settles the stakes on it. The banker takes matched stakes and pays the rest. The deal ends when a card matches the dealer's own.
britannica-1911-lettres-de-cachet:
Lettres de cachet were sealed letters that bore the order of the French king. The 1911 Britannica entry defines them as papers signed by the king. A minister signed them too, and the royal seal closed each one. In form they could carry any order at all from the throne. They bound groups to meet or to do a set act at once.

The most famed kind were the penal letters of that name. By them the king jailed a subject with no trial at all. No chance to plead a defence was given to the victim. A man might be sent to a state prison or to exile. He might be shut in a convent, a hospital, or a colony.
britannica-1911-logan-john-poet:
John Logan (1748-1788) was a Scottish poet born at Soutra in Midlothian. His father farmed and held with the Burgher sect. Musselburgh school and Edinburgh University formed the son. Tutor work at Ulbster came in 1768-1769. He left the Secession church and won a preacher's licence in 1770.

South Leith took him as minister in 1771, though ordaining came two years on. Poet Michael Bruce died young, and Logan took his papers to print. The 1770 book of Bruce's poems held work by other hands, unmarked. Doubt on that score has clung to Logan since. Church hymn work filled 1775 to 1781. His talks on the philosophy of history drew crowds at St Mary's Chapel. Own poems came in 1781, with the Ode to the Cuckoo among them. Some had first shown in the Bruce book.
britannica-1911-malplaquet:
Malplaquet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a village of France and its battle. The village lies in the department of the Nord. It stands close to the Belgian frontier, south of Mons. It is famous as the scene of a battle in September 1709. The Allies under Marlborough and Prince Eugene fought there. The French were commanded by Marshal Villars in that fight. The Allies were victorious in the encounter.

The country west and south of Mons is ringed by woods. Only two important gaps pierce that wall of woods. The gap of Jemappes lies to the west. The gap of Aulnois, holding Malplaquet, lies to the south. Villars took up his position in that southern gap. He faced north eastward there at the end of August. The forces in presence were over ninety thousand on each side.
britannica-1911-martineau-harriet:
Harriet Martineau, an English writer who lived from 1802 to 1876, gets a long life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Norwich, where her father made cloth, she came of Huguenot stock and Unitarian faith. She had no sense of taste or smell and grew deaf while young. A stay with an aunt at Bristol gave her happier years.

Her father died in 1826, and the family soon lost all its means. Deafness barred teaching, so she took to writing in earnest. Her Illustrations of Political Economy came out in 1832 after many refusals and sold at once in huge numbers. From then her success was secure. In 1834 she paid a long visit to America, where her open stand for abolition gave deep offence.
britannica-1911-martinet:
Martinet is a word for a strict drill master in an army. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it to one French officer. Jean Martinet died in 1672 while serving King Louis the Fourteenth. He drilled the king foot regiments as inspector of infantry.

His work helped build the first model regular army in Europe. He also brought in copper pontoons for bridging rivers. At the siege of Duisburg his own guns killed him by chance. A court joke of the day mocked that double loss. His age saw hired soldiers of fortune fade from armies. Enlisted recruits in standing regiments took their place instead. Set drill and training on one system followed from that change. Martinet thus stands as a forerunner of the Prussian drill kings.
britannica-1911-mazamet:
Mazamet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a mill town of France. The town lies in the department of Tarn in the south west. A count from 1906 gives the town 11,370 people. The wider commune held 14,386 in that count. It sits on the north slope of the Montagnes Noires. The Arnette stream runs by it, a feeder of the Agout.

Many works in the town spin wool for cloth. They make flannels and a cloth called swan-skins in the text. Cloth for troops and hosiery are also made there. Large tanneries and leather dressing works stand in the town. Glove making and dye works add to the trade. A wide commerce runs in wool and raw hides. Those goods come from Argentina, Australia, and Cape Colony.
britannica-1911-minuet: Minuet is a dance for two, in three beat time, whose name hints at the short steps it needs. The word comes through French and Italian forms from a Latin term for small. At its peak the dance was slow, grave, and full of grace. The name is also used for a tune in the same time. The dance move sits in sets by great hands. Haydn put it in the large form, where it in time grew to a more brisk move.
britannica-1911-moresnet:
Moresnet is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a small neutral state on the borders of Prussia and Belgium. It lies four miles south west of Aix la Chapelle and covers nearly fourteen hundred acres. Its only village holds twenty eight hundred people. Just across the frontiers lie a Prussian and a Belgian place of the same name.

Under the hill of Moresnet sits a very rich zinc mine, held by a Belgian company, the entry says. Customs profit is split between the two states that guard it. The odd state grew out of the European settlement of 1815. No one could agree who owned the small district, so it was made neutral under Prussia and Belgium jointly. In 1841 it gained a rule of its own, under a burgomaster and council.
britannica-1911-motet:
Motet, a key form of church music, is explained in a music entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word has a murky root and more than one old use. Its one clear sense is the church piece of the sixteenth century. Such pieces run in one or two joined movements, on Bible or church prose texts in Latin.

Most motets do not form a fixed part of the mass, though the best known kind is bound to it. Those motets were sung between the Credo and the Sanctus on a holy day. They were built on the chant tones of their texts. The mass for the day was built on the same themes, which gave the service a unity of music. The entry notes loose uses of the word as well.
britannica-1911-northfleet:
Northfleet, a town in Kent in England, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Thames within the borough of Gravesend, east of London by rail. About thirteen thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. Its church of Saint Botolph has a Norman base.

The nave of that church is most of all in the Decorated style, and the chancel is Perpendicular. Its tower fell down and was rebuilt in 1628. A brass from the fourteenth century and other monuments fill the church. Huggens College, with homes for poor ladies, was set up in 1847. Work in the town covers chalk, lime, cement, and bricks, with a shipyard as well. Nearby Swanscombe is tied by tale to a camp of the Danish king Sweyn.
britannica-1911-paulet:
Paulet, also spelled Poulett or Powlett, is an English family traced in a 1911 Britannica article. The stock is an old Somersetshire one. The surname comes from the parish of Pawlett, near Bridgwater. The family rose by a run of marriages with heiresses.

Those matches brought manors and lands in four counties. Land came in Somersetshire, Wiltshire, Devonshire, and Hampshire. A match with a Denebaud in the early fifteenth century brought the manor of Hinton St George. That house stayed the seat of the elder line, the earls Poulett. One ancestor, Sir Amias Paulet, was knighted in 1487 after the battle of Stoke. He was treasurer of the Middle Temple in 1521. The article shows how marriage, more than war, built the fortunes of a county family.
britannica-1911-philaret:
Philaret, born Theodore Nikitich Romanov, was patriarch of Moscow and for years the joint ruler of Russia. A life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his dates as about 1553 to 1633. He was a cousin of Tsar Theodore the First. He won a name both as a soldier and as an envoy.

When that tsar died with no child, Philaret was the folk choice for the throne. He gave way to Boris Godunov, who later forced him and his wife to take monastic vows. He spent eight years as a prisoner in Poland, which he would not own as ruler of Russia. Freed in 1619, he was set on the patriarch's throne. From then till his death he ruled beside his son, Tsar Michael. His tax reforms filled the treasury, and he bound the peasants to the soil.
britannica-1911-philo-poet:
Philo, a Jewish poet who wrote in Greek, is the subject of a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the author of an epic poem in Greek hexameters on the history of Jerusalem. Almost all that survives of his work comes through later writers. Alexander Polyhistor quotes several passages of the poem.

Those extracts are preserved in the work of Eusebius, the entry explains. The poet is probably the Philo named by Clemens of Alexandria and by Josephus. Josephus calls him the elder, to set him apart from others of the name. A modern study of Philo and a fellow Jewish poet is cited at the close.
britannica-1911-picket:
Picket, also spelled piquet or picquet, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a French term for a pointed stake or peg. In military use it means an outpost or guard. The use is said to have begun in the French army about 1690, on outpost duty.

On such duty, musketeers spread out to watch while a small group of pikemen stayed in reserve. In Britain the word is now kept for an infantry post on the outpost line. In the United States a picket means the same as a sentry. The picket line is the farthest line from which an army keeps watch. A body of men held ready for duty inside a camp is also a picquet. In its plain sense, a picket is a peg or stake, used in horse lines or stockades.
britannica-1911-privet:
Privet is the common name for Ligustrum, a group of shrubs and low trees. Its plant entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group holds about thirty five kinds, mostly from warm and mild parts of Asia. Only the common privet is native to Europe as a wild plant.

Plants in the group bear paired plain leaves that stay green or near green. Dense clusters of small white tube shaped blooms come first in the year. Small round berries, most often black, follow the blooms in due course. The entry names prized kinds for hedges, sea coasts, and town gardens. Forms with yellow leaves, yellow fruit, and weeping limbs are also listed.
britannica-1911-puket:
Puket, a port in Siam on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is also known by the Chinese name Tongkah. The town stands on the east side of the island of Junk Ceylon. About thirty thousand people lived there, more than a third of them Chinese.

Tin ore lies beneath the town and all round it, worked by Chinese hands from ancient times. Most local people still earn their living from that ore. In 1907 a European company began to dredge for tin in the harbour. European merchants have traded at Puket since the sixteenth century. In old wars between Siam and Burma the town was attacked more than once. Each time forces from the mainland relieved it in good time. A branch of the Siamese mining office sits there under European officers.
britannica-1911-rambouillet:
Rambouillet, a town of northern France, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the chief town of a district south west of Paris, on the rail line to Chartres. Its town count in nineteen hundred and six was near four thousand, with the wider commune past six thousand. The entry says the town draws all its pull from one great house.

That house is an old great home first built in the thirteen hundreds and rebuilt many times. One big tower with slots for defence is all that stands of the first work. Fine rooms with good wood work draw note too. A park of three thousand acres and a vast wood ring the house. Grounds in both French and English styles hold a walk of rare trees found in no other place in Europe. A state sheep farm sits in the park as well.
britannica-1911-ricochet:
Ricochet is a military article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the rebound of a shot that strikes a hard surface. The French word's origin is unknown. Its earliest known use, in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, meant repetition, as in an oft-told tale. From there it passed to the flat stone skimmed along water, the game of ducks and drakes, and at last to gunnery.

The article explains the old art of ricochet fire. A shot fired at a small angle struck the ground and went on in a series of leaps and falls. The method, credited to Vauban at Ath in 1697, let a besieger skip shot over each traverse. Field guns of the eighteenth century relied on it too. The article closes with its decline: once guns used case shot and shell, ricochet vanished.
britannica-1911-rochet:
Rochet is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a white church vestment worn by high clergy. The robe is made of fine linen or muslin and falls to about the knee. Its sleeves are narrow and close fitting, unlike the loose sleeves of the surplice.

The entry traces the name of the robe through old tongues and old lists of church dress. Bishops and high clergy hold the right to wear it, though the pope can grant that right to others. The robe is worn at choir prayers and at mass over daily dress. Old lists show its use as far back as the ninth century. Its use spread from Rome to the rest of Europe in time.
britannica-1911-rocket:
Rocket is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a word with two chief senses. The first sense names two plants grown or known in gardens. One is an annual with white blooms veined in purple. Its sharp leaves are used in salads in southern Europe.

The second sense is a tube of paper, board, or metal. It is filled with a powder mix that bursts with force. Such rockets serve for firework shows of stars and coloured balls. They also serve as signals and in life-saving gear for wrecks. Big war rockets had a vogue early in the nineteenth century. Sir William Congreve is named as their maker and first user.
britannica-1911-saidapet: Saidapet is a town of British India, the head town of Chingleput district in Madras. It stands on the South Indian railway, five miles south west of Madras city. A line of tanks, or ponds, splits it from that city. Its people numbered fourteen thousand two hundred fifty four in nineteen o one. The state teachers college there has a boarding house for Brahmans, opened in eighteen ninety seven. The farm college began in eighteen sixty five as a model farm. It has since moved to Coimbatore.
britannica-1911-sheet:
Sheet, a word with a sail in its past, is traced in a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. One sense is a flat, thin spread of stuff of any kind. The other sense is a rope tied to the foot of a sail. Old English held three kin words from the root of shoot. That root means to dart, let fly, or thrust forth.

Skeat takes the first sense to be a thing that shoots out. From a corner or fold of cloth the word grew wide. It came to mean the whole cloth spread out flat. Kin words in Iceland and Germany hold the same spread of senses. Bed linen, paper, and broad ice all take the name now.
britannica-1911-sherbet: Sherbet is the Turkish form of an Arabic word for a drink. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it first as an Oriental drink of fruit juice. Lemon or citron juice was dropped on a cake of sugar for it. Snow or other cooling then partly froze the mix. In western use the word covers a water ice left softer than common ice. Fruit juice or spirit flavors that form in most cases. A cheap fizzy sweet drink also bears the name.
britannica-1911-skirret: Skirret is the subject of a short plant article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Skirret is a lasting plant with fleshy roots, in the carrot family. Its roots are boiled and served like salsify. The plant needs free, deep, and much enriched soil. It is raised in most cases from seed. Seed should be sown in drills a foot apart near the end of March. The bed must be well watered in dry weather. Roots are ready near November and keep fresh through winter if stored with care.
britannica-1911-spinet:
Spinet is a name given in England to small keyboard instruments, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Such instruments have one string to a note, plucked by a quill or a plectrum of leather. Shape does not govern the name, which covers all small forms of the kind. The earliest name on record for the instrument is clavicymbalum, found in rules of 1404.

In Italy the usual early model was five sided or seven sided in form. It was kept in an outer case and taken out to be played at need. Some of the oldest oblong cases hold a five sided spinet with its corners not filled in. In the 1500s Italian makers shaped oblong spinets on the cassone, or wedding chest, as their model. The head breaks off in that account, with German, French, and Italian forms of the name all noted at its start.
britannica-1911-stirling-william-alexand:
William Alexander, Earl of Stirling, a Scots poet and court man, fills a long life in the 1911 Britannica. Born near Stirling near fifteen sixty seven, he came of an old line at Menstrie House. He may have learned at Glasgow and at Leiden. He toured France, Spain, and Italy with the Earl of Argyll. At court he won the grace of King James and wrote a poem on prince craft for Prince Henry.

James gave him vast lands in America in sixteen twenty one, the lands of Nova Scotia and more. He was named heir lord of the new colony on that grant. His terms for settlers were too mean, and few came. Verse, court posts, and a failed silver mine fill the rest of the shown text.
britannica-1911-sylhet:
Sylhet is a town and district in the Surma vale of east Bengal and Assam. The town stands on the right bank of the Surma on high ground in groves. Its count of folk in nineteen one was near fourteen thousand. Mats, carved ivory, and home goods are made there.

The district is a broad flat plain cut by streams and drains. In the north, vast rain turns miles of land to a lake each wet span. Tea grows well in the south hills. A great quake in eighteen ninety-seven broke each stout build in town. The tract passed to British hands in seventeen sixty-five.
britannica-1911-tiaret:
Tiaret is a town of Algeria in the Tell Atlas, in the department of Oran. The 1911 Britannica article places it one hundred and twenty-two miles south-east of Mostaganem by rail. The town holds a key pass through the mountains, at a height of 3,552 feet. Its count in 1906 was 5,778 people, of whom 3,433 were Europeans. The Wadi Tiaret runs through the town in a chain of falls.

The upper town, where most homes stand, lies on the right bank of the stream. A citadel crowns a hill of its own across the wadi. The chief trade quarter lies in the lower town. The entry in the hosted text follows a long piece on the papal tiara, a quirk of the scan order. Its own facts on the town's site, people, and stream are plain and full.
britannica-1911-tophet:
Tophet is treated in a brief article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name comes from the Hebrew Bible, in the Books of Kings and Jeremiah. It marks a spot in the valley of Ben Hinnom, near Jerusalem. There, in the days of kings Ahab and Manasseh, children were offered to Molech and other heathen gods.

King Josiah defiled the place as part of his reforms, the article relates. It then became a spot for dumping and burning refuse. In later use the name stood for Gehenna itself, a place of dread. The piece closes by noting that the root of the word is unsure. It points readers to the discussion under Molech in a Bible encyclopaedia for the rival views.
britannica-1911-velvet:
Velvet is a silk cloth with a short dense piled face on it. Its cloth entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The art of velvet weaving most likely began in the Far East. No note of the cloth shows till the early fourteenth century in Europe.

Rich dye hues on velvet showed depth yet stayed soft to view. That trait marked it for church robes, royal dress, and grand hangings. Italian velvets were the grandest cloths of medieval times in that line. Makers varied pile hue and length and wove in gold ground thread. Lucca, Genoa, Florence, and Venice led as sources of fine velvet.
britannica-1911-violet:
The violet is a large genus of plants, named Viola in botany. More than two hundred kinds have been set out in print. They are found chiefly in the mild or hill regions of the northern half of the globe. They grow as well in the hills of South America and of south and tropical Africa. Most kinds are low herbs with leaves that stand in turns along the stem.

Violet flowers stand alone, or at times in pairs, at the end of thin stalks from the leaf axils. The flower is far from regular in form. It has five sepals and five petals. The lowest petal is the largest and bears a spur. Honey made by the spurs of two stamens gathers in that spur. The ovary sits above the other parts and has one cell with many seeds inside.
britannica-1911-wellington-somerset:
Wellington, a market town in Somerset in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits at the foot of the Blackdown hills near the river Tone, on the Great Western rail line from London. The town held just over seven thousand people in 1901. Its church of St John dates from the fifteenth century.

The church has a fine tower and holds a grand tomb for Sir John Popham, a chief justice under Queen Elizabeth and King James. Chief buildings are a county school and a home for aged poor folk founded by Popham in the sixteen hundreds. A tower on the highest Blackdown peak honours the duke of Wellington. The town makes woollen goods and has iron works and brick and tile yards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-frig:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Frigolet describes the monastery of St. Michael. Conrad the Pacific, King of Arles, founded it about 960 on a hill between Tarascon and Avignon. Monks of Montmajour, Augustinians, Hieronymites and last Reformed Augustinians held it in turn, until the French Republic shut it and sold it with all French monasteries.

After changing hands often, Frigolet was bought by Rev. Edmund Boulbon, a former Trappist of Bricquebec who wished for a more active life. On St. Norbert's feast in 1856 he received the white habit at Prémontré, and Pius the Ninth backed his plan to bring back the Norbertine Order in France. The entry follows Frigolet from royal foundation to Norbertine revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrien-baille:
Adrien Baillet was a French author born in 1649 at Neuville-en-Hez near Beauvais, who died at Paris in 1706. His parents were poor. La Garde's Cordeliers, struck by the boy's piety and alert mind, took him into their monastery. They had him admitted to Beauvais College, where he later taught humanities. Ordained priest in 1676, he served as curate of Lardieu and canon of Beaumont, but neither post satisfied him.

After four years, learning's pull took him to Paris, where he became librarian to celebrated de Lamoignon. An insatiable reader and rigid ascetic, he spent his life in study and austerity, making an analytical catalogue of Lamoignon's library in thirty-two folios. His writings fall into erudition, history, and religion, including Jugements des savants of 1685. His criticisms drew fire, notably from Menage, and a later work savoured of Jansenism to the Bishop of Gap.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amulet:
An amulet is an object, often inscribed with secret formulas, worn on the body as a guard against sickness and witchcraft. Pliny is the earliest writer to mention such charms. The word likely comes from the Arabic hamala, to carry, since the power lay in bearing the object. Eastern peoples used them widely, and the habit spread through the Roman Empire as those peoples entered it.

The Church forbade amulets yet allowed emblems that would call a doctrine to mind. Clement of Alexandria urged symbols such as the fish, the dove, and the anchor on seals and rings. Surviving medals show a martyr on a gridiron, the monogram of Christ, and the sacrifice of Abraham. Gnostics used amulets most of all, calling on Adonai, Sabaoth, Jao, Michael, Raphael, Uriel, and Gabriel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-comel:
A priest and thinker from Berga in Catalonia, Antonio Comellas lived from 1832 to 1884 and taught philosophy and theology at Solsona after his ordination in 1856. He first drew notice with two pamphlets. One offered a fresh account of the procession of the Three Divine Persons, the doctrine of how Father, Son, and Holy Spirit relate. The other translated a Protestant writer on reunion with Rome. In 1871 he gave up his chair of theology to devote himself to philosophy at home in Berga.

His best known book argued for harmony between Catholic religion and science, answering William Draper's Conflict Between Science and Religion. A fuller introduction to philosophy followed in 1883. The entry sketches a provincial scholar who chose quiet study over a teaching post. His apologetic work, a reasoned defence of faith, aimed to show that science need not threaten belief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-magl:
Augustin Magloire Blanchet was a Canadian-born missionary bishop, brother of Francois Norbert Blanchet, first Bishop of Walla Walla-Nesqually. He was born near Saint-Pierre in Canada in 1797 and died at Fort Vancouver in 1887. After village school and study at Quebec, he was ordained in 1821 and served in the Magdalen Islands, Cape Breton, and the Gulf provinces. Recalled to Montreal, he pastored four parishes in turn.

In 1846, while a canon of Montreal cathedral, he was named Bishop of the new Diocese of Walla Walla in what is now Washington State. The next spring he traveled overland with one priest and two students, gathering more clergy at St Louis, and reached Fort Walla Walla in September 1847. From The Dalles he built missions across a vast, hard frontier, enduring wild beasts and wilder men. He later became titular Bishop of Ibora, and he is revered as the Apostle of Washington.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-jose:
Benedict Joseph Flaget, first bishop of Bardstown in Kentucky, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in France in 1763 and orphaned young, he joined the Sulpicians, a society of priests who train clergy, and was ordained in 1787. The French Revolution closed his teaching posts, and in 1792 he sailed for the American mission.

Kentucky became his life's work. Sent first to Vincennes on the frontier, he later became bishop of a vast diocese that grew into Louisville. He built churches and a seminary, guided clergy across rough country, and laid the cornerstone of the Louisville cathedral in 1849. He died in 1850, mourned as the father of Kentucky Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-francis-re:
Blessed Francis Régis Clet, a Lazarist missionary martyred in China, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1748, tenth of fifteen children of a Grenoble merchant, he was martyred in 1820. Jesuit schooling at Grenoble and seminary under the Oratorians led him to the Lazarists at Lyons in 1769, with ordination in 1773.

Sent to China, he laboured in disguise through persecution, ministering to scattered Christians for decades. Arrested in old age, he was strangled after torture rather than renounce his faith. His surviving letters, French and Latin both, reveal a cultivated mind behind the missionary's endurance. The entry presents a martyr of the China missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-briconnet:
Guillaume Briconnet, French cardinal and minister of Charles VIII, pushed France into Italy through ambition and finance. A younger son of the king's secretary, he ran Languedoc's finances under Louis XI with integrity and skill. Charles VIII made him treasury secretary and first in council, undertaking nothing, says Guicciardini, without Briconnet's advice.

Widowed and newly Bishop of Saint-Malo, he backed Ludovico Sforza's bid to draw Charles toward Naples, lured by promises of a cardinal's hat. He beat the council's opposition, signed a secret treaty with Sforza, and funded the war despite an empty treasury. Alexander VI offered him the hat to stop Charles, but he pressed on. His betrayal of the Pisans to Florence nearly got him killed by his own troops. He died at Narbonne on 14 December 1514.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celebret:
A celebret is a letter a bishop gives a priest so that he may obtain permission to say Mass in another diocese. It testifies that its bearer stands clear of canonical censures. Trent's council laid down that no strange cleric should celebrate the divine mysteries without commendatory letters from his own ordinary, and no bishop should receive him without them.

Ordinarily a priest from another diocese is not given leave to say Mass unless he shows this signed and sealed certificate. The seal is the safer guard against forgery. A priest in good standing, or certainly known to be so, may celebrate while he takes time to comply with the rule. The Third Plenary Council of Baltimore added a decree against fund collectors, barring them from celebrating even once until they had received permission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-cleme:
Charles Clemencet was a Benedictine historian born at Painblanc in Burgundy in 1703 and dead at Paris in 1778. He joined the Congregation of Saint-Maur young. He served briefly as lector of rhetoric at Pont-le-Voy. Soon called to Paris, he shared in nearly all his congregation's major literary labours. His superiors first set him to edit Photius's Myriobiblion. He soon left that task for a chronological work prepared by his confrère Dantine.

That chronology, his principal work, bore a long title. It promised an art of verifying dates from charters, chronicles, and ancient monuments. It added tables of years, indictions, and paschal cycles, a perpetual calendar, and short histories of councils, popes, emperors, and kings. Clemencet also shared in an edition of St. Gregory of Nazianzus begun by Prudentius Maranus. Its first volume appeared at Paris in 1778, still valuable and far above its predecessors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-use:
An entry on the Christian use of the alphabet, tracing how Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters served the liturgy. During Holy Week, the Lamentations of Jeremiah at Matins are sung with each verse headed by a Hebrew alphabet letter. The letters carry only a numerical value and might be replaced by numbers. The chant is now uniform, with the oldest known setting in the Romano-Gregorian liturgy and a twelfth-century Naples codex giving varied melodies by verse.

Greek letters served a second use in the litterae formatae, letters of commendation. To block fraud, the Council of Nicaea was said to have ordered such letters to carry letter series whose values, added up, would prove their origin. Those initials covered the Trinity, the pope, writer, recipient, cycle letter, and Amen. Scribes often added badly, as a Metz letter shows, so the check soon failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-maltre:
Claude Maltret, a French Jesuit also spelled Maltrait, was born at Puy on 3 October 1621 and died at Toulouse on 3 January 1674. He entered the Society of Jesus on 12 October 1637. After his studies he taught belles-lettres and rhetoric for eleven years, winning wide fame as a classical scholar. He then held a professorship in Sacred Scripture for nine years. In 1662 he became rector of the College of Montauban.

The next year he published his greatest work, Procopius's Histories in an edition with a critical commentary. It passed through many editions, was augmented by other scholars, and entered the Synopsis of Byzantine History printed at Venice. From 1672 to 1674 he served as rector of the Toulouse novitiate. His principal works are Procopius in eight books, the Secret History as a ninth book, and four books on the Gothic War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clouet:
Several generations of painters bear the family name Clouet. Jean the Younger, born at Tours in 1485 and dead probably at Paris between 1541 and 1545, was son of Jean the Elder. The Elder, a Flemish painter, came to Paris from Brussels in 1460 and settled at Tours. Francis the First made his son court painter at Paris and, in 1518, valet de chambre. The court called him Janet, a name that became generic, covering his father, his son Francois, and many imitators.

Jean's portraits of royalty and nobility follow the antique, or Gothic, style of the Van Eycks, with sharp outlines and great attention to detail. He painted his sitter faithfully and avoided theatrical effects, producing portraits simple, reticent, and naive. In 1524 he painted Francis the First in full armour on horseback, and in 1528 a bust now at Versailles. Some authorities count only the Louvre portrait of Francis the First authentic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cruet:
A liturgical entry describes the cruet, a small vessel holding the wine and water for Mass. Two are always used. The Roman Missal directs glass as the best material, since it cleans easily and its transparency prevents confusing water with wine. Gold, silver, and other metals are also used.

In that case a V for wine and an A for water mark the vessels apart. No shape is prescribed, but each cruet needs a firm base, a fairly wide neck for cleaning, and a cover against flies. Long ago the faithful brought the wine in a jar-shaped vessel, taken by the deacon for pouring into the chalice. A trace of that custom survives at a bishop's consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-discipline-of:
The Discipline of the Secret names the early Church custom of hiding its deeper mysteries from pagans and even from those still learning the faith. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses that the custom itself is beyond dispute, though the name is modern, first used in the disputes of the seventeenth century. Its root lies in the words of Christ about not casting pearls before swine.

Catechumens were kept from the inner rites until baptism opened the door, and the habit shaped early worship, teaching, and church building. The entry weighs rival views of how far the secrecy ran and leans on the learned work of Funk, who dated the discipline with care. It offers a clear guide to a practice that guarded the sacred from profane eyes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dom-augustin-:
Dom Augustin Calmet was a celebrated Bible scholar, born at Menil-la-Horgne in Lorraine on 26 February 1672. He was schooled at the Benedictine priory of Breuil and joined the order at Toul in 1688. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him to teaching posts at Moyen-Moutier, where with his brethren he began gathering matter for a Bible commentary. He finished the work at Munster in Alsace as sub-prior and professor of exegesis.

The first volume of his Literal Commentary on all the books of the Old and New Testament appeared at Paris in 1707. Twenty-three quarto volumes followed, making him the most famous Catholic commentator of his age. He died at the abbey of Senones in 1757, leaving a work that shaped Bible study for generations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enguerrand-de:
Enguerrand de Monstrelet was a French chronicler born about 1390 or 1395 and dead in July 1453. Most likely a native of Monstrelet in the Somme, he spent his life at Cambrai in the service of Philip, Duke of Burgundy and Count of Flanders. In 1436 he was lieutenant of the gavenier, collecting the gavenne tax in the Cambresis from church tenants in return for Philip's protection.

From June 1436 to January 1440 he was bailiff of the Cambrai chapter, provost of Cambrai from 1444 to 1446, and bailiff of Walincourt from March 1445 until his death. He took no personal part in the wars of his agitated age, and his Chronicle keeps an impartial tone. It runs from the coronation of Charles VI in 1380, truly from Easter 1400 where Froissart ends, to 1444. It covers other lands besides France, with many documents and details of great religious events as well as battles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-binet:
Etienne Binet, a Jesuit author, was born at Dijon in France in 1569 and died at Paris in 1639. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1590, led the colleges at Rouen and Paris as rector, and served as provincial of Paris, Lyons, and Champagne. Forty-five published works came from his pen, and the first, on devotion to the Blessed Virgin, ran through eleven editions.

Flowers from the Psalms of 1615 reached readers in Italian and Latin translations. Consolation and Joy for the Sick and Afflicted of 1616 saw fourteen republications inside eight years. An Essay on Nature's Wonders of 1621, a popular scientific work, passed through 24 editions before 1658. In 1622, the year Ignatius and Francis Xavier were canonized, he published their Lives. A clear, graceful style and original thought mark his works, which abound in quotations from Scripture and the Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exultet:
Exultet is the Easter-vigil hymn praising the paschal candle, sung by the deacon at the Easter vigil. In the missal its title is Praeconium. Use of the paschal candle looks very old outside Rome, in Italy, Gaul, Spain, and perhaps Africa. The Liber Pontificalis credits Pope Zosimus with bringing it into the Roman Church.

The Praeconium formula was not always the Exultet. The Gelasian Sacramentary instead has Deus mundi conditor, with its famed praise of the bee. The steady metrical cursus points to a date from the fifth to the seventh century. The earliest manuscripts are Gallican, from the seventh and eighth centuries. The hymn invites all to join the deacon. It parallels old and new Passovers with the candle as pillar of fire, calls Adam's sin a happy fault, and ends praying for clergy, pope, and rulers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-fra:
Ferdinand Donnet was a French cardinal and long-serving archbishop of Bordeaux. Born in 1795, he was ordained a priest in 1819. He worked six years in missions, then served as pastor at Irigny and Villefranche. Named to Bordeaux in 1837, he ruled the great see for forty-one years.

Donnet resumed provincial councils and restored shrines and the Pey Berland tower. Made cardinal in 1852, he also sat as Senator of the Empire. At the Vatican Council he stood openly with the Ultramontane party. Loved for his affable and cheerful temper, he died at Bordeaux in 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-etie:
Francois-Etienne Caulet, also called M. de Foix from an abbey he held, was a French bishop and Jansenist born at Toulouse in 1610 and dead at Pamiers in 1680. After studies at La Fleche he worked under Pere de Condren of the French Oratory, joined M. Olier in founding the Vaugirard Seminary and the Company of Saint-Sulpice, and when Olier took Saint-Sulpice parish in 1642, Caulet practically headed the seminary. In 1644 Louis XIV, on St. Vincent de Paul's advice, made him Bishop of Pamiers.

He had not sought the honour, but as bishop he reformed clergy, visited his diocese yearly, held synods, and founded schools, one for training teachers. Later he resisted royal encroachment on church rights, the regale, was betrayed by his metropolitan and despoiled by the king, and appealed to Innocent XI, whose briefs praised his courage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-norb:
Francois Norbert Blanchet, son of a Canadian farmer, was born near Saint-Pierre, Riviere du Sud, Quebec, on 30 September 1795 and died at Portland, Oregon, on 18 June 1883. He was missionary and first Archbishop of Oregon City. After village school he went with his brother Augustin Magloire, later first Bishop of Nesqually, to Quebec Seminary in 1810 and was ordained on 18 July 1819. A year at the cathedral preceded seven years at Richibucto, New Brunswick, among Micmac Indians and Acadian settlers, in poverty, isolation, and hardship.

Recalled to Montreal in 1827 as pastor of Saint-Joseph de Soulanges, he won a Protestant testimonial for fearless service in the cholera epidemic of 1832. In 1837 Archbishop Signay made him vicar-general for the Oregon mission, a vast region no priest had visited. On 3 May 1838 he set out with Modeste Demers on the Hudson's Bay Company's annual express.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-picq:
Francois Picquet, born at Bourg in Bresse on 4 December 1708 and dead at Verjon in 1781, was a celebrated Sulpician missionary in Canada, called le Canadien. He entered the Lyons seminary in 1727, was ordained deacon in 1731, won his doctorate at the Sorbonne, and became a Sulpician priest at Saint-Sulpice in Paris. He begged for Canada, reaching Montreal in July of the year he was ordained and serving there five years from 1734 to 1739.

 In the war of 1743 to 1748 his influence kept the Five Nations, old English allies, neutral, while other peoples fought for France. After peace he volunteered for a post on the Presentation, later Ogdensburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-anselm:
George Anselm Touchet, a Benedictine born at Stalbridge in Dorset, traded a profligate youth for the cloister and the queen's chapel. Second son of Mervyn, Earl of Castlehaven, he was professed at Saint Gregory's, Douai, in November 1643 under the name Anselm. Sent on the English mission's southern circuit, he became chaplain to Queen Catherine of Braganza in 1671.

Touchet lived at Somerset House until banishment in 1675, and Parliament's 1678 act confirming his brother's earldom expressly barred him from the succession. In London he published Historical Collections from Protestant historians on religion's changes in 1674, with a second edition in 1686. In 1680 came his translation of The Secret Paths of Divine Love from the French of Barbason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-de-:
Guillaume de Nogaret, a lawyer from St. Félix-en-Lauragais who died in 1314, was Philip the Fair's chief counsellor and the sharpest weapon in the king's war on the papacy. A doctor and professor of law, he became royal judge at Beaucaire in 1294 and keeper of the seal in 1307. He held that Roman law gave the king absolute supremacy and let nothing check it.

In March 1303 he attacked Boniface VIII before the Louvre assembly, then seized and mistreated the pope at Anagni that September, escaping full punishment only by Boniface's death weeks later. He then drove the Templars' arrest of October 1307, drew up the case against them, and steered the measures that ended with Jacques de Molay's execution in 1314.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-beaufor:
Henry Beaufort, cardinal and Bishop of Winchester, was John of Gaunt and Katherine Swynford's second illegitimate son, legitimized by Richard II in 1397. His career moved between church and state: dean of Wells, Bishop of Lincoln, chancellor of Oxford, chancellor of England, and Bishop of Winchester from 1404. Under Henry V he served again as chancellor and attended the Council of Constance. There his diplomacy with Emperor Sigismund cleared the way for electing a new pope and ending the Western Schism.

Created cardinal by Martin V, Beaufort guarded the infant Henry VI and served as the pope's legate to Germany, Hungary, and Bohemia during the Hussite War. He crowned Henry VI as King of France in Paris in 1431. He fought off an attempt to strip him of his see, financed the war party with large advances, and completed Winchester Cathedral, where he is buried.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-garnet:
Henry Garnet, an English Jesuit martyr born about 1553, broke with his conformist upbringing at twenty and entered the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1575. He studied under Bellarmine and Suárez before teaching Hebrew and mathematics. Sent to England in 1586 with Robert Southwell, he became superior of the English mission the next year when Father Weston was arrested, and held that office until his death. Under his prudent management the Jesuits in England grew from one to forty.

Garnet's later years were entangled in the Wisbech Stirs, a prison dispute among Catholic clergy that he helped settle. They were entangled also in the Appellant Priests controversy over the archpriest George Blackwell, whose authority Garnet advised but did not secretly control, as the account carefully corrects. A prolific correspondent, he translated Canisius's catechism and wrote on Christian renunciation and equivocation, works that circulated in secret print before his execution in 1606.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-capet:
Hugh Capet was king of France and founder of the Capetian dynasty, born about the middle of the tenth century and dead about 996. Hugh the Great's second son, born to the count of Paris and Hedwig, sister of Emperor Otto I, he inherited Paris and the duchy of France at about ten. About 970 he married Adelaide of Aquitaine, and by 985 Gerbert could write that Lothair governed only in name, while Hugh was truly king.

When Louis V died in May 987, Archbishop Adalberon of Reims and Gerbert secured Hugh's election. At Senlis, Adalberon urged crowning the duke, most illustrious by exploits, nobility, and forces, insisting the throne came not by hereditary right but by worth of soul. A unanimous vote followed, and Hugh was crowned at Noyon on 3 July 987, an accession one historian calls above all an ecclesiastical achievement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignace-bourge:
Ignace Bourget was the first bishop of Montreal and titular archbishop of Marianopolis, born at Point Lévis in Quebec in 1799 and dead near Montreal in 1885. Remarkable for piety and learning, he played a potent part for sixty years in Canada's religious and even civil life. Eleventh of thirteen children of Pierre Bourget and Thérèse Paradis, he spent sixty-two years in priesthood and almost fifty as bishop.

Schooled at home and at Point Lévis, then at Quebec Seminary, he stood out for strength of character and brilliant intellect. After two years of theology he entered Nicolet College, took the subdiaconate in 1821, and that same year Archbishop Plessis chose him as secretary to Bishop Lartigue of Montreal. Even before holy orders, Bourget had begun an active life that would shape Montreal for nearly thirty-six years as bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-babin:
French physicist Jacques Babinet was born at Lusignan on 5 March 1794. He died at Paris on 21 October 1872. He began studies at the Lycée Napoléon. There his teacher Binet turned him from law, his family's plan, toward science. He continued at the Polytechnic School. He left in 1812 for the military school at Metz. He served for a time with the Fifth Artillery Regiment.

At the Restoration he left the army and began teaching. He taught mathematics at Fontenay-le-Comte, then physics at Poitiers and later at Lycée Saint-Louis. From 1825 to 1828 he lectured on meteorology. In 1838 he succeeded Savary at the Collège de France. In 1840 he joined the Academy of Sciences. His fame rests chiefly on optics, though his work ranged wider. The entry sketches a teacher-physicist of nineteenth-century France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-benig:
Celebrated French bishop and pulpit orator Jacques Bénigne Bossuet was born at Dijon on 27 September 1627. He died at Paris on 12 April 1704. For over a century his forebears on both sides had held judicial office. He was the fifth son of Bénigne Bossuet, a Dijon parlement judge, and Madeleine Mouchet. He began classical studies at Dijon's Jesuit Collège des Godrans.

When his father moved to the Metz parlement, young Bossuet stayed at Dijon under his uncle Claude, a noted scholar. His ardent study sparked a schoolboy joke linking his name to an ox used to the plow. He soon mastered Greek and Latin classics. Homer and Virgil were favorites, while the Bible became his bedside book. He often said he would grow old among the Scriptures. The entry opens the life of France's great preacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-phili:
French mathematician and astronomer Jacques Philippe Marie Binet was born at Rennes on 2 February 1786. He died at Paris on 12 May 1856. After two years at the École Polytechnique, he became a student-engineer in bridges and roads in 1806. Teaching soon attracted him more. For a time he taught mathematics at Lycée Napoléon. At the École Polytechnique he rose in turn through posts in descriptive geometry, examining, mechanics, and general inspection of studies.

In 1823 he succeeded Delambre in the astronomy chair at the Collège de France. Intense devotion to Charles X cost him his Polytechnique post under the July Government of 1830, though it let him keep his Collège de France chair. He had joined the Société Philomathique in 1812, and in 1843 he was elected to succeed Lacroix in the Academy of Sciences, a teacher-astronomer caught in political change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-longstr:
Soldier and Catholic convert James Longstreet was born at Edgefield, South Carolina, on 8 January 1821. He died at Gainesville, Georgia, on 2 January 1904. In 1831 he moved to Alabama with his parents. From there he was appointed to West Point, graduating in 1842. For Mexican War service he was brevetted major. In 1852 he became a captain. At the Civil War's outbreak he resigned in June 1861 and entered Confederate service.

There he became one of its greatest fighters and won his soldiers' unbounded confidence and affection. He at once received brigadier general's rank. He served with distinction at First Bull Run, then became major general in 1862. At Antietam on 17 September 1862 he commanded the right wing of Lee's army. As lieutenant general he headed a corps in later campaigns. The entry presents a Confederate corps commander turned Catholic convert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-antoine-:
Jean-Antoine Nollet, a French physicist born in 1700 at Pimpré and dead in Paris in 1770, began life toward the priesthood before science took hold of him. With Dufay and Réaumur he turned to physics, above all to electricity, and he first saw how sharp points help discharge it, a point later used in the lightning rod.

Nollet studied how charge moves through tubes, smoke, steam, and living things, and found water passing through a bladder into alcohol, the start of the study of osmosis. Admitted to the Royal Society in London in 1734, he taught experimental physics in Paris at his own cost from 1735, held a public chair from 1738. He tutored the dauphin at Versailles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Gonet, a French Dominican theologian born about 1616 at Béziers and dead there in 1681. He entered his order at seventeen and rose through Bordeaux to a doctorate and a chair of scholastic theology. Pupils prized him as a brilliant teacher, and in 1671 his province chose him its head.

Gonet ranks among the chief voices of his day for Thomas Aquinas. He set out Thomist teaching with rare clarity and skill, though with sharp words for rivals. He lived when theologians tired of beaten paths and built new systems, and his zeal for doctrinal purity sometimes outran even Aquinas. His works still mark the high point of seventeenth-century French Thomism.

Jean-Baptiste Gresset, a French poet born in 1709 and dead at Amiens in 1777, made his name with a comic poem about a parrot. Schooled by Jesuits, he joined the order and taught literature at Moulins, Tours, Rouen, and Louis-le-Grand in Paris. His Vert-Vert of 1734 tells how a convent's pet bird picks up coarse talk on a journey and shocks the nuns.

The poem's light touch and lifelike convent scenes won wide praise, and more verses followed. A later poem steeped in Epicurean ideas cost Gresset his place in the Society, though he parted with gratitude. Turning to the stage, he failed with tragedy and drama but triumphed in 1747 with Le Méchant, still judged the best verse comedy of its century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-crasset:
Jean Crasset, a French Jesuit writer on the spiritual life born at Dieppe in 1618 and dead in Paris in 1692. He joined the Society in 1638, taught humanities and philosophy, and led a famed Paris sodality for twenty-three years while preaching with success.

Crasset's devotional books include a method of prayer, Christian thoughts for each day, and talks for youth, plus a work on the Sibylline oracles that drew attack. His 1689 History of the Church of Japan, drawn largely from Solier and carried from 1624 to 1658, was judged heavy and imprecise, though widely translated. An Orléans interdict over a sermon in 1656 was later lifted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-denis-at:
Jean-Denis Attiret, a French painter born at Dole in 1702 and dead at Peking in 1768. He studied art in Rome, won repute as a portraitist, and entered the Jesuits as a lay brother. Specimens of his novice work survive at Avignon cathedral and its sodality chapel.

Attiret joined the Jesuit painters in China in 1737 and soon outshone them all, becoming the emperor's painter, whose studio the emperor visited daily. He made him a mandarin against his will. To please his patron he dropped oil and shading, painting in watercolour on glass and silk. His sixteen battle scenes for the Tatar wars were engraved in France, though he died before they arrived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François-Albert du Pouget, marquis de Nadaillac, born in 1817 and dead at Rougemont in 1904, was a Frenchman of old family who became a leading student of early humankind. After able service as prefect of the Basses-Pyrénées in 1871 and Indre-et-Loire in 1877, he retired to private study.

Nadaillac threw himself into prehistory and anthropology, above all American questions, and helped explore the caves of southern France. He ranked foremost on cave drawings and the art of their makers, warned France early against falling birth rates, and weighed science against faith. Learned societies worldwide honoured a man famed for courtesy and kind heart.

Jean-François Millet, a French painter born near Cherbourg in 1814 and dead at Barbizon in 1875. He was himself a peasant's son who began as a farm labourer and never lost touch with the soil. His family, stern and pious readers of Pascal and Bossuet, gave him a gravity that shaped his art.

Taught by his parish priest in Virgil and the Bible, Millet studied at Cherbourg, won a town pension for Paris, and entered Delaroche's studio in 1837, haunting the Louvre instead. Italian primitives moved him deeply, yet he turned to field labourers, sowers, and gleaners, painting them with a dignity that made peasant life a fit subject for great art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-garet:
Jean Garet, a Benedictine of Saint-Maur born at Le Havre about 1627 and dead at Jumièges in 1694, professed in 1647 at twenty and lived at Saint-Ouen in Rouen. There he prepared an edition of Cassiodorus, printed at Rouen in 1679.

Garet based his text on Fournier's 1579 edition, adding changes of his own, and Mommsen later judged the Variae harshly as work without skill or learning. His preface argued Cassiodorus was a Benedictine, and Migne reprinted Garet in his Latin Fathers. That made it the fullest modern edition of its day, though it lacks the Complexiones found later by Maffei.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jouvenet:
Jean Jouvenet, called the Great, was a French painter born at Rouen in 1644 and dead in Paris in 1717. Painting ran in his Italian-descended family: his grandfather may have taught Poussin, and his father gave him his first lessons before sending him to Paris in 1660.

Jouvenet painted the 1673 May offering for Notre-Dame, a Cure of the Paralytic, which drew Lebrun's eye and work at Versailles. Elected to the Academy in 1675 and professor in 1681, he rose fully only after Lebrun's death in 1692. As French painting freed itself from Rome and Bologna toward Rubens's colour and life, Jouvenet led the new native manner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jehan-fouquet:
Jehan Fouquet, a French painter and miniaturist born at Tours about 1415 and dead about 1480, was perhaps son of Huguet Fouquet, who worked for the dukes of Orléans. French painting then stood at a brilliant pitch, heralding the Renaissance, yet monarchy's disasters drove art from Paris to Burgundy and the Loire.

In the Loire valley, the nation's true heart in crisis since Saint Martin, grew the first painter with a clear French face. Fouquet, contemporary of Joan of Arc, was as national in character as she was. His style blends Burgundian and Flemish roots, seen in Sluter and the Van Eycks, with Italian touches. Court portraits and book miniatures made him the founder of French Renaissance painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joachim-bouve:
Joachim Bouvet, a French Jesuit missionary born at Le Mans and dead at Peking in 1732, was among the first Jesuits Louis XIV chose for China. Before sailing, he and his companions joined the Academy of Sciences, charged to take star readings, fix places, and gather scientific data, sailing from Brest in March 1685.

Reaching Peking in February 1688, Bouvet and Gerbillon became Emperor Kangxi's mathematics tutors, writing treatises in Tartar that the emperor had turned into Chinese with his own prefaces. Kangxi gave them a palace site for church and residence, finished in 1702. Later he sent Bouvet to France for more missionaries, bearing forty-nine Chinese volumes for the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-colet:
John Colet was the Dean of St. Paul's who founded St. Paul's School in London and befriended Erasmus and Thomas More. Born in London in 1467, eldest son of a twice Lord Mayor, he studied at Oxford, toured France and Italy in 1493, and was ordained in 1498. His Oxford lectures on St. Paul's epistles broke with purely textual commentary to study Paul's personality and the text as a whole.

Meeting Erasmus at Oxford in 1498 began an intimacy that deepened the Dutchman's distrust of the later schoolmen. Made Dean of Saint Paul's in 1504, Colet administered the cathedral vigorously. On his father's death in 1505, he spent his inheritance founding the great school in 1509, where Greek ranked with Latin and William Lilly served as first head master. Accused of advanced views in 1512, he saw the charges dismissed by Archbishop Warham as frivolous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-anthon:
Joseph Anthony de La Rivière Poncet was a French Jesuit missionary in Canada and the Caribbean. Born in Paris in 1610, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at nineteen and studied at Clermont, Rome, and Rouen. In 1639 he sailed to Canada with Madame de la Peltrie and Marie de l'Incarnation.

Sent at once to the Huron mission, he founded a mission to the Algonquins on St. Mary's Island in 1645. Iroquois captors were torturing him when a rescue party intervened, though his companion was burned at the stake. After church disputes sent him back to France, he served at Loreto and died at Martinique in 1675.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-de-gal:
Joseph de Gallifet was a French Jesuit called the Apostle of devotion to the Sacred Heart. Born near Aix in 1663, he joined the Society of Jesus at fifteen and came under Father de la Colombière, confessor of Margaret Mary Alacoque. A near-fatal fever during his probation led a fellow priest to vow that Gallifet would spend his life for the Sacred Heart.

He kept that vow through rectorships at Vesoul, Lyons, and Grenoble and as assistant for France in Rome. His 1726 book De Cultu Sacrosancti Cordis Dei pleaded for a feast of the Sacred Heart, granted only in 1765, after his death. He lived to see over seven hundred confraternities of the devotion founded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-pablo-bo:
Juan Pablo Bonet was a Spanish priest who pioneered teaching the deaf to speak. Born late in the sixteenth century, he became secretary to the High Constable of Castile, whose brother was deaf and mute. Bonet took the boy's education in hand, inventing visible signs and breathing exercises to shape lips, tongue, and teeth for each sound.

His manual alphabet, hand signs for letters, and his account of the vocal organs' positions let his pupil grasp words and utter them with fair success. He set out the method in Reducción de las letras y arte para enseñar á hablar los mudos, published at Madrid in 1620. Later teachers, from de l'Epée to Gérando, built on his early work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-feuille:
Louis Feuillet was a French Franciscan geographer and explorer, born at Mane in 1660 and dead at Marseilles in 1732. Skilled in mathematics and astronomy, he won the Academy of Sciences' notice and sailed to the Levant with Cassini in 1699 to fix the positions of ports and cities.

A voyage to the Antilles followed in 1703, with a cruise along South America's north coast and a haul of plant specimens. As royal mathematician he rounded Cape Horn in 1707, worked up the west coast to Callao, and studied months at Lima. Home in 1711, he gained a pension and a Marseilles observatory, and published journals of physical, mathematical, and botanical observations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-francoi:
Louis Francois de Bausset was a French cardinal, writer, and statesman, born at Pondicherry in 1748 and dead at Paris in 1824. Schooled at La Fleche and St. Sulpice, he became vicar-general of Aix, administrator of Digne, and Bishop of Alais in 1784.

Refusing the clergy oath, he fled to Switzerland, was jailed on return, and freed at Robespierre's fall. After the Concordat he resigned his see, and Napoleon made him a canon of St. Denis and a university councillor. Under the Restoration he led the university council, entered the Academy, and became cardinal in 1817. His lives of Fenelon and Bossuet remain his chief literary works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-joliet:
Louis Joliet was a Canadian explorer, born at Quebec in 1645 and dead in Canada in 1700. Son of a wagon-maker, he shone in mathematics at the Jesuit school, took minor orders in 1663, then traded the classroom for the wilderness and Indian trade.

Frontenac sent him in 1672 to find the great river beyond the Lakes. With Marquette he wintered at Mackinaw, then paddled down the Fox and Wisconsin to the Mississippi on 17 June 1673. A month south proved the river reached the Gulf of Mexico, not the Pacific, and the party turned back, having mapped a waterway that reshaped France's American dreams.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marc-antoine-:
Marc-Antoine Muret was a French humanist born at Muret near Limoges in 1526 and dead at Rome in 1585. He studied at Poitiers under Scaliger's influence, then taught at Poitiers, Bordeaux, and Paris. Friend to Dorat, du Bellay, and the Pleiade poets, he published a French commentary on Ronsard's Amours in 1553 and Latin verses called Juvenilia.

Accusations of heresy and loose living forced him out of Paris to Toulouse, then on to Lombardy. At Venice he taught four years, editing Horace, Terence, Catullus, Tibullus, and Propertius for Paulus Manutius. His Variae lectiones of 1559 broke his friendship with Lambinus over plagiarism charges. Later he served Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, reached Rome in 1563, and spent his last years expounding Aristotle, Cicero, Plato, Juvenal, and Tacitus, besides teaching law. Ordained in 1576, he won fame as a modern master of Latin style, imitating Cicero by temper rather than by laborious copying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-bouque:
Martin Bouquet was a learned Benedictine of the St Maur Congregation, born at Amiens in 1685 and dead at Paris's Blancs-Manteaux monastery in 1754. As a boy he meant to become a secular priest, but shunning worldly dangers he chose the Benedictines. He took vows at St Faron, Meaux, in 1706, when St Maur flourished.

Soon after priesthood his superiors made him librarian at St Germain-des-Pres, then holding some sixty thousand volumes. French history sources had been gathered before, but St Maur now took up Dionysius de Sainte-Marte's project and set Bouquet to run it. He issued eight volumes covering France's history from earliest days to 987, drawing on chronicles, charters, and letters with care for authentic texts. Later Maurists carried the Recueil des historiens des Gaules et de la France further, past Bouquet's death. His work remains the groundwork for French medieval history, praised for range and scholarly order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-motet:
A motet is a short piece of music set to Latin words. It is sung instead of or just after the Offertory, or as a detached number in extra-liturgical services. Its name most likely comes from Latin motus, movement, though French mot, word or phrase, has also been proposed. The Italian mottetto began in the thirteenth century as a secular polyphonic form.

Philip de Vitry, who died Bishop of Meaux, wrote an Ars compositionis de motetis about 1320. It holds the oldest surviving sacred motets, which stayed in vogue for over two centuries. Between 1390 and 1435 composers such as Dunstable, Power, Dufay, Brasart and Binchois raised the form to new artistry. The entry follows it through Palestrina and the later masters to its modern revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-olivet:
Mount Olivet, in English Bibles the Mount of Olives, is the hill east of Jerusalem beyond the brook Cedron. It lies a Sabbath day's journey from the city. It was named in antiquity for the olive groves that flourished there and still leave traces. Medieval Arab writers called it Tur ez-Zeitun, whence the modern Jebel et-Tur.

It is less a single hill than a range running north to south, from Scopus at 2,686 feet through Ras el-Madbase to the Jebel et-Tur proper. That peak has three summits Christians call the Men of Galilee, the Ascension and the Prophets. The last takes its name from rock tombs. The entry maps its shrines, the Garden of Gethsemane at its foot, the Ascension church and the places of Christ's Passion week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-bone:
Nicholas Bonet, Friar Minor, theologian and missionary, died in 1360, his birth date uncertain. Probably French by birth, he taught theology with great success at Paris, earning the title Doctor Pacificus, the Peaceful Doctor, for his suave and tranquil lecturing. He played an important part in the beatific vision dispute, warmly debated under John XXII and settled by Benedict XII's decree Benedictus Deus.

As a member of Benedict XII's papal embassy to Kublai Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, Bonet traded a theology professor's ease for a missionary's arduous and perilous labours. Franciscan missions in Tatary began as early as 1245 under Lorenzo da Portogallo and Giovanni da Pian Carpino, and continued under Archbishop John of Monte Corvino. The great khan, wishing the work kept up and extended, sent an embassy seeking new labourers, and Benedict commissioned four Friars Minor as legates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-jose:
Nicholas Joseph Laforet, Belgian philosopher and theologian, was born at Graide on 23 January 1823 and died at Louvain on 26 January 1872. After theology at Namur's seminary, he entered Louvain University, studying Oriental languages, Scripture and philosophy. In 1848 he took the moral philosophy chair and received his theology doctorate. Two years later he became president of the College du Pape.

On Mgr de Ram's death, Belgium's bishops chose Laforet as university rector. His main undertakings included founding and organising civil engineering, industry and mines schools, and establishing the Justus Lipsius Institute, a new literary and pedagogical school. His example and advice constantly encouraged professors and students. He was prothonotary Apostolic, honorary canon of Namur, officer of the Order of Leopold, and commander of the Order of Christ. He also belonged to Belgium's Royal Academy and Rome's Academy of the Catholic Religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-triv:
Nicholas Trivet, a Dominican friar born around 1258, wrote history, theology, and notes on classical authors in medieval England. He studied at Oxford and Paris, served at one point as prior of his order in London, and taught at Oxford.

His best known book traces six kings descended from the counts of Anjou from 1136 to 1307, with a rich account of Edward I. Trivet also wrote a French chronicle later linked to Chaucer, plus commentaries on Scripture, a treatise on the Mass, and notes on Seneca and Augustine. Only two of his many works appear in print, the chronicle and part of his commentary on Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-corne:
French theologian Nicolas Cornet, head of Navarre College and syndic of the Sorbonne, set the Jansenist dispute on its road to Rome. Born at Amiens in 1572 and doctored at Paris in 1626, he reported seven suspect propositions to the Sorbonne in 1649, two from Arnauld and five from Jansenius.

Despite fierce opposition and appeals to Parliament, Cornet pressed on until the Assembly of the Clergy sent the five Jansenist propositions to Innocent X, who condemned them in 1653. Bossuet later praised him, and he died at Paris in 1663. He left no writings of his own, though he is said to have worked with Richelieu on controversial method.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolet:
Nicolet, a diocese in Quebec, Canada, took shape when it split from Trois-Rivières in 1885. Named for its town on the south bank of the Saint Lawrence, opposite Trois-Rivières, it covers Nicolet, Yamaska, Arthabaska, and Drummond counties, with parts of two more.

Its first bishop, Elphège Gravel, served until 1904, when Joseph-Simon-Herman Brunault succeeded him. The entry lists its seminary, founded in 1803, its teaching and nursing orders, its 500 parish schools with 20,000 pupils, and a Catholic population near 90,000. Its religious orders teach, nurse, and keep house across the diocese, from Nicolet to Drummondville.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ninian-winzet:
Scottish controversialist Ninian Winzet, born at Renfrew in 1518, defended the old faith against John Knox with wit and learning. Ordained in 1540 and master of Linlithgow school, he publicly disputed Knox in 1559 and lost his posts when Scotland changed religion in 1560.

On Mary Stuart's arrival he published Certane Tractatis, addressed to queen, clergy, nobles, and Knox himself. Driven out when his Last Blast was seized, he fled to Louvain, wrote from Antwerp, and ended as Benedictine abbot at Ratisbon, dying in 1592. He seems for a time to have been Mary’s confessor before his flight to Louvain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olympe-philip:
French bishop Olympe-Philippe Gerbet, born at Poligny in 1798, moved from Lamennais's circle to orthodox leadership without losing his friend's esteem. Ordained in 1822, he went to Lamennais at La Chesnaie in 1825, then accepted the encyclicals condemning traditionalism and withdrew to Juilly in 1836.

A decade in Rome gathering material for his Sketch of Christian Rome ended with posts as a Sorbonne professor, Amiens vicar-general, and bishop of Perpignan in 1854. His 1860 pastoral on current errors modeled Pius IX's Syllabus, earning him the name Fénelon of the nineteenth century. He spent 1839 to 1849 in Rome gathering data for his Sketch of Christian Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-baillo:
Pierre Bailloquet was a French Jesuit missionary among Canada's Indians, born at Saintes in 1612. He entered the Society at Bordeaux in 1631 and reached Quebec in summer 1647. For forty-five years he laboured and suffered among tribes roaming from Acadia in the east to Illinois country in the west, enduring hardships the Relations call well-nigh incredible.

Earth served him for bed and mattress, bark strips for a palace filled less with air than smoke, and zeal often put him in danger of tomahawk or stake. Near eighty and grievously infirm, he still dragged himself across snow for leagues to reach huts whose dwellers could not come to him. He died in the Ottawa missions on 7 June 1692, in his eightieth year and his sixty-first in religious life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-daniel:
Pierre Daniel Huet was a celebrated French scholar and bishop, born at Caen on 8 February 1630, son of a sheriff converted from Calvinism. Orphaned young, he loved Latin poetry, geometry, and mathematics, studied law solidly, and admired Descartes before Samuel Bochart's sacred geography drew him to biblical studies. Learning Greek and Hebrew, he followed Bochart to Sweden in 1652 with Queen Christina and found Origen fragments at Stockholm.

Fifteen years of labour at Caen produced his edition of Origen's exegetical works. He founded an academy at Caen, became bishop of Avranches, and spent his last twenty years at the Paris Jesuit house in piety, learned company, and writing. His works span literary essays, Caen's origins, ancient commerce, the Demonstratio evangelica of 1679, and attacks on Descartes culminating in a posthumous fideist treatise on the mind's weakness. He died at Paris in 1721, aged ninety-one, leaving his great library to the Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-herman:
Pierre Herman Dosquet was the fourth Bishop of Quebec, born at Liège in Flanders in 1691. After two years in Canada from 1721 to 1723, he became superior of Lisieux Seminary in France and helped preserve it from Jansenism. At Rome he became vicar apostolic of part of India and titular Bishop of Samos, consecrated by Benedict XIII in 1725.

He stayed at Rome until named coadjutor to Bishop Mornay of Quebec in 1729. He legislated wisely for women's religious communities and zealously suppressed the liquor traffic. Succeeding to Quebec in 1733, he promoted primary and classical education and entrusted Acadia, the Gulf islands, Cape Breton, and Newfoundland to the Holy Ghost Congregation, endowing it generously. Ill health forced him from Quebec in 1735, though his resignation was accepted only in 1739. He then lived chiefly at Rome. He died at Paris in 1777.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-jean-d:
Pierre-Jean de Smet was a Belgian Jesuit who became the best-known Catholic missionary among the Native peoples of the American West. He was born at Termonde in 1801 and emigrated to the United States in 1821. He helped found the Missouri province of his order at Florissant. From 1840 he made the Rocky Mountain tribes the centre of his life's work.

His travels took him to the Flatheads, Nez Percés, Crows, and Sioux. He founded missions such as Saint Mary's on the Bitterroot River. He also acted again and again as a peacemaker between tribes and with the United States government. The peoples he served had first asked Saint Louis for a priest in black robes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-millet:
Pierre Millet was a French Jesuit missionary among the Iroquois of New York State in the late seventeenth century. He was born at Bourges in 1635 and entered the order in 1655. He studied at La Flèche and Paris and was sent to Canada in 1668, where he was assigned to the Onondagas.

He quickly learned enough of their language to lead prayers and teach the catechism. The Onondagas gave him the name Teahronhiagannra, meaning one who looks up to heaven. Later he laboured among the Oneidas until 1685 and served as chaplain at Fort Niagara. He was taken prisoner during the wars of the period and ended his days at Quebec in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-puget:
Pierre Puget of Marseilles, born 31 October 1622 and dead there 2 December 1694, worked as painter, sculptor, architect, and ship designer. A shipbuilder took him on at fourteen, and his promise soon showed. Walking to Italy in 1637, he earned a living in Florence making furniture for a duke. In Rome he learned painting from Pietro da Cortona. Back in France by 1643, Toulon called him to construct a warship.

He returned to Italy in 1646 beside a Feuillant friar, sent by Anne of Austria to sketch old monuments, and the task drew him toward architecture. By 1653 he was back in France painting altarpieces, among them the Annunciation and Visitation at Aix. After Fouquet fell he stayed on in Genoa, carving works such as Saint Sebastian and the Rape of Helen. The Louvre holds his Hercules, Perseus delivering Andromeda, and Milo of Crotona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayer-of-qui:
The Prayer of Quiet counts with all writers on mystic theology as one of the grades of contemplation. It stands midway between affective prayer and the prayer of union. In it the soul tastes rare peace and rest, with delight in gazing on God as present. God gives the soul knowledge of His presence and a sense of true touch with Him, though dimly. The sense of Him grows clearer as union with God climbs higher.

This gift cannot be won by effort, for it is supernatural. God Himself makes His presence felt in the soul's depths. The gift of wisdom works here, as in each grade of contemplation. Scaramelli holds this gift renders God present to the soul, more so as the gift grows. Some writers add this is not common wisdom, but wisdom as one of the rare charismata.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pustet:
Pustet is the name of a family of well-known Catholic publishers. This encyclopedia entry traces them from the Republic of Venice, where the name Bustetto remains common. The founder of the Ratisbon line likely moved to South Germany in the seventeenth century. His descendant Anton Pustet lived as a poor bookbinder at Hals, near Passau, late in the eighteenth century. Anton's son Friedrich was born there on 25 March 1798.
