Friedrich learned bookbinding from his father, opened a small bookshop at Passau in 1819, and founded a printing house in 1822. Energy and skill let him move the publishing business to Ratisbon in 1826. Ties with prominent Catholic authors widened the firm's reach. Branch houses followed in New York in 1865, Cincinnati in 1867, and Rome in 1898, carrying a Bavarian family firm across the Atlantic and to the papal capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-massuet:
René Massuet, Benedictine patrologist of the Congregation of Saint Maur, was born on 13 August 1666 at Saint Ouen de Mancelles in the diocese of Evreux. He died on 11 January 1716 at Saint Germain des Prés in Paris. His profession came in 1682 at Notre Dame de Lire; Bonnenouvelle in Orléans was where he studied, showing more than ordinary ability. After teaching philosophy at Bec and theology at Saint Stephen's in Caen, he took bachelor and licentiate degrees in law.

He taught a year at Jumièges and three years at Fécamp, and spent 1702 in Rome studying Greek. In the following year he moved to Saint Germain des Prés, teaching theology there until his death. His principal work, undertaken rather reluctantly, was the Paris edition of Saint Irenaeus of 1710. He also left in manuscript an Augustinus Graecus, gathering every passage of Saint John Chrysostom on grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rochet:
The rochet is an over-tunic of fine white linen, usually cambric, reaching to the knees. Its sleeves are always tight-fitting, unlike the surplice's fairly wide ones. It is trimmed with lace or embroidered borders. Tulle or lace throughout is discouraged.

Unlike the surplice, the rochet belongs distinctively to prelates. Other clergy may wear it only where the use of the rochet has been granted by special papal indult, as for some cathedral chapters. It has no liturgical character as a sacred vestment. A decree of Urban VII and a decision of the Congregation of Rites in 1852 bar its use as such at sacraments, where the surplice is required. As choir dress it counts as a liturgical vestment. It grew from the everyday clerical linen tunic, privileged at Rome by the ninth century, and remained common wear for clergy until the fourteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secret:
Near the end of the Offertory in the Roman Mass, the priest says a prayer so quietly that the choir's singing covers his voice. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that hushed prayer. It is called the Secret, from the Latin Secreta. For a long stretch it stood alone as the prayer said at that point of the Mass.

Early evidence shows the priest praying in silence while a psalm was sung. The entry follows the custom through later centuries. The silent Canon took shape over time. Newer offertory prayers reached Rome only in the 1300s. The Secret changes with each feast. It echoes the day's saint or occasion. It almost always asks God to accept the gifts laid on the altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-margaret:
Margaret of Antioch, virgin martyr also called Marina, faced a prefect's lust and a trial's torments without yielding. Daughter of a pagan priest at Pisidian Antioch, she lost her mother soon after birth. A pious woman living five or six leagues from the city nursed her. Embracing Christianity, she found her father cast her off, and her nurse took her in. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows her to Olybrius's court.

Watching her mistress's flocks one day, she caught the eye of the Roman prefect Olybrius. Struck by her beauty, he sought her as concubine or wife. Neither cajolery nor threats moved her to yield, so he tried her publicly at Antioch. Threatened with death unless she renounced faith, she refused to adore the empire's gods. Flames, the Acts say, left her unhurt. Bound and cast into boiling water, her bonds broke at her prayer and she stood uninjured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-oliver-plu:
Oliver Plunket, archbishop of Armagh and primate of Ireland, was executed at Tyburn in the Popish Plot scare. Born at Loughcrew in County Meath in 1629, he studied at the Irish College in Rome, shone in philosophy, theology, and law, and served the Irish bishops as their agent in Rome. In 1669 Propaganda named him to Armagh, and he was consecrated at Ghent.

Entering his diocese in 1670, he confirmed nearly forty-nine thousand people in four years, often outdoors in wind and rain, and opened a school at Drogheda with Jesuit teachers. Arrested on false charges of plotting rebellion, he was tried in London, condemned, and hanged on 11 July 1681. Canonised in 1975, he remains a symbol of a persecuted Irish Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stephen-of:
Stephen of Muret, founder of Grandmont, built an order of extreme austerity in the Limousin hills. Born in 1045, he died at Muret on 8 February 1124. The traditional story of his youth presents serious chronological difficulties. The entry exposes them: a pilgrimage to Bari before its relics arrived, and twelve years under an archbishop who held office too briefly.

What stands firm is his settlement at Muret. His rule stressed silence, poverty, and solitude modelled on the Calabrian solitaries. A community grew around him. After his death his disciples were organised as the Order of Grandmont, with houses across France. The entry offers a candid study of a founder whose legend outran its dates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-bec:
Thomas Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, moved from royal chancellor to martyr in a quarrel over church liberty. Born at London on 21 December 1118 to Norman settlers of some standing, he learned to read at Merton Abbey and studied at Paris. After secretarial work, he entered Archbishop Theobald's household about 1141 and became his most trusted clerk.

Henry II made him chancellor, and the two men were close friends until Henry named him archbishop in 1162. Becket then defended church rights against the Constitutions of Clarendon, fled into exile in France, and returned to Canterbury in 1170. Four knights, taking the king's angry words as command, murdered him in his cathedral on 29 December 1170. Canonised in 1173, he became England's most popular saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-gar:
Thomas Garnet, protomartyr of St Omer's College, was executed at Tyburn in 1608 for priesthood alone. Born at Southwark about 1575 to Richard Garnet of Balliol College, Oxford, he attended Horsham grammar school and served as page to half-brothers of Philip Howard, earl of Arundel. At the opening of St Omer's College in 1592 he was sent there.

By 1595 he was judged fit for the new English seminary at Valladolid, sailing in January with five companions and a disguised Jesuit, William Baldwin. Storms, a search by Elizabeth's ships in the Downs, and capture dogged the voyage. Ordained and returned to England as a Jesuit priest, he was arrested, tried, and hanged at Tyburn on 23 June 1608, the first martyr of his college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoret:
Bishop and theologian Theodoret of Cyrus, Antioch's learned, embattled churchman, is the figure examined here. Born at Antioch about 393, dying about 457, he counted his birth an answer to monk Macedonius's prayers. His mother vowed him from birth to God's service, and monks Macedonius and Peter educated him. Lector while very young, he studied Diodorus, Chrysostom, and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

Syriac and Greek he knew, Hebrew and Latin not at all. At twenty-three, both parents dead, he gave his fortune to the poor and spent seven years as a monk at Nicerte near Apamea. Against his will, about 423, he became Bishop of Cyrus, a diocese of nearly 800 parishes suffragan to Hierapolis, and wrote histories, commentaries, and letters that still define his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-marie-:
Thomas-Marie-Joseph Gousset, French cardinal and theologian, was born at Montigny-les-Charlieu in 1792, the son of a vine-grower, and died at Reims in 1866. He worked in the fields and began his studies only at seventeen. Ordained priest in 1817, he taught moral theology at Besancon's Grand Seminaire until 1830, earning a name as an expert teacher and casuist.

His early books treated church teaching on lending at interest, civil law in relation to moral theology, and a defence of Liguori. Named Bishop of Perigueux in 1835, he protested the university monopoly in his Observations on freedom of teaching. Called to Reims in 1840, he still finished his Moral Theology for parish priests in 1844 and a dogmatic theology that ran through many editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-somers:
Thomas Somerset, a Catholic confessor born about 1530, spent close to twenty years in prison for printing and for treason charges. Second son of Henry, second Earl of Worcester, he was sent to the Fleet prison in June 1562 for translating and printing, without licence, an oration by the Cardinal of Lorraine. Brought before the Council at Greenwich, he refused to submit and was sent back to the Fleet.

Released on bail in February 1582 to handle legal business in Monmouthshire, he was too ill to travel that May. He stayed at liberty until October 1585, when he was in the Tower on a charge of high treason. A man of property in Gloucestershire and Monmouthshire, he paid his own prison costs, so his name never appears in the Tower bills. He died in the Tower in May 1587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tibet:
Tibet is a vast high plateau of about 463,320 square miles, running 1,240 miles east to west and 740 miles north to south, at heights between 13,000 and 16,500 feet. Chinese estimates put its people at about six and a half million, though other counts fall as low as two or three million. It is bounded by the Kunlun Mountains and the Gobi in the north, the Himalayas with Everest in the south, and China and India on its flanks.

From its heights flow the Indus, the Brahmaputra, the Yellow River, the Yangtze, the Irrawaddy, the Salween and the Mekong. The entry surveys its five provinces, its lamaist hierarchy and civil rule, its history from the sixth-century kings, and the missions that reached Lhasa by roads from Sining, Szechwan and India. It also weighs Tibet's tangled relations with China, Russia and England.
caught-in-the-net:
Emile Gaboriau's Paris crime novel, dated 1868 in this edition, opens on a bitter February day at the Hotel de Perou, a cheap lodging house. The landlady worries over her top-floor tenants: old Daddy Tantaine, young Paul Violaine, and Rose, a girl she judges far too pretty for the house.

Money, blackmail, and hidden pasts draw those lodgers into a web worked by harder hands. A banker who says cruel things in honeyed tones shows the world the tenants are caught in. Twenty-seven chapters tighten the net by stages, through pressure, pursuit, and disclosure. Gaboriau builds the tale from small lodgings and small sums up to ruin and revenge.
colonel-thorndyke-s-secret:
Colonel Thorndyke's Secret, by G. A. Henty, is an adventure novel whose own prefatory summary lays out the plot. A bracelet of diamonds, stolen from a Hindu idol by a British soldier in India, comes into Colonel Thorndyke's hands. Wounded, he is sent home to England, and the secret passes to his brother, a country squire.

The family soon learns it is being watched. Highwaymen crowd the district, so the watchers might be knights of the road, or Lascars sworn to recover the god's property. A mysterious death takes the one man who knew the hiding place. The young hero joins the London police as a detective to clear the mystery. The bracelet is at last unearthed and taken to the diamond cutters of Amsterdam.
dave-porter-at-star-ranch-or-the-cowboy-:
A western outing fills Dave Porter at Star Ranch, by Edward Stratemeyer, issued at Boston in August 1910 by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard. Lyle T. Hammond drew the pictures. Dave and his chums open the tale at home, and a stray shot starts the fun.

Niagara Falls, a robbery, and a street waif crowd the road west. At Star Ranch come a horse race, fine trout fishing in mountain streams, and Phil's boast that it is the best he ever saw. A cowboy's secret gives the book its second title and its late turn. Stratemeyer, king of the boys' series, keeps the pace fast and the tone clean for his young trade.
diary-of-a-pedestrian-in-cashmere-and-th:
Captain Knight of the Forty-eighth Regiment walked through Cashmere and Thibet with a notebook, and this diary prints what he wrote on the road. Richard Bentley published the book in London in 1863. Knight, a British army officer, traveled on foot where no excursion trains or printed guides yet existed. He kept the diary's daily shape, with little editing afterward.

Entries record mountain passes, river crossings, temples, markets, and meetings with local officials and villagers. Knight describes Cashmere's lakes and gardens, then the colder, thinner air of Thibet beyond the passes. Notes added later cover the architecture of Cashmere, drawing on Captain Cunningham's essay, and a closing sketch treats the life of Krishna. Spelling of place names follows the sounds as Knight heard them. Walkers and armchair travelers alike get a ground-level picture of Himalayan travel before roads, hotels, or tour parties reached the region.
doe-osti-17198190-uncertainty-and-sensit:
Uncertainty and sensitivity analysis inside the GDSA framework is the subject of Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-27199R, dated September 30, 2026. The authors are Teresa Portone, Eduardo Basurto, Dusty M. Brooks, and Paul E. Mariner, writing for the Department of Energy's Office of Nuclear Energy. The GDSA framework models the safety of deep geologic disposal for spent fuel and high-level waste.

The year's priority was direct disposal of used fuel in dual-purpose canisters set in shale host rock. The team describes its methods and a reference case that follows temperatures and pressures around a single waste package. A 200-sample study measured how uncertain inputs move those results for a generic heat output curve peaking at 4 kilowatts. Newer runs then test hotter packages, near the top of the stored inventory.
doe-osti-1764912-region-specific-merchan:
CRADA project CRD-18-00751 closed with National Laboratory of the Rockies report NREL/TP-6A20-78011, issued in February 2026. Technical contacts Richard Boardman, Mark Ruth, Bethany Frew, and eight colleagues came from Idaho National Laboratory, the Rockies laboratory, Argonne, Southern Company, Exelon, and Xcel Energy. Together they sized up merchant hydrogen markets region by region and priced hydrogen made by electrolysis.

The study starts from a grid problem: cheap renewables, cheap gas, and flat demand have cut power prices, while baseload plants are costly to turn down. Making hydrogen from power that would otherwise be curtailed is one outlet. Each utility territory gets its own market and cost assessment, ending in a go or no-go judgment. High-temperature electrolysis, running at 600 to 850 degrees Celsius, is covered alongside lower-temperature routes.
doe-osti-2589169-defining-a-platform-app:
Harsha Padullaparti, Priti Paudyal, and Tom Harris of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5D00-96576, from September 2025. It covers Project 1, Modification 1 of CRADA CRD-21-21469. The topic is market participation for a medium voltage solid-state transformer platform. Its synthetic inertia and voltage stability controls need data driven business models.

A solid-state transformer is a power electronics device, not iron and copper. It can actively steady a grid that is losing the inertia of spinning machines. The project priced that value stakeholder by stakeholder under updated grid rules for distributed energy. Two use cases anchor the study: corridor charging for electric vehicles, and solar plus storage aggregated under FERC Order 2222. Customers span utilities, installers facing interconnection rules, balancing authorities, and aggregators. The warning underneath: distribution transformers, never designed for two-way power flow, could limit vehicle and DER growth.
doe-osti-2589619-uncertainty-and-sensiti:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11744R, dated August 2025, advances the math used to judge a future nuclear waste repository. Authors Laura Swiler, Eduardo Basurto, Dusty Brooks, and co-authors at Sandia and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory work in the GDSA framework, the Department's simulation system for geologic disposal safety. Their package covers uncertainty and sensitivity methods: how unsure a result is, and which inputs drive that doubt.

Work ties into companion packages that build the framework, run repository cases, and develop the PFLOTRAN flow code. Model meshes are checked with a quality score, with values above 0.6 treated as acceptable; a few drift-region cells scored lower but stayed in range. Decision makers get repository forecasts with honest error bands, plus a ranked list of what to measure next.
doe-osti-3002178-application-of-raman-sp:
Tashiema Ulrich, Luke Sadergaski, Donald Kovacic, Francisco Parada, and co-authors test a light-based assay in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4131, dated October 2025. The assay uses Raman spectroscopy, which reads how laser light scatters off molecules, to find the uranium content of ADUN solution. ADUN is acid-deficient uranyl nitrate, a liquid form of uranium handled in fuel processing. Fast, in-line uranium readings support material accounting.

The team built calibration data linking Raman signals to known uranium levels in the solution. A working method would let plant staff measure uranium without drawing samples for slow laboratory analysis. That speed matters where solutions move through pipes during processing. The report adds to a line of Oak Ridge work on optical sensors for nuclear process streams, aimed at safeguards and plant control alike.
doe-osti-3005574-optimization-of-scintil:
Ashlyn Kaylee Van Pelt, a University of Texas at Austin researcher working at Los Alamos, optimizes a camera in report LA-UR-25-31393, issued November 19, 2025. The camera images MeV X-rays: a scintillator converts the X-rays to light, and the light forms the picture. Such radiography inspects dense objects and severe-accident experiments that ordinary X-rays cannot penetrate.

Detector choices trade brightness against blur and speed. The study works through scintillator options and detector configurations, drawing on medical imaging physics and recent fast MeV imaging upgrades. Scintillator research from Lawrence Livermore's imaging program feeds the comparison. The goal is a detector matched to its experiments rather than a general-purpose compromise. Student reports of this kind document design reasoning that senior staff can audit and reuse.
doe-osti-3008148-determination-of-scale-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/CFCT-25/37, by Zhi-Gang Mei, Carolyn Tomchik, Aaron Oaks, and Kun Mo, dated December 2025, determines the scale bar for metallography images in the AGHCF data collection. Old micrographs of irradiated fuel and cladding carry printed scale bars whose own calibration method has been lost.

One method measured cladding of known 381 micrometre thickness across 986 pixels, giving 0.386 micrometres per pixel, about 5.4 percent larger than the legacy bar's 0.367. A second method matched pairs of bubbles between images: one pair 258 micrometres apart spanned 691 pixels. Cross-checked scales let modern measurements be taken from the archived images with confidence.
doe-osti-3008387-2023-annual-explosives-: The 2023 annual explosives count at Lawrence Livermore is closed out in LLNL-TR-2014307 by Eric Bukovsky, lead of the lab's Explosives Safety Program Office. The count ran from May 18 to September 27, 2023 and was checked the next day under the lab's Explosives Materials Inventory Plan. Since a 2020 Inspector General audit, such stocks count as sensitive property under federal rules. The memo also notes the High Explosives Inventory Tracking System being extended to all sites holding such stocks.
doe-osti-3025065-carbon-neutral-steel-pr:
Kevin Bush of Molten Industries led award DE-EE0010869, from October 2023 to October 2025, on carbon-neutral steel through methane pyrolysis feeding direct reduced iron. Pyrolysis splits methane into hydrogen and solid carbon instead of carbon dioxide. The hydrogen then reduces iron ore, and the carbon comes out as a handleable solid rather than a gas the plant must bury.

Milestones record practical calls made with industry advisers. The product will be stored as direct reduced iron pellets, since hot briquetted iron is mainly needed for long sea voyages. Pellets cut complexity and energy use for a pilot mine-to-mill demonstration. A full energy balance of the iron-making process, counting the energy in hydrogen recycle, was used to size how much preheating the iron, hydrogen, and carbon streams can supply.
doe-osti-3380293-multilayer-membrane-ele:
Multilayer Membrane-Electrode-Sub Gasket-Ptl Assembly, shortened to MESPA, is the subject of CRADA final report NLR/TP-5900-99717 from July 2026, under agreement CRD-24-30512. Peter Rupnowski, Guido Bender, and Ken Hansen are the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts and cited authors. Funding came from the Hydrogen Fuel Cell Technologies Office.

PEM electrolysis stacks split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and building them means stacking many delicate layers in exact alignment. MESPA pre-assembles the membrane, electrode, sub-gasket, and porous transport layer into one multilayer unit, so the stack goes together more easily and with fewer handling errors; the title's word is facile assembly. The report closes the cooperative work on that assembly and its role in electrolysis stack manufacture.
doe-osti-3394856-leveraging-solar-therma:
Firestone Walker Brewing Company's quarterly progress report for award DE-EE0011498, covering April 1 to July 1, 2026, advances its Leveraging Solar Thermal Energy for Net-Zero Brewing project. Mark Fischer, director of operations, is principal investigator. The project period runs from January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2027. The brewery, in Paso Robles, California, makes one million barrels a year and needs up to five megawatts of process heat as saturated steam.

Brewing is a heat business, and steam is where its carbon sits. Firestone Walker has set a goal of cutting the brewery's carbon emissions by half. The project's first major goal is measurement: quantify the thermal and electrical energy demands of a million-barrel brewery precisely, so solar thermal equipment can be sized against real loads rather than estimates. This report is the first quarterly installment of that work.
doe-osti-3398694-role-of-neutrals-versus:
Massachusetts Institute of Technology's final technical report for award DE-SC0021629, by principal investigator Jerry Hughes with Saskia Mordijck of William and Mary, studies what sets the density pedestal at a tokamak's edge. The project ran from May 2021 to April 2025 under the Office of Fusion Energy Sciences. Plasma density drives the fusion reaction rate. The pedestal's height therefore feeds straight into predicted gain.

The open question is division of credit. How much of the edge density profile is built by transport, and how much by direct ionization of fueling neutrals? The team validated computational neutral models against measurements on the DIII-D and Alcator C-Mod tokamaks. There, edge ionization rates were measured under varied fueling. The team also ran interpretive transport modeling with neutral penetration altered to mimic future reactor conditions. The aim is a pedestal predicted, not prescribed, for burning plasma devices.
elsie-at-nantucket:
Martha Finley sends the Dinsmore and Raymond families to the sea in Elsie at Nantucket, dated 1884. The book is billed as a sequel to Elsie's New Relations. Her preface owns the source. She spent six weeks on Nantucket herself, with the town as headquarters. She also borrowed from Northrup's 'Sconset Cottage Life to fill out the picture of the old cottages.

Captain Raymond opens the tale at breakfast at Ion. He has one month's leave certain and hopes of more. He moves at once that the summer outing be planned and carried out. The families sail for the island's odd little dwellings and surf. A homecoming scene shows the captain gathering little Grace in his arms. Violet asks how he came back so soon. The book doubles as a resort guide in story dress, full of beaches, drives, and family devotion.
enter-bridget:
Thomas Cobb brings a suspected adventuress into a London drawing room in Enter Bridget, published by Mills and Boon in 1912. Bridget Rosser divides opinion from the outset. Mark Driver leans to more than tolerance; Lawrence calls her a pretty woman on the make, before he has seen her face. Carrissima Faversham tries to hold the balance even.

Twenty-eight chapters play out the comedy through birthdays, excursions, and a carpet-buying afternoon that ends where it began. Mark pays the bill for the bronze and black Childema rug at Mabred's after a wasted search. Proposals, confidences, and open confession lead to Mrs. Jimmy and exeunt omnes. The novel keeps its quarrels light and its ending tidy.
essays-on-paul-bourget:
Mark Twain aims these two essays at the French critic Paul Bourget, whose book on America had been greeted by American newspapers as a divine light breaking on the land. The contents are the pair: What Paul Bourget Thinks of Us, and A Little Note to M. Paul Bourget. Twain quotes the famous summary himself: in Boston they ask how much a man knows, in New York how much he is worth, in Philadelphia who his parents were.

His question is about the observer's equipment and method. Bourget, he argues, collected Americans as a naturalist collects bugs, then classified, grouped, and deduced a nation of seventy million. A pleasant system, Twain grants, but subject to error, and the bug was never consulted. The essays are a defence of the observed against the observer.
fair-margaret:
Haggard's Fair Margaret is a historical romance set between England and Spain. H. Rider Haggard, author of King Solomon's Mines and She, wrote the tale. J. R. Skelton supplied fifteen illustrations for the 1907 London edition. Peter, the hero, meets a Spaniard in the opening chapter.

John Castell and his secret stand near the plot's heart. Chapters carry Peter through farewell, news from Spain, and a chase. The Meeting on the Sea and The Adventure of the Inn add pace. Betty shows her teeth and later pays her debts in key chapters. Isabella of Spain appears in person late in the book. The Holy Hermandad and a baker's oven bring danger. Haggard blends love, faith, and intrigue in Tudor dress.
four-day-planet:
Piper sets this novel on Fenris, a planet whose day runs so long that settlements huddle against killing cold and heat. A ship from Terra opens the story, and a young reporter works the city levels. Monster killing, a tallow-wax fire, and civil war postponed mark the chapters.

Cast away in the snow, the party plans to pack a boat's stern with wet snow and let it freeze. Ramón Llewellyn warns they have seventy hours before the heater fails and they freeze around it. Joe Kivelson and the bandaged Abdullah set to work on the engines. H. Beam Piper published Four-Day Planet in 1961.
gloria-and-treeless-street:
Annie Hamilton Donnell's 1910 tale sets rich, idle Gloria, seventeen and content on her broad veranda, against the poor families of Treeless Street. Each day she watches a queer little figure hurry past with a bag, always at the same hour, and longs to know where she goes. Her aunt and uncle guard her easy life, and she has never had to think about want.

Curiosity draws Gloria across the wide street into small, bare rooms. There she meets a nurse, a mother named Rose, and a frail baby called Hunkie. She watches the nurse mend a broken stair rail with clothesline, doing work no one expected of her. The tale is a gentle lesson in sympathy: a sheltered girl learns what her neighbors' lives cost. Donnell writes it warmly, for young readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISocietyofFor: An article called Hoover's Loyal Legion profiles the Society of Former Special Agents of the FBI, the organization of men who once served under J. Edgar Hoover. The nickname in the title is the point: loyalty to the old director outlasted his tenure. The surviving record gives the subject and title but no author or date, so the piece stands as an undated portrait of the Bureau's alumni society.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RifleandBullet_:
Remington Arms Company issued this Remington-Peters catalog for 1971. It lists the company's sporting firearms and ammunition for that year. Shotguns and rifles are presented with their models and prices. High-velocity ammunition gets its own place in the line. The catalog is a sales book, made for dealers and sportsmen planning a season.

A manufacturer's catalog fixes a year's products exactly: names, gauges, barrel lengths, and prices in print. Gun catalogs sit in assassination files because the Oswald rifle was a mail-order product of the same world. This one is valuable on its own terms. It preserves Remington's 1971 line entire, the sporting market as the maker chose to present it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
On December 17, 2014, Presidents Barack Obama and Raúl Castro announced a breakthrough in United States-Cuba relations. Behind that public moment lay years of secret contacts. Peter Kornbluh edited this major collection, announced in December 2017 near the third anniversary of that date.

The documents chart the history of secret communications between the two governments. Back channels let enemies talk when open diplomacy is frozen, and this set preserves how those talks worked in practice. It is a useful record for anyone studying how long-hostile states begin, quietly, to change course.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Sav:
After the Bay of Pigs invasion failed, more than a thousand invaders sat in Cuban prisons. Getting them home took long negotiation, and this National Security Archive posting examines one strange thread of it. Did President John F. Kennedy send Fidel Castro a secret warning through Brazil?

A warning routed through a third country would fit the odd diplomacy of the prisoner talks. Each side needed messages it could deny in public. The posting lays out the question and the evidence around it, and it shows how much of the rescue effort happened out of sight.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_environm:
In October 1986 a Soviet nuclear submarine carrying nuclear weapons sank north of Bermuda. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, number 562, published on the thirtieth anniversary. Top secret minutes of a Politburo discussion anchor the record.

The minutes show Soviet leaders applying lessons from the Chernobyl disaster months earlier. Communication between Washington and Moscow about the accident stayed open. That openness came on the eve of the Reykjavik summit between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev. The documents catch two rivals handling a nuclear accident at sea with unusual candor, days before a meeting that nearly changed the arms race.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
Area 51, the secret Nevada test site, became famous through the CIA's U-2 spy plane history, declassified in 2013. This briefing book, posted that October, argues the site's role was even larger. Documents show it served as a center for top secret stealth aircraft work in the 1970s and 1980s.

The site also hosted Soviet MiG fighters obtained in secret during the Cold War. American pilots could test their own aircraft against the real enemy machines. That double life, stealth development plus foreign fighter testing, makes Area 51 a genuine crossroads of intelligence and aviation history, beyond its flying-saucer fame.
hamlet:
William Shakespeare's Hamlet, Prince of Denmark stands here in an early electronic text that keeps the old printing's spelling, with u and v exchanged as the executive director's notes explain. The notes warn readers that odd spellings come from the printers' type cases, not from errors. The play itself opens on Elsinore's platform: Who's there?

Hamlet meets his father's ghost, feigns madness, stages the play within the play, and argues with his mother, Ophelia, and himself in the great soliloquies. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern carry his forged commission to England, sealed with his father's signet. Old spelling slows the eye slightly and rewards it, bringing readers closer to how Shakespeare's first audiences saw the text.
heart-of-the-sunset: Rex Beach's novel is set in sun-baked ranch country of mesquite, dust and water-holes, where Texas Rangers, ranchers and Mexican neighbours live close to violence. Chapters follow Dave Law, Judge Ellsworth and the outlaw Luis Longorio through ambushes at the water-hole, an evening at Las Palmas, a rodeo and a crash of loyalties. Land, water and pride drive the feud at its heart.
honey-sweet:
Edna Turpin published this girls' novel in 1911, with pictures by Alice Beard. Anne is an orphan whose doll, Honey-Sweet, shares her name and her heart. A plate shows Anne pale and wordless at a hard moment. The orphan home, under Miss Farlow, rules Anne's days.

Anne's temper and hunger for love drive the small scenes. She dumps chocolates before Miss Farlow for the old orphans in one burst. Then she sobs to Honey-Sweet over one tiny piece she could not take. Turpin writes tenderness without syrup, mostly. Young readers got an orphan tale with real sting in its sweetness.
in-secret:
In Secret, by Robert W Chambers, is a war novel of enemy intrigue in America, written while the First World War still shaped its readers' fears. Chambers, listed on his title page as the author of The Common Law and Lorraine, opens with a set of comic verses in dedication. They thank a police chief and a woman called Arethusa for fighting pneumonia, flu, and the Hun with clubs, guns, and bottles of disinfectant.

Behind the joking front matter sits a sterner story of secrets moving through wartime society. Chambers builds his plot from hidden agents, watched houses, and information carried across drawing rooms and offices. The dedication's gallows humor tells the truth about the book's world: everyone is performing calm while suspecting everyone else. Readers of his earlier romances get the same social polish here, wired for espionage and sudden arrest.
in-the-days-of-the-comet:
H. G. Wells imagined a comet remaking nature in In the Days of the Comet, a novel framed as a memoir. Vapors from a comet's tail sweep Earth and trigger the Change, a clearing of minds. Narrator Willie Leadford, once a clerk, tells how the world woke up kinder and saner. Wells uses the tale to test his socialist hopes.

Dust in the shadows opens the story, with Willie poor, angry, and in love with Nettie Stuart. A revolver, a rival lover, and a war scare push him toward murder as the comet nears. Green vapors knock humanity out cold, and everyone wakes with envy washed away. Cabinet councils and love after the Change fill the last book. Beltane festivals and a deathbed close the memoir before the epilogue. Readers meet Wells the utopian, arguing that people fail from arrangements, not souls, and that a wiser world stays possible.
king-alfred-s-viking-a-story-of-the-firs:
King Alfred's Viking, a Story of the First English Fleet, is Charles W. Whistler's historical novel. Whistler's preface explains his sources: the details come from Asser's Life of Alfred. Alfred employed Norsemen whose names the record never gives. Whistler links them to Rolf the Ganger and Harald Fairhair's age.

He argues over battle sites with care, naming Ethandune and Kynwith and citing Bishop Clifford's identifications. Alfred's refuge at Athelney, the preface says, lies in scenes he could test himself. Whistler wrote many such tales of Saxon and Viking England. This one joins Alfred's fleet-building to a Norse hero's adventures. The preface shows a novelist checking chronicles like a scholar before daring his story.
lady-audley-s-secret:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret is a famous sensation novel. Its first chapter, titled Lucy, opens at Audley Court. The house lies in a hollow of old timber and rich pasture.

A lime avenue, an old arch, and a one-handed clock set the mood. Lucy herself seems sweet, bright, and harmless. Yet the title promises a secret behind that fair surface. Braddon builds suspense from hidden identity and buried acts. The book helped define Victorian sensation fiction, a genre built on shocks and secrets. Robert Audley, the heroine's nephew by marriage, grows suspicious in time. His slow hunt for proof drives much of the suspense.
legend-of-moulin-huet:
Lizzie A. Freeth published her Legend of Moulin Huet at Guernsey in 1872. She had earlier written The Adventures of Carl Skinflint among the Fairies. Le Lievre printed the book at the Star Office there.

Freeth dedicated it to the Conway boys of the training ship Conway. She stresses that the story itself has no link to them. She simply owed that fine institution much gratitude, she says. The tale draws on Guernsey's own coastal lore. A mill, a bay, and local legend give the small book its charm. The Conway dedication shows Freeth's ties to naval families. Guernsey readers would know the Huet shore she describes.
lombard-street-a-description-of-the-mone:
Walter Bagehot describes London's money market in this famous essay. He names it Lombard Street to deal with concrete realities. Abstract words, he argues, falsely make the subject seem impalpable. Plain words can describe the market as clearly as anything.

Bagehot avoids Peel's Act of 1844 wherever possible. Controversy over that act caused half the supposed difficulty. When he must mention it, he stresses experienced effects only. Theory's refined basis interests him far less than practice. Few will attend to anything else once 1844 is mentioned, he warns. Experienced effects, not abstract theory, govern his treatment throughout.
maggie-miller-the-story-of-old-hagar-s-s:
Maggie Miller is a novel by Mary J. Holmes, subtitled Old Hagar's Secret. Holmes also wrote Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine. Its motto is 'Lead us not into temptation.' The tale opens at the old house by the mill.

Hagar's secret hangs over Hester and the young Maggie. Girlhood, trifles, and expected guests fill the early chapters. Arthur Carrollton enters Maggie's life as the waters trouble. Madam Conway's disasters add comedy and social bite. Holmes was among America's best-selling novelists of her century. Her tales of love, class, and hidden birth thrilled millions. Maggie Miller is a fine sample of her sentimental art.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Elizabeth Charlotte of Bavaria, Duchesse d'Orleans, wrote the memoirs in this set. She was mother of the Regent, as the title page states. Her letters to kin across Europe ran to near eight hundred.

A Brunswick councillor, De Praun, picked the best parts after her death. The first printed set, in 1788, was cut and weakened by censors. Names were struck out, and her bold German turns were softened. This complete set restores the extracts with life and force intact. A life of the princess in a later reprint read like a sermon. This set aims to keep her salt and salt alone.
montlivet:
Alice Prescott Smith published this frontier novel with Grosset and Dunlap in 1907. Its contents begin with a key, a captive, and a scene behind the commandant's door. The action moves into an Ottawa camp, then westward toward the islands. A character named Mary Starling enters midway, and a compact is made.

Later chapters gather over Cadillac's table and in council. Cadillac founded Detroit, and the novel breathes that French Great Lakes world. Storms, mist, and mixed motives fill the middle chapters. Smith writes a romance of the old Northwest, where French officers, traders, and Native nations bargain and fight over the lakes country.
moonfleet:
J. Meade Falkner published this Dorset adventure in 1898. He dedicates it to all Mohunes of Fleet and Moonfleet, living or dead. The contents open in Moonfleet village, with floods and a discovery. A vault, a rescue, and an assault follow in quick succession.

Later chapters bring an auction, a landing, and a judgment. A sea-cave, a funeral, and a well-house deepen the danger. The last named chapters are The Well and The Jewel. Smugglers and a cursed diamond drive the tale. Generations of readers have ranked it among the finest adventure stories in English.
mr-marx-s-secret:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this mystery novel, first issued in 1899 and reprinted in 1916. The title page lists his other tales of intrigue. Chapter one is called News from the Pacific. A frontispiece shows a man vowing to end a beast's misery.

Oppenheim builds the plot around a secret held by Mr. Marx. News, travel, and hidden motives drive the early chapters. His style favors short scenes, talk, and sudden turns. Readers follow who knows the secret and who wants it. The book is an early sample of the spy and crime tales that made Oppenheim famous.
nan-sherwood-at-pine-camp-or-the-old-lum:
Annie Roe Carr sends Nan Sherwood to a winter lumber camp here. Chapter one opens on High Street in Tillbury, by the high school. Bess Harley spots a crowd at the Atwater Mills gate. Nan's merry face clouds at once at the sight.

Nan is rosy-cheeked, brown-eyed, and hard to keep still in class. Yet she is no thoughtless girl, the narrator insists. Trouble at the mill starts her trip to Pine Camp. An old lumberman's secret waits in the snowbound woods. V1 promises snow fun, new friends, and a light mystery, in cheerful series fiction for girls.
nasa-tm-19650025650-analytic-solutions-t:
Richard S Brokaw at Lewis Research Center worked out exact, analytic solutions for how a hydrogen and oxygen mixture ignites. The paper was prepared for a combustion meeting at Cambridge in England in August 1964. Ignition kinetics is the study of the chain of chemical steps that leads to burning. Hydrogen and oxygen react with explosive speed once lit.

Analytic solutions give insight that pure number work cannot. They show which steps control the delay before ignition. Rocket engines burn these same gases, so the timing of ignition matters for safe starts. Brokaw's solutions gave combustion scientists a clean base for checking both theory and engine practice.
nasa-tm-19670002044-the-effects-of-space:
Frederick Gordon Jr. and Harry E. Wannemacher Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report in August 1966. It studies what space radiation does to MOSFET transistors, and what those effects mean for engineers who build with them. Goddard was then putting metal-oxide-semiconductor circuits into spacecraft telemetry systems.

The introduction explains why Goddard chose these devices despite the radiation risk. They saved so much size and power that no rival circuit class could do the same job. Bipolar circuits met the space limits but missed the power limits by a wide margin. Conventional parts met the power limits but not the space limits. The first spacecraft set to fly the devices were the IMP-D and IMP-F satellites, whose orbits would expose them to harsh radiation.
nasa-tm-19670008546-simultaneous-trapped:
Donald J. Williams and Norman F. Ness, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in June 1966. Using satellite data, it watches two things at once. First come energetic electrons trapped in Earth's radiation belts, and the magnetic field in Earth's long magnetic tail. That tail stretches away from the Sun.

Data from the polar-orbiting satellite 1963 38C tracked the high-latitude trapping boundary at 1,100 kilometers from March 15 through June 3, 1964. At the onset of magnetic storms, that boundary suddenly collapsed toward lower latitudes. Meanwhile the IMP-1 satellite measured field strength inside the tail itself. Comparing the two records, three cases matched the latitude drops predicted by an extended tail shape, and one did not. The authors call the results direct evidence that the tail field governs trapped particles in quiet times and storms alike.
nasa-tm-19670014616-rare-earth-analysis-:
C. C. Schnetzler, H. H. Thomas, and John A. Philpotts, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis paper. It presents a new way to measure rare-earth elements in rocks and minerals. The method uses a mass spectrometer with stable isotope dilution. A sample is spiked with known amounts of chosen isotopes to reveal the abundances present.

The technique was already in routine use for europium and the seven even-numbered rare-earth elements. That set, the authors say, is enough to outline the general rare-earth abundance pattern of a rock. Results matched neutron activation analysis in quality, or beat it, while running faster and more simply. As a check, the team determined rare-earth abundances in two standard rocks, known as W-1 and G-1, whose values other laboratories could compare against.
nasa-tm-19680008597-propulsive-potential:
Joseph L. Ansell, of the Delta Project Office at Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in February 1968. It assesses the propulsive potential of residual rocket motor heat. A spent solid rocket motor stays hot after burnout. Ansell asks whether that leftover heat can still do useful work in vacuum.

His scheme sprays an inert quenching fluid into the hot motor, flashing it to gas that escapes as thrust. Three fluids were compared, water, propane, and Freon 12, applied to the Delta launch vehicle's third stage motors. Water proved superior under the conditions assumed. The method appears feasible, the study finds, for fine velocity trimming within six minutes after burnout. A computer program predicts the effect of introducing the quenching fluid at various times after the motor's peak temperature. Planners can thus pick the best moment.
nasa-tm-19700013645-marshall-space-fligh:
William M. Greene of the Space Sciences Laboratory at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on April 15, 1969. It covers the gravity network set up around the center in Huntsville, Alabama. That network supported work on a laser instrument meant to measure gravity with great exactness.

Greene made early field seismic measurements at seven proposed sites in and around Redstone Arsenal. He also set out a local gravity net and a wider one across the state to meet test needs. Every result, he reports, pointed the same way: the instrument site needed shielding from ground vibration. The work ended with an optimum permanent field site chosen for the tests.
nasa-tm-19710018232-experiments-on-the-e:
NASA preprint X-322-71-165 reports experiments on ultraviolet light and contamination inside vacuum systems; the author's name is poorly rendered in the scan. Thin films of stray material can coat hardware inside vacuum chambers and spoil sensitive tests. The experiments ran in an otherwise empty chamber and watched the films with a quartz crystal microbalance.

Data from the microbalance showed that ultraviolet light changes what clean and contaminated even mean inside a chamber. The chamber's past use mattered most, far more than the pumping mechanism. Under ultraviolet exposure, a chamber with a dirty history behaved differently from a clean one. The report recommends checking for contamination with ultraviolet irradiation whenever an experiment is critical.
navajo-silversmiths-second-annual-report:
Washington Matthews, a United States Army doctor, wrote Navajo Silversmiths for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. The piece ran in the bureau's second annual report, for 1880 to 1881, printed in Washington in 1883. Plates show silver objects, a workshop, crucibles, and stone molds.

Matthews says many Navajo smiths work chiefly in silver, though some forge iron and brass. He could not learn when or how the art began among them. Some held that it did not come from Europeans at all. He notes that tools from American and Mexican traders had shaped the craft, and that the work had improved in recent years.
o-flaherty-v-c-a-recruiting-pamphlet:
George Bernard Shaw wrote O'Flaherty V. C. as a recruiting pamphlet in play form. In 1915, he says, this little play was a recruiting poster in disguise. British officers seldom like Irish soldiers, he begins, yet always try to keep a share of them in a battalion. Irish dash, he argues, gives impetus to bold operations.

Irish recruiting in 1915 was badly bungled, Shaw charges. Irishmen were mostly Roman Catholics and loyal Irishmen, which English eyes read as heretics and rebels. Yet they were willing to soldier beside France and see the world. The War Office, he says, approached them from Dublin Castle's view, not their own. Commissions denied to Catholic officers repulsed them.
one-basket:
Edna Ferber gathered thirty-one short stories in this book. An introduction opens the collection for readers. The first tale is The Woman Who Tried to Be Good. It is dated 1913 in the table of contents. Blanche Devine owns the House with the Closed Shutters.

Blanche trails fine clothes down Main Street in the tale. No man lifts his hat, and no woman bows. Storekeepers overcharge her, and she pays in silence. She has no redress as a woman of her class. Ferber writes with pity for judged and lonely people. Her tales mix humor, pathos, and small-town life.
pinocchio-the-tale-of-a-puppet:
Carlo Collodi's Pinocchio: The Tale of a Puppet is the story of a wooden puppet who laughs and cries like a child and wants to become a real boy. This edition, illustrated by Alice Carsey, was published by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin, in 1916.

The first chapter asks how a piece of wood could laugh and cry like a child, and from there Pinocchio runs through one scrape after another. He is famous for the nose that grows when he lies, and for learning, slowly and painfully, to be good. Generations of children have met him first in some edition like this one.
poems-and-ballads-third-series-taken-fro:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Poems and Ballads, Third Series, appears here as taken from the third volume of his collected poetical works, published by William Heinemann in London. Swinburne was the most musical and provocative English poet of his generation, famous for verse that celebrated pagan feeling and challenged Victorian respectability. The collected edition arranged his output across six volumes, from the first Poems and Ballads through songs, roundels, and dramatic poems.

Within that scheme the third series continues the ballad and lyric work that made his reputation, full of the rushing metres and rich sound that readers either loved or condemned. Placed beside the second series and the Songs of the Springtides in the same collected volume, it shows Swinburne in his mature manner. Readers who want the poet whole rather than in selections can follow his career volume by volume here.
rip-foster-in-ride-the-gray-planet:
Blake Savage wrote this Golden Griffon space adventure for boys, copyrighted in 1952 by Western Publishing Company. Golden Press of New York issued the first Golden Griffon printing in 1969. Rip Foster is its hero, and the fourteen chapter titles promise a fast ride through peril in space.

Spacebound and Rake That Radiation open the tale, followed by Capture and Drive and Find the Needle. The Gray World and Rip's Planet give the mission its ground, and Earthbound turns the course homeward. Duck — or Die, Repel Invaders, and Get the Scorpion raise the fighting pitch. Mercury Transit, Peril, and Between Two Fires close the list.
romeo-and-juliet:
William Shakespeare's tragedy of Romeo and Juliet is set out here by acts and scenes, with a list of its persons. Escalus, Prince of Verona, heads that list, with Mercutio, the Prince's kinsman and Romeo's friend, and Paris, a young nobleman, after him. A chorus speaks the prologue and returns in the second act.

The scenes move from a public place and a street to rooms and a hall in Capulet's house, and to Capulet's garden by night. Friar Lawrence's cell recurs through the middle acts. The last act shifts to a street in Mantua and ends in a churchyard, in a monument belonging to the Capulets, where the lovers' story closes.
ruth-fielding-of-the-red-mill-or-jasper-:
Alice B. Emerson's Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, or Jasper Parloe's Secret, is headed with the year 1913. Chapter I, The Red Flame in the Night, opens with the sound of drumming wheels roaring in Ruth's ears for hours. She sits in the last car of the afternoon Limited, whirling from the West to the East through the rich valleys of Upper New York State. Cheslow is not many miles ahead now. She has found it on the railroad timetable and on the map printed on the back of the sheet, and she has spelled out station names with quick eyes until dusk fell.

Ruth is glad to have a seat to herself, since a seatmate might have seen how hard she works to keep back tears. She is by no means one of the crying kind, she insists, and she had banned tears for this occasion weeks ago.
somerset: G. W. Wade and J. H. Wade wrote Somerset. Methuen and Co. printed the London book. It holds thirty-two pictures and two maps. One picture maps the railways of Somerset. An other shows the Pinnacles at Cheddar. The contents open with an introduction in nine heads. They treat the county's lie and reach. Weather and links by road and rail follow. Land shape, rocks, beasts, and plants come next. The past, old remains, trades, and famed folk close the list.
the-alchemist-s-secret:
Isabel Cecilia Williams wrote The Alchemist's Secret, a set of tales printed by P. J. Kenedy and Sons of New York with rights held in 1910. Eleven tales are listed, from The Passing of Tony and The Tramp through Nancy's Tale, Patsy, The Story of Julie Benoit, and God's Way.

The Passing of Tony opens at a small post office, where Tony asks Widow Bascomb if the last mail is in and if it holds a thing for him that night. She knows full well it does not, yet she still turns to the letters in their pigeonhole to check for him. Her sour face and rasping voice soften as she smiles on the lad. Readers get warm, faith-touched tales of poor folk, priests, and small mercies.
the-amulet:
Hendrik Conscience builds The Amulet on an event said to have happened at Antwerp in the sixteenth century. The title page names him as author of The Lion of Flanders, The Conscript, Blind Rosa, and many more tales. The English here was made, the title page states, expressly for this edition. A translator signs the preface with the initials S. J. F. from Baltimore.

That preface calls the tale one of a dark and bloody deed met by swift and dreadful payback. Crafty plots fall apart, it argues, when heaven's justice brings them to light. Good acts, by contrast, bear fruit in this world and shield a person from foes. The first chapter is headed simply Antwerp.
the-anti-slavery-alphabet:
Printed at Philadelphia for the Anti-Slavery Fair in 1847 by Merrihew and Thompson, this small book teaches children the case against slavery letter by letter. A verse at the front speaks to little readers directly. They are young, it admits, but there is much they can do.

Children can plead with grown men not to buy slaves again and to free those they hold. They can talk with playmates on the walk from school about the slave child, motherless and alone. They can refuse candy and cake not made by free hands. The alphabet then begins: A is an abolitionist, and each letter carries its own short lesson in the cause.
the-brighton-boys-with-the-submarine-fle:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys with the Submarine Fleet. Its twenty-six chapters run from Good-by, Brighton and Down in a Submarine to sealed orders in the North Sea. German raiders, a ramming by a destroyer, and a mine field come early. A rescue, fog, Yankee camouflage, and life on the bottom of the sea fill the mid heads. Capturing a U-Boat, a trap, chlorine gas, and the Stars and Stripes close the list.

The tale opens on Jack Hammond, reading a newspaper spread over his knees. Bold type calls for young men to enlist in Uncle Sam's submarine fleet for service in European waters. A great force of young Americans is wanted to man the undersea ships to be sent abroad against Germany. Stirred by the appeal, Jack pulls the paper closer and reads each word.
the-case-of-the-golden-bullet:
The Case of the Golden Bullet is by Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner. It opens not with the case but with an introduction to Joe Muller. Muller is a secret service detective of the Imperial Austrian police. Muller is a small, slight, plain-looking man of indefinite age and humble manner, nothing like the impressive Holmes or the brilliant Lecoq.

The introduction explains that humility. In early youth a miscarriage of justice gave him years in prison. The stigma barred him from honest employment afterward. That threw him back on his peculiar talents. It drove him into the police. Red tape keeps his official rank barely above a policeman's, though kings and councillors consult him, and his modesty asks for nothing but a sufficient income and work he enjoys.
the-chaplain-of-the-fleet: Walter Besant and James Rice wrote this novel together, dated 1881 in its heading. Only the title page and the contents of Part I, headed Within the Rules, are present here. The chapter titles follow a girl named Kitty, who loses her father and her friends, makes engagements, rides to London by coach, first sees the doctor, and witnesses a fleet wedding.The book itself never opens here.
the-chequers-being-the-natural-history-o: James Runciman, author of Skippers and Shellbacks, edited this record, subtitled the natural history of a public house set forth in a loafer's diary, published in London by Ward and Downey. Only the title page, dedication, and the start of the contents are present here. The dedication, addressed to Philip Wood and John Wood of South Shields, calls the book a record of ruined lives. It thanks them for the writer's training from age seventeen in their house, and for their good relations with the police. No diary text follows.
the-figure-in-the-carpet:
Henry James wrote The Figure in the Carpet as a tale of books and the men who read them, printed at London in 1916 from the final text. A young critic tells the tale in his own voice.

The critic recalls the night George Corvick begged him to review a new novel by Hugh Vereker for their paper. He seized the chance, since he would soon meet Vereker at a country house. Praise, pride, and a hunt for the one secret plan said to hide in all Vereker's work drive the tale. James turns a book review into a quiet study of fame and blind spots.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-iii-awakening-to: John Galsworthy wrote Awakening and To Let as volume three of The Forsyte Saga. This copy's heading dates it 1926. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The heads name a meeting and a fine fleur Forsyte. They name Robin Hill, a mausoleum, and the native heath. Figures called Jon and Fleur appear. Parts for mothers and sons and for fathers and daughters follow. No page of the tale itself is included in this portion.
the-great-secret: E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Great Secret. A heading dates the book 1906. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of eighteen chapters. The heads open with Room No. 317 and A Midnight Raid. They name Miss Van Hoyt and A Match at Lord's. They name the mysterious Mr. Guest and Wortley Foote, the spy. Later heads name A Legacy of Danger, Gathering Jackals, and A Dying Man. They name Nagaski's Instinct. They end with In the Death Chamber. No chapter text is present.
the-isles-of-sunset: Arthur Christopher Benson published this volume with Sir Isaac Pitman and Sons in 1908, dedicating it to Hugh Macnaghten. Lines from George Herbert stand as an epigraph. Only the title page, verses, and contents start are present here. The tales themselves do not appear. His verses describe the book's aim. A sequestered song should lead to twilight gardens. Clear waters from secret wells may cool fevered lips. An elder pilgrim tells the tales, tracing a golden stairway west across the sea.
the-last-chronicle-of-barset: Anthony Trollope closed his Barsetshire series with a novel first issued in monthly parts from December 1866 to July 1867. Only the front pages and contents are present here, listing early chapters on Mr. Crawley before the magistrates, Grace Crawley, the archdeacon threat, and dinner at Framley Court. The novel itself, with Crawley cheque trouble and the Proudie household, does not appear in this record beyond those chapter titles.
the-literature-of-arabia-with-critical-a:
Epiphanius Wilson prepared The Literature of Arabia for the Oriental Literature series in 1900, pairing translated selections with critical and biographical sketches. The contents move from The Romance of Antar through Arabian poetry to the Arabian Nights, including the seven voyages of Sindbad and Aladdin's Wonderful Lamp.

The opening selection, translated by Étienne Delécluse and Wilson, begins The Romance of Antar with the Bedouin tribes of the Absians and Adnamians. King Zoheir of the Absians rules so firmly that subject kings pay him tribute, and Arabia itself falls under Absian power. Readers meet a heroic desert romance first, before turning to the poems and the famous Nights tales.
the-little-nugget:
P. G. Wodehouse's The Little Nugget opens in a suite at London's Hotel Guelph, where Mrs. Elmer Ford, late of New York, paces like a caged animal despite every comfort. She takes a framed oil painting from her suit-case and gazes at it hungrily, whispering the name Ogden. The portrait shows a bulgy, overfed boy of about eleven, plainly the spoiled child of parents with far more money than was good for them.

A part summary promises that the Little Nugget will be introduced and plans made for his future by several interested parties. A future Mr. Peter Burns is also touched on, and the part ends with a momentous telephone call. Wodehouse sets up a comic plot around a rich, unlovely child whom everyone seems to want.
the-manor-house-of-lacolle-a-description:
W. D. Lighthall, president of the Antiquarian and Numismatic Society of Montreal, wrote The Manor House of Lacolle. It is a description and historical sketch of the manor of the seigniory of de Beaujeu, or Lacolle, privately printed for him in Montreal. The house stands in a neighborhood on the New York State border. It lies four miles southwest of Lacolle Village, one mile north of Champlain, New York, and some forty miles from Montreal. Lighthall describes the approach: heavy low stone walls, a white gate, a sloping lawn, old trees, gardens on the north side, and a wooded park of some hundred acres.

The manor house is large and wooden, with a stone gabled wing, six tall fluted pillars with Ionic capitals on the verandah, and an oak front door with a brass knocker. Its main part was built in 1825 by a widow from Troy, New York.
the-mormon-prophet:
Lily Dougall's novel The Mormon Prophet was published at Toronto by the W. J. Gage Company in 1899, with copyright held by D. Appleton and Company. Dougall, author of The Mermaid and Beggars All, opens with a preface defending her approach. Studying the rise of the Mormon sect, she found stubborn misconceptions among earnest, well-informed people.

Many, she writes, treat Mormonism as a synonym for polygamy. They take Brigham Young for its chief prophet. They also expect only stories of oppressed women and tyranny from a faith of over two hundred thousand people. Friends warned her that writing without polemic, meaning heated argument, might undermine civilised life. She answers that she offers the simple truth as far as she could discern it.
the-net:
Rex Beach's novel The Net, with four illustrations by Walter Tittle, is present here only in title page and contents, so the story does not appear. Beach is billed as author of The Spoilers, The Barrier, and The Silver Horde. Seventeen chapters are listed.

The Train from Palermo opens the book, followed by A Confession and a Promise and The Golden Girl. A feast at Terranova, a search, and a kidnapping build toward Chapter XII, titled simply La Mafia. The Blood of His Ancestors, The Net Tightens, and The End of the Quest follow. Quarantine and An Obligation Is Met close the visible list.
the-outlet:
Andy Adams wrote The Outlet, a cattle novel with a long historical preface. Adams explains that at the close of the Civil War, Texas held millions of cattle with no market and no real value. Drives to Louisiana ended in fever and loss, Mexico had a surplus of its own, and desert blocked the west. Only a short route through the Choctaw and Cherokee lands to Baxter Springs, Kansas, stood open.

Quoting Emerson Hough, Adams calls the demand for a market imperative. Small outlets at Abilene, Ellsworth, and Wichita in the late 1860s proved that Texas steers wintered in the north made good beef. The preface sets the stage for a trail-driving story.
the-phoenix-and-the-carpet: E. Nesbit wrote The Phoenix and the Carpet for her godson Hubert Griffith and his sister Margaret. A verse letter to Hubert is dated from Dymchurch in September 1904. In it she wishes she could stand on a wishing carpet and fly to him, and laments that no phoenix comes her way. Only this front matter and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list The Egg, The Topless Tower, The Queen Cook, and The Hole in the Carpet.
the-picture-alphabet:
Oliver Spafford's The Picture Alphabet was printed at Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1850. Its opening pages give the alphabet in capitals and small letters. They also give the joined forms used in printing and the numbers from one to ten. Each letter then appears with a pictured animal beside it. Beginners thus join a letter's shape and sound to a creature they can name.

The pairings shown run from A for antelope, B for bull, and C for cat. They go on through dog, eagle, fox, goat, hawk, and ibex. Later letters bring the kite, lynx, monkey, nylghau, owl, and pig. Plain teaching of this kind served young children learning to read at home or in school. The whole alphabet is handled in the same direct way, one letter and one animal at a time.
the-pilgrims-of-new-england-a-tale-of-th:
Mrs. J. B. Webb's The Pilgrims of New England, subtitled a tale of the early American settlers, came from a Hereford printing. Webb is named as the author of Naomi and Julamerk. An epigraph from Hemans describes waves breaking on a stern, rock-bound coast. Exiles moor their bark there on the New England shore.

Chapter I tells of the Mayflower furling her tattered sails on the evening of November 11, 1620. Heavy seas, an unknown coast, and the worn state of the ship had kept the passengers from landing for days. At last the vessel moored in a small inlet beyond the breakers. The Pilgrim families stepped onto a mass of granite at the foot of a steep cliff. They faced a barren shore and a cold welcome, with hope and faith still strong in them.
the-primadonna-a-sequel-to-fair-margaret:
F. Marion Crawford's The Primadonna, a sequel to Fair Margaret, is dated 1908. Crawford is named as author of Saracinesca and Sant' Ilario. Chapter I opens at the opera, where Cordova is singing Lucia's mad scene, her final performance of it that season. She has never sung it better. The narrator pauses to call The Bride of Lammermoor the greatest love-story ever written, and to mock the libretto made from it.

Cordova's face is a mask of powder and her hands chalked like plaster casts. The whole effect adds to the impression of madness. In the fifth row sits an elderly, iron-grey man who has heard great sopranos from Patti to Melba. He judges that none sang the mad scene better than Cordova, on the stage only two years. He first met her at a breakfast aboard a Greek financier's yacht.
the-psychology-of-management-the-functio: L. M. Gilbreth's The Psychology of Management, subtitled The Function of the Mind in Determining, Teaching and Installing Methods of Least Waste, was published by Macmillan in 1914. The title pages of the 1921 printing are followed by a contents heading. The leaves provided end there, at seven hundred-odd characters; Gilbreth's chapters on the mind in management are not shown.
the-rebellion-of-margaret: Geraldine Mockler, author of a St. Bede's girls' story, published her novel with Jarrold and Sons at London, illustrated by Arthur Twidle. Contents follow Margaret from a dream friend and an overheard conversation onto a journey where she makes a friend, meets Eleanor Carson, and changes names with her. Here only the title pages and chapter list are present, so the impersonation plot itself does not appear.
the-red-planet:
William J. Locke opens with a narrator who will never walk again, attended by Sergeant Marigold, his old comrade from the South African War. A motto warns that the red planet Mars hides not only over battlefields but over sheltered home valleys as well.

The same Boer shell crippled both men, and each keeps a bit of its shrapnel as a token of their shared brush with death. The narrator jokes about Marigold refusing to pity his paralysed legs. War at home, told by a wounded officer with humor and restraint, is the ground of this First World War novel.
the-shewing-up-of-blanco-posnet:
Bernard Shaw dated The Shewing-Up of Blanco Posnet to 1909. A long preface on the censorship precedes the play. This little play is really a religious tract in dramatic form, Shaw declares. If the silly censorship would permit its performance, it might help loose-lived playgoers, he argues. It could set their perverted conscience right-side-up.

As matters stand, the preface tells another story instead. A select committee of both Houses sat last year to enquire into the censorship, Shaw recounts. He calls its report a readable bluebook. Few books of 1909 were cheaper or more entertaining, he claims. The report contains long interviews with famous witnesses. Archer, Barrie, Galsworthy, Pinero, and Chesterton all appear in his list. Shaw himself testified as well.
the-silent-bullet:
Arthur B. Reeve's The Silent Bullet gathers twelve Craig Kennedy stories, its contents say. The scientific cracksman, the bacteriological detective, and the deadly tube appear early. The diamond maker, the black hand, and the steel door come later. A prefatory section called Craig Kennedy's Theories opens the book in dialogue.

Kennedy lays down his evening paper and fills his pipe. It has always seemed strange to him, he says, that no university has endowed a professorship in criminal science. The narrator, his old college roommate, now works on the Star's staff. He argues that crime is just crime, and detection belongs to the born detective. Kennedy replies earnestly that science has a distinct place in detection. The Continent is far ahead in that respect, he insists.
the-stokesley-secret:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this family story, transcribed here from the 1902 Macmillan edition that paired it with Countess Kate. Chapter one opens at a children's tea-table. Five-year-old David Merrifield sits boosted on a Latin dictionary. He asks how a pig can pay the rent. His brother Sam holds up a slice. Sam protests that Mary has served bread and scrape, not bread and butter.

Susan pleads that the butter hides only in the little holes, and Miss Fosbrook, making tea, gently rebukes the grumbling of the Merrifield children, whose parents are away. A second record of the same 1902 edition, under a longer file name, opens with exactly the same scene.
the-story-of-miss-moppet:
Beatrix Potter, author of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, published this little picture book with Frederick Warne in 1906. Its kitten heroine, Miss Moppet, thinks she has heard a mouse, while the mouse peeps out behind the cupboard and makes fun of her, quite unafraid of a kitten.

Miss Moppet jumps just too late. She misses the mouse. She bangs her own head. She decides that it is a very hard cupboard. The mouse watches her from the cupboard top. Miss Moppet ties a duster round her head. She sits before the fire. The book is a tiny comedy. A hunter is outwitted by her prey. Potter tells it in a sentence or two to a page.
the-story-of-the-amulet:
E. Nesbit continues the adventures of Cyril, Robert, Anthea, and Jane in a story dedicated to Dr. Wallis Budge of the British Museum for his help. A contents list promises much. It names the half amulet, the past, and Babylon. Atlantis, Pharaoh, and the heart's desire follow. Chapter one recalls an earlier find. The children first met the Psammead in a sandpit. The pit lay between their white holiday house and a chalkpit.

The Psammead, Nesbit reminds readers, is a sand-fairy with eyes on long horns like a snail's, ears like a bat's, a tubby spider-like body in thick fur, and monkey's hands and feet. It lay buried for thousands of years. It kept the fairy power of granting wishes. The children found those wishes came true in troublesome ways. From that start they travel through time. They search for the amulet's other half.
the-third-violet:
Stephen Crane, author of The Red Badge of Courage, published The Third Violet with D. Appleton in 1897. A train bellows up a winding mountain valley under grey crags, then releases its passengers at a little station. They burst out with the enthusiasm of escaping convicts. Village idlers and philosophers examine the city consignment while stage drivers and families throng together in the bustle.

Down the steps climbs Hawker, a young painter loaded with clothes case, paint-box, and a swinging easel. The easel knocks a small boy's head, and Hawker waits politely while the child studies him. Crane sets a summer-resort romance in motion with quick, ironic strokes, city people and country watchers sizing each other up on one crowded platform.
the-title-market: Emily Post's Title Market, published by Dodd, Mead in 1909 with illustrations by J. H. Gardner Soper, appears here in its front leaves only. A frontispiece caption quotes an Italian prince declaring that his people live, endure, and die for woman and love. Post dedicates the novel to her mother, 'Madre Mia,' whose daily companions the Sanseveros, Nina, and John had been for months. The contents open with Prince Sansevero diminishing the fortunes of his house. Post's society romance of American money and Italian titles is announced, not begun.
the-two-elsies-a-sequel-to-elsie-at-nant: Martha Finley's Two Elsies, book ten of the Elsie books and a sequel to Elsie at Nantucket, dated 1868, is represented here only by the publisher's catalogue of Finley's works. That list runs through twenty-five Elsie volumes, from Elsie Dinsmore to Elsie at Home, plus the Mildred Keith series and titles such as Casella and Our Fred. The catalogue documents the reach of Finley's Christian family saga, a nineteenth-century steady seller. The two Elsies themselves appear only in the titles listed here.
the-white-gauntlet:
Captain Mayne Reid opens The White Gauntlet, in a printing dated 1864, with a woman encountered alone in a wood. A gipsy or peasant girl would challenge curiosity, he says, but a high-born, bright-haired beauty stirs admiration bordering on adoration. Marion Wade is all of these, mounted on a white horse with a hawk on her hand and a hound following.

Marion is mistress of the stately mansion inside Bulstrode Park, ancient as Alfred the Great, so she cannot be lost. Yet she checks and urges her palfrey, stopping to listen as if expecting someone. A hoof-stroke answers her: a horseman rides the forest track toward the great beech at the glade's centre. Reid suspends the meeting under autumn noon light.
the-wing-and-wing-or-le-feu-follet:
J. Fenimore Cooper prefaces The Wing-and-Wing, or Le Feu-Follet, with an argument about belief and unbelief. The world, he says, holds as much presumptuous cavilling at revelation as blind belief in dogma. France at the height of her revolutionary mania was charged with the cavilling, yet Cooper doubts the nation deserved it, blaming a few bold and unquiet spirits instead.

Revolution loosed the audacious from the church's healthful restraints onto a sea of speculation and conceit. Young men especially imbibe a taint of unbelief before reaching humbler perceptions of their own insignificance. Cooper calls the demand that belief conform to crude private notions of reason the greatest stumbling-block of the young. His sea tale is framed as a study of faith tested.
the-younger-set: Robert W. Chambers's The Younger Set is represented here by a list of his other works and an illustration caption. His novels listed include The Fighting Chance and The King in Yellow. Children's books such as Garden-Land and Forest-Land also appear. A frontispiece caption quotes a line about giving soul and body into keeping. The novel's own pages do not appear in the pages present in this record.
to-let: John Galsworthy closed the Forsyte Saga with this volume, as his author's note states. The saga comprised The Man of Property, Indian Summer of a Forsyte, In Chancery, and Awakening. Contents divide the novel into three parts, opening with an encounter and Fine Fleur Forsyte at Robin Hill. Later headings follow Jon and Fleur, a mausoleum, a Goya, Soames's private life, and June taking a hand. Galsworthy's short note and the chapter list are what is included in this record, so the novel itself does not appear.
voodoo-planet: Andre Norton wrote Voodoo Planet, billed on its cover as a complete novel under the banner Duel of the Cosmic Magicians. Pages present here hold cover matter and a cast of characters only, so the story itself is not shown. A cover quote pits Dane Thorson of the spaceship Solar Queen against Lumbrilo, the mental wizard of the planet Khatka, in a fight between reason and hypnotic witchcraft. The cast names Medic Tau, part physician and part magician, and Chief Ranger Asaki, who fears mad animals, real or imagined.
western-worthies-a-gallery-of-biographic:
J. Stephen Jeans, editor of the Evening Star, wrote Western Worthies in Glasgow in 1872. The book gives short lives of noted men from the west of Scotland. Jeans says the public wants to know more about the men it looks up to. He also hopes young readers will learn from their hard work.

Jeans admits that short sketches cannot do full justice to any one life. He leans toward facts over views, so readers can judge for themselves. The pages mix life stories with brief critical notes. For readers now, the book is a window on whom Glasgow praised in its own day.
with-marlborough-to-malplaquet: The front pages here hold the title page, a series list, and the first lines of a note. The book is Herbert Strang and Richard Stead's With Marlborough to Malplaquet, and the tale is not begun. The series mates the book with tales of Edward the Third and Queen Elizabeth. The story is set in the reign of Queen Anne. Four colored pictures and a map aid the text. The note begins by stating the series aim: to stir a taste for history. The book came out in London in 1908.
with-steyn-and-de-wet: Only the title page and a contents list with page numbers are present here. The book is Philip Pienaar's With Steyn and De Wet, printed by Methuen in London in 1902. His account does not appear. Pienaar served in the Transvaal telegraph service. The contents open at Thomar and the eleventh of October. First impressions, Colenso, Platrand, and Spion Kop follow. A chapter called Glorious War sits mid-list. Tapping the wires and a meeting with De Wet come later. Roodewal closes the part shown.
zweig-the-burning-secret:
At an Austrian resort, a suave baron befriends a lonely twelve-year-old boy as a path to the boy's mother. Stefan Zweig's The Burning Secret, from 1911 and presented here in English, turns on the moment the child understands the game. Jealousy and betrayal follow, and innocence ends in a single burning insight.

Zweig tells the story from inside the boy's awakening mind with unbearable precision. The mother's romance, the baron's polish, and the child's fury interlock like gears. Few novellas anywhere study childhood's end so exactly. The Burning Secret made Zweig's early reputation across Europe. It still reads as a small masterpiece of psychological fiction, perfectly paced to its final reconciliation.
